pages.title: Linear Independence, Bases and Dimension

items.title: Linear independence: a finite list $v : n \to V$ is independent when $\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i = 0_V$ forces every $\lambda_i = 0_F$, and a subset $S \subseteq V$ is independent when every injective finite list into $S$ is
items.strategy: TWO NOTIONS, DEFINED TOGETHER AND RELATED, because the page needs both: lists carry ordered bases and coordinates, subsets carry the Zorn argument. (1) The finite sum is the one page 68 already fixed: [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read additively in the abelian group $(V,+,0_V)$, exactly as [[def-linear-combination-and-span]] does. Do not introduce a second finite sum, and do not reach for [[def-finite-sum]], which is stated for sequences into the complete ordered field. (2) THE INJECTIVITY CLAUSE IN THE SUBSET DEFINITION IS LOAD-BEARING AND MUST BE STATED. A linear combination in [[def-linear-combination-and-span]] is indexed by an arbitrary list $v : n \to S$, which need NOT be injective; if repetitions were allowed, $1_F v + (-1_F) v = 0_V$ would make every nonempty $S$ dependent. Quantifying over injective lists is what makes the subset notion the intended one. [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]] then shows the clause is not an extra hypothesis for LISTS -- the vanishing condition forces a list to be injective by itself. (3) BOUNDARY CASES ARE REAL CASES: $n = 0$ makes the empty list independent and $\varnothing \subseteq V$ independent (vacuously), and $\{0_V\}$ is dependent, since $1_F \cdot 0_V = 0_V$ with $1_F \ne 0_F$ ([[def-field]], [[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]). $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, so state both. (4) Dependent means not independent; define the word here so no later item has to.

items.title: An independent finite list is injective and takes no value $0_V$; every sublist of an independent list is independent; and every subset of an independent set is independent
items.strategy: direct, with the witnesses written out. INJECTIVITY: if $v_j = v_k$ with $j \ne k$, take $\lambda_j = 1_F$, $\lambda_k = -1_F$ and $\lambda_i = 0_F$ otherwise; the sum is $0_V$ by (F1) and (F3) of [[def-sum-of-linear-subspaces]] -- CITE THOSE, they are exactly the finite-sum facts page 68 proved so that this page would not rebuild them -- while $1_F \ne 0_F$. NO ZERO VALUE: if $v_j = 0_V$, take $\lambda_j = 1_F$ and the rest $0_F$. SUBLISTS and SUBSETS: extend a witnessing scalar list by zeros and use (F3). Record the consequence used constantly below: an independent list $v : n \to V$ is a bijection onto its range, so its range is a subset with exactly $n$ elements ([[def-equinumerous]], [[lem-pigeonhole]] clause 3), and independence of the list and of its range are the same condition.

items.title: A subset $S \subseteq V$ is linearly dependent if and only if some $s \in S$ lies in $\operatorname{span}(S \setminus \{s\})$
items.strategy: both directions direct. ($\Rightarrow$) A witnessing injective list with some $\lambda_j \ne 0_F$ can be solved for $v_j$, multiplying by $\lambda_j^{-1}$, which exists because $F$ is a field ([[def-field]]); the remaining terms are a linear combination of the other entries, which are distinct from $v_j$ by injectivity, hence lie in $S \setminus \{v_j\}$. Use (F2) and (F3) of [[def-sum-of-linear-subspaces]] for the rearrangement, and [[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]] to land in the span. ($\Leftarrow$) Reverse it. CHECK THE EDGES: $S = \varnothing$ has no $s$ and is independent; $S = \{0_V\}$ is dependent and $0_V \in \operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$ by [[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]], so the equivalence holds there too and must be checked in the proof rather than waved at.

items.title: $S \subseteq V$ is linearly independent if and only if every finite subset of $S$ is; consequently the union of a nonempty chain of independent subsets of $V$, ordered by inclusion, is independent
items.strategy: direct, and this is the lemma that makes Zorn applicable, so it must be proved in full rather than assumed. FINITE CHARACTER: an injective list $v : n \to S$ has finite range, and independence of $S$ is by definition a condition on such lists. CHAINS: let $C$ be a nonempty chain of independent subsets under $\subseteq$ ([[def-chain]], [[def-partial-order]]) and let $v : n \to \bigcup C$ be injective; each $v_i$ lies in some $A_i \in C$, and by induction on $n$ ([[thm-induction-principle]]) using comparability, all $n$ of them lie in a single member $A \in C$ -- WRITE THIS INDUCTION OUT; 'by comparability' is not a proof, and it is the only place the chain hypothesis is spent. Then independence of $A$ gives the conclusion. Note the induction needs $n$ finite, which is why finite character is stated first.

items.title: If $S \subseteq V$ is independent and $w \notin \operatorname{span}(S)$ then $S \cup \{w\}$ is independent and $\operatorname{span}(S) \subsetneq \operatorname{span}(S \cup \{w\})$; and if $w \in \operatorname{span}(S)$ then $\operatorname{span}(S \cup \{w\}) = \operatorname{span}(S)$
items.strategy: contradiction for the first clause. Note $w \notin S$, since $S \subseteq \operatorname{span}(S)$ ([[lem-span-monotone-and-idempotent]] clause 1). Given a dependence on $S \cup \{w\}$, the coefficient of $w$ cannot be $0_F$ (else $S$ would be dependent) and cannot be nonzero (else $w \in \operatorname{span}(S)$ by the solving step of [[lem-dependent-iff-a-vector-lies-in-the-span-of-the-others]]). The second clause is monotonicity and idempotence of the span ([[lem-span-monotone-and-idempotent]]). This lemma is the engine of both [[thm-steinitz-exchange]] and the Zorn argument of [[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]]; state it once, here.

items.title: Basis of a vector space: a linearly independent spanning subset; and ordered basis: an injective finite list whose range is a basis
items.strategy: Definition, with the naming decision recorded. NAMING: the bare id `def-linear-basis` is free, and the library's other basis -- a basis for a topology -- is already namespaced as [[def-topology-basis-subbasis]] with alias `def-basis-top`, so no collision arises; say so in Remarks, in the dictionary style page 68 used for `linear subspace`, and note that the two notions share nothing but the word. CONTENT: $B \subseteq V$ is a basis when $B$ is independent ([[def-linear-independence]]) and $\operatorname{span}(B) = V$ ([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]). $\varnothing$ IS A BASIS OF THE ZERO SPACE, since $\operatorname{span}(\varnothing) = \{0_V\}$ ([[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]]) -- state this, it is the $n = 0$ case that every later induction on this page starts from. An ORDERED basis is a list $v : n \to V$, $n \in \mathbb{N}$, that is injective and whose range is a basis; by [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]] the injectivity is equivalent to asking only that the list be independent and span. Also fix the word SPANNING SET here if page 68 has not: it has -- [[def-linear-combination-and-span]] defines it -- so cite rather than redefine.

items.title: A finite list $v : n \to V$ is an ordered basis if and only if every $x \in V$ equals $\sum_{i<n} \lambda_i v_i$ for exactly one $\lambda : n \to F$; those scalars are the coordinates of $x$ in the ordered basis
items.strategy: both directions direct; this is the well-definedness obligation for coordinates and must be proved, not assumed. EXISTENCE is spanning ([[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]]). UNIQUENESS: subtract two representations using (F2) of [[def-sum-of-linear-subspaces]] to get $\sum_{i<n} (\lambda_i - \mu_i) v_i = 0_V$, then independence. CONVERSE: unique representation gives spanning at once and independence by comparing a vanishing combination with the all-zero one, which represents $0_V$ by (F1). The list is injective by [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]]. State plainly that the coordinates depend on the ORDERED basis and not on the basis as a set -- reordering the list permutes the coordinates -- and leave the map $x \mapsto \lambda$ un-named: it is a linear map, and linear maps are order 72. LANDMARK.

items.title: For $B \subseteq V$ the following are equivalent: $B$ is a basis; $B$ is a maximal linearly independent subset of $V$; $B$ is a minimal spanning subset of $V$ — maximality and minimality being in the inclusion order
items.strategy: three implications, direct. Basis implies maximal independent: any $w \notin B$ lies in $\operatorname{span}(B) = V$, so $B \cup \{w\}$ is dependent by [[lem-dependent-iff-a-vector-lies-in-the-span-of-the-others]]. Maximal independent implies basis: if some $w \notin \operatorname{span}(B)$ existed, [[lem-adjoining-a-vector-outside-the-span]] would contradict maximality. Basis implies minimal spanning, and back, by the same lemma applied to $B \setminus \{b\}$. Use [[def-maximal-element]] and [[def-partial-order]] for the words `maximal` and `minimal`, in the inclusion order on the relevant family of subsets -- name the poset explicitly, because [[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]] feeds Zorn the very same poset.

items.title: The Steinitz exchange lemma: if $L \subseteq V$ is linearly independent and $S \subseteq V$ spans $V$ with $S$ finite of size $n$, then $L$ is finite with $|L| = m \le n$, and there is $T \subseteq S$ with $|T| = n - m$ such that $L \cup T$ spans $V$
items.strategy: induction, on $m$, exchanging one vector at a time. THE EXCHANGE STEP: if $L' \cup T'$ spans $V$ and $w \in L \setminus L'$, then $w$ is a combination of $L' \cup T'$ ([[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]]) with some coefficient on a $t \in T'$ nonzero -- if every coefficient on $T'$ vanished, $w$ would lie in $\operatorname{span}(L')$, contradicting independence of $L$ via [[lem-dependent-iff-a-vector-lies-in-the-span-of-the-others]] -- so solve for that $t$ and replace it by $w$, the new set still spanning by [[lem-adjoining-a-vector-outside-the-span]] and [[lem-span-monotone-and-idempotent]]. THE BOUND $m \le n$ falls out because $T'$ cannot run out before $L$ does. SIZES ARE NATURALS AND ARE HANDLED BY [[lem-pigeonhole]]: a finite set is equinumerous with exactly one natural (clause 3), which is what makes $|L|$ and $|T|$ meaningful; $n - m$ is the unique natural $k$ with $m + k = n$ ([[def-nat-addition]], [[thm-nat-linear-order]]). ALSO PROVE $L$ IS FINITE rather than assuming it: if $L$ were infinite it would contain an independent subset of size $n+1$, which the bound forbids ([[lem-independent-list-is-injective]] for subsets). LANDMARK.

items.title: If $V$ has a spanning set with $n$ elements, then every linearly independent subset of $V$ is finite with at most $n$ elements; in particular $V$ has no independent subset equinumerous with $\mathbb{N}$
items.strategy: direct, from [[thm-steinitz-exchange]]. The last clause is the one later items use to say a space is infinite-dimensional, and it needs [[lem-pigeonhole]] clause 4 ($\mathbb{N} \not\approx n$) plus [[lem-independent-list-is-injective]] to cut a subset of size $n+1$ out of an infinite independent set.

items.title: If $V$ has a basis with $n$ elements and a basis with $m$ elements then $n = m$; and if $V$ has one finite basis then every basis of $V$ is finite
items.strategy: direct, applying [[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]] twice, in each direction, then antisymmetry of the order on $\mathbb{N}$. This is well-definedness obligation #12 and it is what licenses [[def-dimension]] to speak of THE dimension. Sizes are compared through [[lem-pigeonhole]] clause 3. THE INFINITE CASE IS NOT CLAIMED: this page does NOT assert that any two infinite bases are equinumerous, and it must not, because the standard proof needs cardinal arithmetic and [[def-cardinal]] is homed on `ordinals-and-transfinite-recursion` at order 183, one hundred and thirteen pages above this one. Say in Remarks that the invariance proved here is the finite one, in the 'not available at this point in the reading order' form -- never 'this library does not develop it'. LANDMARK.

items.title: Finite-dimensional vector space, and its dimension $\dim_F V$; infinite-dimensional means having no finite basis
items.strategy: Definition resting on [[thm-any-two-finite-bases-have-the-same-size]], which is a PREREQUISITE and belongs in `deps`, not in `justified_by`: it does not depend on this item. $V$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ when it has a finite basis, and then $\dim_F V$ is the unique natural $n$ with a basis of $n$ elements. $\dim_F$ IS SUBSCRIPTED BY THE FIELD and the Remarks must say why: page 68's [[lem-restriction-of-scalars]] makes the same set a vector space over a subfield, and the dimension changes when the field does. $\dim_F \{0_V\} = 0$, with basis $\varnothing$. INFINITE-DIMENSIONAL is defined as the negation, with NO cardinal attached -- do not write $\dim V = \infty$ and do not cite [[def-cardinal]] (order 183). Note that the definition is stated relative to a field and a space, so 'the dimension of $V$' is incomplete language, exactly as page 68 says of 'the vector space $V$'. LANDMARK.

items.title: Zorn's lemma gives a basis between any independent set and any spanning set containing it: if $L \subseteq S \subseteq V$ with $L$ independent and $\operatorname{span}(S) = V$, there is a basis $B$ of $V$ with $L \subseteq B \subseteq S$
items.strategy: constructive via Zorn, and the two hypotheses are stated together on purpose so that the two classical statements are corollaries rather than two separate Zorn arguments. THE POSET: $P := \{\, A : L \subseteq A \subseteq S,\ A \text{ independent} \,\}$ ordered by inclusion, a poset by [[def-partial-order]]. NONEMPTY: $L \in P$. EVERY CHAIN HAS AN UPPER BOUND -- and the EMPTY CHAIN MUST BE HANDLED SEPARATELY, its upper bound being $L$, because the union of the empty chain is $\varnothing$, which need not contain $L$; [[thm-zorn]] as published quantifies over every chain, so this case is not optional. For a nonempty chain the union is in $P$: independent by [[lem-independence-has-finite-character]], and between $L$ and $S$ because every member is. [[thm-zorn]] then yields a maximal $B \in P$. FINALLY $\operatorname{span}(B) = V$: if some $s \in S$ had $s \notin \operatorname{span}(B)$ then $B \cup \{s\} \in P$ by [[lem-adjoining-a-vector-outside-the-span]], contradicting maximality; so $S \subseteq \operatorname{span}(B)$ and $\operatorname{span}(B) \supseteq \operatorname{span}(S) = V$ by [[lem-span-monotone-and-idempotent]]. CHOICE IS DECLARED, not hidden: [[thm-zorn]] assumes [[def-axiom-of-choice]], which this library has adopted, and the Statement should say the theorem is proved from Zorn's lemma. LANDMARK.

items.title: Every spanning subset of a vector space contains a basis
items.strategy: direct: apply [[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]] with $L = \varnothing$, which is independent by [[def-linear-independence]]. Note the finite case needs no choice at all -- a minimal spanning subset of a finite spanning set exists by [[lem-pigeonhole]] and downward induction -- and say so, since the library is careful elsewhere about what a proof actually costs.

items.title: Every vector space has a basis
items.strategy: direct: apply [[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]] with $L = \varnothing$ and $S = V$, noting $\operatorname{span}(V) = V$ by [[lem-span-monotone-and-idempotent]] clause 4. The zero space is included, its basis being $\varnothing$. REMARKS, and this is a decision the orchestrator should confirm: the CONVERSE -- that 'every vector space has a basis' implies the Axiom of Choice -- is a theorem of Blass (1984) which this library does not prove. State that in PLAIN PROSE with a real entry in `sources.references` and NO wikilink and NO `external_refs` entry, exactly as the number-theory scaffold orients readers forward without linking; the self-contained-scope rule forbids resting on it, and nothing here does. LANDMARK. See the batch notes: the published [[rem-choice-ledger]] currently says of this statement that 'neither direction is proved here', which THIS ITEM FALSIFIES, and the amendment is recorded in `research/level9-mixed-batch-2.notes.md`.

items.title: The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(j) = 1_F$ for $j = i$ and $0_F$ otherwise is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$
items.strategy: direct, via [[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]: for $x \in F^{n}$ the list $\lambda_i := x(i)$ is the unique one with $x = \sum_{i<n} \lambda_i e_i$, checked by evaluating both sides at each $j < n$, which is legitimate because equality in $F^{X}$ is pointwise ([[def-function-space]]). INDEXING: $F^{n}$ is $F^{X}$ with $X = n = \{0,\dots,n-1\}$ the von Neumann natural, so entries run $x_0,\dots,x_{n-1}$ and the list starts at $0$ ([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]); $n = 0$ gives $F^{0}$, whose single element is the empty function, and the empty list is its ordered basis. Evaluating a finite sum pointwise needs induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]) on the defining clauses of [[def-monoid-finite-product]]; do not assert it.

items.title: If $\dim_F V = n$ and $U$ is a linear subspace of $V$, then $U$ is finite-dimensional, $\dim_F U \le n$, and $\dim_F U = n$ if and only if $U = V$
items.strategy: direct. $U$ is finite-dimensional: an independent subset of $U$ is independent in $V$, hence has at most $n$ elements ([[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]]); take one of maximal size, which exists because the sizes form a nonempty set of naturals bounded by $n$ ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]] or the bounded-above form), and it is a basis of $U$ by [[lem-basis-iff-maximal-independent-iff-minimal-spanning]] applied inside $U$ -- note that maximality among independent subsets OF $U$ is what is needed, and that the span in $U$ and in $V$ agree because $U$ is a linear subspace. EQUALITY CASE: if $\dim_F U = n$ and $U \ne V$, pick $w \in V \setminus U$; a basis of $U$ together with $w$ is independent by [[lem-adjoining-a-vector-outside-the-span]] and has $n+1$ elements, contradicting the bound. FINITENESS IS ESSENTIAL and the companion page carries the witness: in infinite dimension a proper subspace can have a basis equinumerous with a basis of the whole space.

items.title: Every linear subspace $U$ of a vector space $V$ has a complement: a linear subspace $W$ with $V = U \oplus W$
items.strategy: constructive, from [[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]]. Take a basis $A$ of $U$ ([[cor-every-vector-space-has-a-basis]] applied to $U$, which is a vector space in its own right by [[def-linear-subspace]]), extend it to a basis $B$ of $V$ with $A \subseteq B \subseteq V$, and put $W := \operatorname{span}(B \setminus A)$. Then $U + W = V$ by [[lem-sum-is-span-of-union]] and [[lem-span-monotone-and-idempotent]], and $U \cap W = \{0_V\}$ because a vector in both has two representations in the basis $B$, contradicting [[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] unless it is $0_V$ -- for an infinite $B$ argue with the finite lists that actually occur, via [[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]], rather than with an ordered basis. Conclude with the two-summand form of [[def-internal-direct-sum]], which that definition states as $U + W = V$ and $U \cap W = \{0_V\}$, and record that the complement is NOT unique -- the companion page of order 69 already exhibits three lines in $F^{2}$ pairwise meeting in $0$.

items.title: The dimension formula: for finite-dimensional linear subspaces $U$ and $W$ of $V$, $\dim_F(U+W) + \dim_F(U \cap W) = \dim_F U + \dim_F W$
items.strategy: constructive. Take a basis $A$ of $U \cap W$ -- which is a linear subspace by [[lem-intersection-of-linear-subspaces]] and finite-dimensional by [[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]] -- extend it to a basis $A \cup A_U$ of $U$ and to a basis $A \cup A_W$ of $W$ ([[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]]). Prove that $A \cup A_U \cup A_W$ is a basis of $U + W$: it spans by [[lem-sum-is-span-of-union]], and independence is the crux -- a vanishing combination puts a vector of $\operatorname{span}(A_U)$ into $W$, hence into $U \cap W = \operatorname{span}(A)$, forcing its $A_U$ coefficients to vanish. Then count, the three pieces being pairwise disjoint (prove that, do not assume it). Arithmetic of naturals: [[def-nat-addition]] and [[lem-pigeonhole]] clause 3 for sizes. CHECK THE EDGES: $U \cap W = \{0_V\}$ gives $A = \varnothing$ and the formula reads $\dim(U \oplus W) = \dim U + \dim W$; $U = W$ gives an identity. LANDMARK.

items.title: If $V = \bigoplus_{i<n} U_i$ with every $U_i$ finite-dimensional, then $V$ is finite-dimensional and $\dim_F V = \sum_{i<n} \dim_F U_i$; in particular $\dim_F(U \oplus W) = \dim_F U + \dim_F W$
items.strategy: induction on $n$, from [[thm-dimension-formula]] and the defining condition of [[def-internal-direct-sum]], which says each $U_j$ meets the sum of the OTHERS only in $0_V$ -- that is what makes the intersection term vanish at each step, and the pairwise condition would not suffice ([[lem-direct-sum-criterion]], and the order-69 counterexample). BASE $n = 0$: the empty direct sum is $\{0_V\}$ and the empty sum of naturals is $0$, so the formula holds; state the base rather than starting at $1$. The sum of naturals is the finite sum of [[def-monoid-finite-product]] read additively in $(\mathbb{N},+,0)$.

pages.title: Bases and Dimension: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The vector $(1,2) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}$ has coordinate list $(1,2)$ in the standard ordered basis, $(2,1)$ in its reversal, and $(2,-1)$ in the ordered basis $\bigl((1,1),(1,0)\bigr)$
items.strategy: Compute all three coordinate lists from [[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]], verifying each by expanding the sum. TITLE MUST BE FIXED BY THE AUTHOR: recompute the third list before writing the title -- the scaffold deliberately leaves the arithmetic unverified so it is checked rather than copied, and a title asserting a wrong triple would be a published falsehood. The point of the item, and it should be stated: coordinates are attached to an ORDERED basis, not to a basis, and the same vector has different coordinate lists under different orderings of the same set. This is the concrete half of the distinction that order 74 will formalise as change of basis.

items.title: The standard unit families $e_i \in F^{\mathbb{N}}$ form a basis of the linear subspace of eventually zero families, an explicit infinite basis
items.strategy: B PAGES ARE LEAVES, so this item may NOT depend on page 69's `ex-sequence-space-and-eventually-zero-subspace`, which lives on another examples page; build the eventually zero subspace natively from [[lem-linear-subspace-criterion]] (three lines) and record the agreement with that example in Remarks ONLY, with no `deps` entry. Then prove SPANNING as it does, and add what is new, namely INDEPENDENCE: an injective list $e_{i_0}, \dots, e_{i_{n-1}}$ with $\sum \lambda_k e_{i_k} = 0$ evaluates at $i_k$ to $\lambda_k = 0_F$, the evaluation being legitimate because equality in $F^{X}$ is pointwise ([[def-function-space]]). Then it is a basis by [[def-linear-basis]], and the space is infinite-dimensional by [[cor-independent-set-is-no-larger-than-a-finite-spanning-set]] together with [[lem-pigeonhole]] clause 4. This is the counterweight to [[cor-every-vector-space-has-a-basis]]: here an infinite basis is written down, no choice principle is used, and the contrast with [[ex-hamel-basis-of-r-over-q]] is the item's point.

items.title: $\mathbb{R}$ as a vector space over $\mathbb{Q}$ has a basis, and every such basis is infinite; the existence proof exhibits none
items.strategy: EXISTENCE: [[ex-r-as-a-vector-space-over-q]] (order 69) makes $\mathbb{R}$ a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space by restriction of scalars, and [[cor-every-vector-space-has-a-basis]] supplies a basis. INFINITUDE, primary argument: a basis with $n$ elements would give a unique coordinate list in $\mathbb{Q}^{n}$ for each real ([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]), hence an injection $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{Q}^{n}$; $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable ([[thm-rationals-countable]]) and finite products of countable sets are countable ([[thm-product-of-countable]]), so $\mathbb{R}$ would be countable, contradicting [[thm-r-uncountable]]. SECOND CLAUSE, OPTIONAL AND TO BE CUT IF IT DOES NOT COME OUT CLEANLY: no basis is countably infinite either, because the set of finite $\mathbb{Q}$-combinations from a countable set is a countable union of countable sets ([[thm-countable-union-of-countable]], which costs countable choice and must be flagged as such via [[def-countable-choice]]). SCOPE DISCIPLINE: say that the proof of existence is non-constructive and exhibits no basis; do NOT write that no basis can be exhibited, which is a metamathematical claim this library has not established, and do NOT mention non-measurable sets -- that clause was withdrawn under the self-contained-scope rule. Do not cite [[rem-banach-no-countable-hamel-basis]] or [[rem-hahn-banach-hamel-basis-open]]: both are recorded-not-proved items, the first is still a draft, and depending on either is forbidden.

items.title: The standard unit families $\{e_i : i \in \mathbb{N}\}$ are linearly independent in $F^{\mathbb{N}}$ but do not span it: the constant family $1$ is not a finite linear combination of them
items.strategy: Refutes: an infinite independent set in an infinite-dimensional space must span. Independence is as in [[ex-basis-of-the-eventually-zero-families]]. NON-SPANNING: every element of the span is a FINITE linear combination ([[lem-span-is-the-set-of-linear-combinations]]) and therefore vanishes outside a finite set of indices, while the constant family $1$ vanishes nowhere -- make the finiteness argument explicit, since it is the whole content. Conclude that this set is independent but not a basis ([[def-linear-basis]]), and note that [[thm-every-independent-set-extends-to-a-basis]] says it EXTENDS to one, which does not contradict anything here.

items.title: $\{(1,0), (0,1), (1,1)\}$ spans $F^{2}$ and is linearly dependent, so a spanning set need not be a basis; each of its three two-element subsets is a basis
items.strategy: Refutes: a spanning set of a space of dimension $n$ is a basis. Spanning is immediate from the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], [[lem-span-monotone-and-idempotent]] monotonicity). Dependence: $(1,0) + (0,1) - (1,1) = 0$, so it is dependent by [[def-linear-independence]], and equally by [[lem-dependent-iff-a-vector-lies-in-the-span-of-the-others]]. Then verify each two-element subset is a basis, which makes [[cor-every-spanning-set-contains-a-basis]] concrete and shows the contained basis is not unique. NOTE THE FIELD: over $F = \mathbb{F}_2$ the identity $-1 = 1$ changes nothing here, but say which field is meant, since page 68 insists the field is part of the data.

items.title: Inside the space of eventually zero families, the subspace spanned by $\{e_i : i \ge 1\}$ is proper and has a basis equinumerous with a basis of the whole space, so "equal dimension forces equality" fails without finite dimension
items.strategy: Refutes: a linear subspace whose basis is equinumerous with a basis of the ambient space equals it. $U := \operatorname{span}\{e_i : i \ge 1\}$ is a proper subspace of the eventually zero families, since $e_0 \notin U$ by the pointwise evaluation argument of [[ex-basis-of-the-eventually-zero-families]]. Both $\{e_i : i \in \mathbb{N}\}$ and $\{e_i : i \ge 1\}$ are bases, of the whole space and of $U$, and they are equinumerous ([[def-equinumerous]]) via $i \mapsto i+1$, which is a bijection $\mathbb{N} \to \{i : i \ge 1\}$. THE POINT: [[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]] states the equality case only for FINITE dimension, and this shows the hypothesis is not decoration. Say explicitly that this item does not compare infinite dimensions as cardinals -- it compares two specific bases through an explicit bijection -- because [[def-cardinal]] is order 183 and no dimension is assigned to either space here.

items.title: Three distinct lines $U_0, U_1, U_2$ in $F^{2}$ have $\dim(U_0+U_1+U_2) = 2$ while the inclusion-exclusion analogue of the dimension formula predicts $3$, so the two-subspace formula does not extend
items.strategy: Refutes: $\dim(U_0+U_1+U_2) = \sum \dim U_i - \sum_{i<j} \dim(U_i \cap U_j) + \dim(U_0 \cap U_1 \cap U_2)$. Take the three lines spanned by $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$ and $(1,1)$ over a field with more than two elements -- CHECK THE FIELD: over $\mathbb{F}_2$ these are still three distinct lines and the computation still works, but say which field is used. Each has dimension $1$ ([[lem-span-of-a-single-vector]], [[def-dimension]]), pairwise intersections are $\{0\}$ ([[lem-span-of-a-single-vector]] clause 3), the triple intersection is $\{0\}$, and the sum is $F^{2}$ of dimension $2$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]); the right-hand side is $3 - 0 + 0 = 3$. Pair this in the prose with the order-69 [[cex-pairwise-trivial-intersection-is-not-a-direct-sum]], which uses the same three lines for the neighbouring failure -- SAME WITNESS, DIFFERENT FAILURE, and saying so is what stops it reading as a duplicate.

items.title: FALSE: the union of two linearly independent subsets of a vector space is linearly independent
items.strategy: Refutation in $F^{2}$: $\{(1,0),(0,1)\}$ and $\{(1,1)\}$ are each independent, and their union is dependent, since $(1,0) + (0,1) - (1,1) = 0$ ([[def-linear-independence]], [[lem-dependent-iff-a-vector-lies-in-the-span-of-the-others]]). Verify independence of each part from the definition. Note the true statements nearby, so the reader knows what survives: a SUBSET of an independent set is independent ([[lem-independent-list-is-injective]]), and adjoining a vector OUTSIDE the span preserves independence ([[lem-adjoining-a-vector-outside-the-span]]) -- the false claim is what you get by dropping the second hypothesis.

pages.title: Matrices, the Matrix of a Linear Map, and Change of Basis

items.title: Rectangular matrix multiplication and the identity matrix $I_n$, including zero-sized shapes
Matrix multiplication is associative, unital, distributive, and compatible with scalar multiplication
items.strategy: Compare entries. Associativity interchanges the two finite summations and uses associativity and distributivity in the field; the identity, zero, distributive, and scalar laws follow from the same entry formula. Retain empty sums for every zero-sized intermediate dimension.

items.title: $M_n(F)$ is a ring under entrywise addition and matrix multiplication, including the zero ring $M_0(F)$
items.strategy: Combine the published vector-space addition with the matrix multiplication laws and check the ring axioms; for $n=0$ the unique empty matrix is both zero and identity, which the ring convention permits.

items.title: Matrix units $E_{ij}$ and the Kronecker delta
$E_{ij}E_{k\ell}=\delta_{jk}E_{i\ell}$
items.strategy: Evaluate the product entrywise: the finite sum has a nonzero term only at the common middle index, and that term exists exactly when $j=k$.

items.title: $M_n(F)$ is noncommutative for every $n\ge2$
items.strategy: Use $E_{01}E_{10}=E_{00}$ and $E_{10}E_{01}=E_{11}$ and distinguish the two matrices at entry $(0,0)$.

items.title: The transpose $A^{\mathsf T}$ of a matrix
Transpose is linear and involutive, and $(AB)^{\mathsf T}=B^{\mathsf T}A^{\mathsf T}$
items.strategy: The entrywise and involution claims are immediate from swapping indices. For products, expand the $(j,i)$ entry of $AB$ and compare it with the $(j,i)$ entry of the reversed product.

items.title: The space $\mathcal L(V,W)$ of linear maps with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication
$\mathcal L(V,W)$ is a vector space over the common scalar field
items.strategy: Show pointwise sums and scalar multiples remain linear, then inherit every vector-space axiom pointwise from $W$; include empty-domain and zero-space cases.

items.title: Invertible linear maps, linear isomorphisms, and inverse linear maps
Identity maps and composites of linear maps are linear
items.strategy: Substitute a general linear combination into the identity and composite, applying linearity first to the inner map and then to the outer map.

items.title: Coordinate columns $[v]_{\mathcal B}$ and matrices $[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}$ of linear maps relative to ordered bases
$[T(v)]_{\mathcal C}=[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}[v]_{\mathcal B}$
items.strategy: Expand $v$ in the domain basis, apply linearity, expand every image of a basis vector in the codomain basis, and identify each resulting coefficient with the corresponding row-by-column entry.

items.title: $T\mapsto[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}$ is a vector-space isomorphism $\mathcal L(V,W)\cong M_{m\times n}(F)$
items.strategy: Linearity follows columnwise. Injectivity follows because equality on a basis determines a linear map; for surjectivity, use the columns of an arbitrary matrix to prescribe images of the domain basis and extend by the unique-coordinate formula. Include $m=0$ and $n=0$.

items.title: $\dim_F M_{m\times n}(F)=mn$ and $\dim_F\mathcal L(V,W)=(\dim_FV)(\dim_FW)$ for finite-dimensional $V,W$
items.strategy: The $mn$ matrix units form an ordered basis of the matrix space, by reading one entry at a time. Transport that basis across the matrix-representation isomorphism and substitute the lengths of the chosen bases of $V$ and $W$, including either zero dimension.

items.title: $[S\circ T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal D}=[S]_{\mathcal C}^{\mathcal D}[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}$
items.strategy: Apply the coordinate-action theorem first to $T$ and then to $S$, use associativity of matrix multiplication, and identify the representing matrix by uniqueness or by evaluation on every basis column.

items.title: $\operatorname{End}_F(V)$ is a ring and matrix representation is a ring isomorphism $\operatorname{End}_F(V)\cong M_n(F)$
items.strategy: Use pointwise addition and composition on endomorphisms. The identity map is the multiplicative identity, composition distributes over addition, and the representation is already a bijective linear map that preserves composition and the identity matrix.

items.title: Invertible matrices and the general linear group $\operatorname{GL}_n(F)$
A square matrix is invertible exactly when its multiplication map is a linear isomorphism; matrices preserve inverses of linear isomorphisms
items.strategy: An inverse matrix gives an inverse multiplication map. Conversely, represent the inverse linear map and use the composition formula to obtain both matrix inverse equations. Apply the same argument to an arbitrary finite-dimensional linear isomorphism in chosen bases.

items.title: Two finite-dimensional vector spaces over $F$ are linearly isomorphic if and only if they have the same dimension
items.strategy: An isomorphism sends a basis to a basis, so dimensions agree. Conversely, when the dimensions agree, send one ordered basis termwise to the other and extend by unique coordinates; the reverse basis assignment is its linear inverse, including dimension zero.

items.title: $\operatorname{GL}_n(F)$ is a group under matrix multiplication, including the trivial group $\operatorname{GL}_0(F)$
items.strategy: Identify $\operatorname{GL}_n(F)$ with the units of the ring $M_n(F)$ and apply the published units theorem; in the zero ring the sole empty matrix is its own inverse.

items.title: The change-of-basis matrix $P_{\mathcal C\leftarrow\mathcal B}=[\operatorname{id}_V]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}$
$[v]_{\mathcal C}=P_{\mathcal C\leftarrow\mathcal B}[v]_{\mathcal B}$ and $P_{\mathcal B\leftarrow\mathcal C}=P_{\mathcal C\leftarrow\mathcal B}^{-1}$
items.strategy: Apply coordinate action to the identity map for the coordinate formula, then represent the two identity compositions in both orders to obtain the two inverse equations. The empty-basis case gives the empty identity matrix.

items.title: $[T]_{\mathcal B'}^{\mathcal C'}=P_{\mathcal C'\leftarrow\mathcal C}[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}P_{\mathcal B\leftarrow\mathcal B'}$
items.strategy: Factor $T$ as the identity from the new codomain coordinates to the old codomain coordinates, followed by $T$ in the old bases, followed by the identity from the new domain basis to the old domain basis; apply the composition formula twice and check matrix shapes.

items.title: Similar matrices: $B=P^{-1}AP$ for an invertible $P$
Similarity is an equivalence relation, and two matrices represent the same endomorphism in two bases exactly when they are similar
items.strategy: Use $I$, $P^{-1}$, and products of conjugating matrices for reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity. The operator-to-matrix direction is the change-of-basis formula; conversely, use the columns of $P$ as a new ordered basis of $F^n$ and apply the same formula.

items.title: The trace $\operatorname{tr}(A)$ as the sum of the diagonal entries
Trace is a linear functional on $M_n(F)$
items.strategy: Apply entrywise addition and scalar multiplication on the diagonal and the finite-sum laws in the additive group of the field; the empty sum gives the unique map $M_0(F)\to F$ with value zero.

items.title: For $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and $B\in M_{n\times m}(F)$, $\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)$
items.strategy: Expand both traces as the same finite double sum, commute the scalar factors in the field, and interchange the two finite index sets. The formula remains valid when either dimension is zero.

items.title: Similar matrices have the same trace
items.strategy: If $B=P^{-1}AP$, apply $\operatorname{tr}(XY)=\operatorname{tr}(YX)$ to $X=P^{-1}A$ and $Y=P$, then simplify $PP^{-1}=I$.

items.title: A matrix represents a map $F^2\to F^3$ by its images of the standard basis vectors
items.strategy: Compute the two image columns, multiply the resulting $3$ by $2$ matrix by a general coordinate column, and recover the stated linear map.

items.title: The same operator has two different matrices in two ordered bases
items.strategy: Fix one explicit operator on $F^2$, compute its matrix in the standard basis and in a second displayed basis, compute the transition matrix, and verify the conjugation formula numerically. Keep the operator fixed throughout.

items.title: The quarter-turn $(x,y)\mapsto(-y,x)$ on $\mathbb R^2$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and square $-I_2$
items.strategy: Apply the map to the two standard basis vectors, assemble the columns, multiply the matrix by itself, and interpret the square as the half-turn.

items.title: Two explicit $2$ by $2$ matrices do not commute
items.strategy: Use $E_{01}$ and $E_{10}$, compute both products, and display the different diagonal results.

items.title: A nonzero square-zero matrix is not similar to any diagonal matrix
items.strategy: Take $N=E_{01}$ in $M_2(F)$. If $N=P^{-1}DP$ with $D$ diagonal, then $0=N^2=P^{-1}D^2P$, so every diagonal entry of $D$ squares to zero and hence is zero in a field; this would force $N=0$.

items.title: Changing both domain and codomain bases of a map $F^2\to F^3$ uses both sides of the formula
items.strategy: Choose explicit old and new bases in both spaces, compute the two transition matrices and the old matrix of the map, multiply in the prescribed order, and independently recompute the new matrix from images of new basis vectors.

items.title: A $2$ by $3$ matrix and a $3$ by $2$ matrix give square products of different sizes but equal traces
items.strategy: Multiply one explicit pair in both orders, display the resulting $2$ by $2$ and $3$ by $3$ matrices, and compare their diagonal sums.

items.title: Elementary row operations and row equivalence for finite matrices over a field
Every elementary row operation has an elementary inverse, so row equivalence is an equivalence relation

items.title: Elementary matrices obtained by applying one elementary row operation to an identity matrix
Applying an elementary row operation is left multiplication by its elementary matrix

items.title: Matrix equation $Ax=b$, its solution set, consistency, homogeneous systems and the augmented matrix $[A\mid b]$
Elementary row operations on an augmented matrix preserve exactly the solutions of its linear system

items.title: Row echelon form, reduced row echelon form, leading entries, pivots, pivot positions and pivot columns
Gaussian elimination reduces every finite matrix over a field to row echelon form

items.title: Finite rectangular matrices over a commutative ring, their entries, rows and columns
Entrywise ring-matrix operations, rectangular matrix products, identity matrices and transpose
Matrix arithmetic over a commutative ring is associative, unital and distributive, and transpose reverses products
items.strategy: entrywise calculation

items.title: Invertible square matrices and similarity over a commutative ring
For a field, the ring-matrix operations, invertibility and similarity agree exactly with the established field-matrix interface

items.title: Column-multilinear, alternating, normalized and antisymmetric functions on square matrices over a commutative ring
Every alternating multilinear matrix function is antisymmetric under a column swap
items.strategy: polarisation without division

items.title: Every alternating multilinear $F$ satisfies $F(A)=F(I)\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_i a_{\sigma(i),i}$

items.title: For $n\ge1$, the determinant over a commutative ring by the Leibniz formula, and $|\det A|$ for a real matrix

items.title: The Leibniz determinant is column-multilinear, alternating and normalized over every commutative ring

pages.title: The Determinant of a Linear Operator, Cofactors and Cramer's Rule

items.title: An alternating top-degree form is determined by its value on one ordered basis
items.strategy: Let B=(b_0,...,b_{n-1}) be an ordered basis of the positive-dimensional space V. For an alternating n-linear form omega, define F(A) by applying omega to the vectors whose B-coordinate columns are the columns of A. Then F is alternating and column-multilinear, so the published rigidity lemma gives F(A)=F(I_n)det(A). Substituting the coordinate matrix M_B(v_0,...,v_{n-1}) yields omega(v_0,...,v_{n-1})=omega(B)det(M_B(v_0,...,v_{n-1})). No exterior power is introduced.

items.title: The determinant of an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space, defined from its matrix in an ordered basis
On a positive-dimensional space, det(T) is the unique scalar by which T scales every alternating top-degree form
items.strategy: For an alternating n-linear form omega on a positive-dimensional n-dimensional space, put omega_T(v_0,...,v_{n-1})=omega(Tv_0,...,Tv_{n-1}). Apply the preceding coordinate formula first to omega_T and then to omega on the tuple (Tb_0,...,Tb_{n-1}); the coordinate matrix of that tuple is [T]_B, so omega_T=det([T]_B)omega=det(T)omega. For uniqueness, use the normalized coordinate form delta_B(v_0,...,v_{n-1})=det(M_B(v_0,...,v_{n-1})) and evaluate at B. Thus the theorem gives the honest top-form characterisation without defining exterior powers.

items.title: The determinant of a linear operator is independent of the chosen ordered basis
items.strategy: In positive dimension, the preceding theorem characterises the matrix-defined determinant as the unique scalar by which T scales every alternating top-degree form, a condition with no basis in its statement. Hence two ordered bases give the same scalar. Treat the zero-dimensional convention det(T)=1 separately.

items.title: For endomorphisms S and T of one finite-dimensional vector space, det(ST)=det(S)det(T)
items.strategy: For every alternating top-degree form omega, apply the scaling theorem first to S and then to T: omega(STv_0,...,STv_{n-1})=det(S)det(T)omega(v_0,...,v_{n-1}). Uniqueness in the same theorem identifies the scalar with det(ST). The zero-dimensional case reads 1=1 times 1.

items.title: The determinant of an operator can be computed from any representing matrix by row reduction while tracking swaps and row scalings
items.strategy: Choose any basis, row-reduce its representing matrix to echelon form, and use the published determinant effects of row operations and the diagonal product for a triangular matrix. Basis independence licenses the initial choice; row additions contribute no factor.

items.title: Deleted-row-and-column minors, cofactors, the cofactor matrix and the adjugate over a commutative ring
Laplace expansion computes the determinant along every row and every column over a commutative ring
items.strategy: For a fixed row, partition the Leibniz sum according to the selected column, delete that row and column, and identify the permutation sign with the cofactor sign. Obtain the column formula either by the same partition or by applying the row formula to the transpose and using determinant invariance under transpose. Include n=1 using the empty-minor convention.

items.title: For every positive-sized square matrix over a commutative ring, A adj(A)=adj(A) A=det(A) I
items.strategy: Compute each entry of A adj(A). A diagonal entry is the Laplace expansion along the corresponding row; an off-diagonal entry is the same cofactor sum for a matrix with one row replaced by another, hence has determinant zero by alternation. Apply the column version for adj(A)A. Do not infer the off-diagonal zeros merely from singularity over a ring.

items.title: A positive-sized square matrix over a commutative ring is invertible if and only if its determinant is a unit
items.strategy: The forward implication is the published unit-determinant corollary. Conversely, if u=det(A) is a unit, multiply the adjugate identity by u^{-1} to exhibit u^{-1}adj(A) as a two-sided inverse.

items.title: If det(A) is a unit, then A^{-1}=det(A)^{-1} adj(A)
items.strategy: Scale both sides of the two adjugate identities by the inverse of det(A), and invoke uniqueness of a two-sided matrix inverse.

items.title: For A in M_n(R) and columns u,v over a commutative ring, det(A+uv^T)=det(A)+v^T adj(A)u
items.strategy: Expand det(A+uv^T) multilinearly in its columns. The empty choice gives det(A); every term choosing two or more columns from uv^T vanishes because those columns are scalar multiples of u. For the singleton choice j, expand the determinant with column j replaced by u along that column, obtaining v_j sum_i C_ij u_i. Summing over j is v^T adj(A)u. State n>=1 explicitly.

items.title: Over a commutative ring, adj(P^{-1}AP)=P^{-1}adj(A)P for every invertible P
items.strategy: Put C=P^{-1}AP. Compare det(C+uv^T) in two ways. The rank-one update formula gives det(C)+v^T adj(C)u. Similarity invariance rewrites it as det(A+(Pu)(v^T P^{-1})), and a second rank-one update gives det(A)+v^T P^{-1}adj(A)Pu. Cancel det(C)=det(A), then choose u and v to be standard coordinate columns to identify every entry. This works for singular A and avoids any undeveloped rational-function field.

items.title: For A in M_n(R), the coordinate endomorphism T_A:R^n to R^n, with det(T_A):=det(A) and adj(T_A):=T_adj(A)
Cramer's rule over a commutative ring: every solution satisfies det(A)x_j=det(A_j(b)), and a unit determinant gives the unique quotient formula
items.strategy: For Ax=b, replace column j of A by b and use b=sum_k x_k A_k. Column multilinearity kills every term except k=j, giving det(A_j(b))=x_j det(A). If det(A) is a unit, the adjugate formula constructs the solution with those coordinates and invertibility gives uniqueness. State n>=1 and do not divide by a merely nonzero non-unit.

items.title: Over a field, for each right-hand side b, Ax=b has a unique solution exactly when det(A) is nonzero, and then Cramer's quotient formula holds
items.strategy: If det(A) is nonzero, it is a unit and the ring theorem supplies the unique Cramer solution. Conversely, if Ax=b has one unique solution x, every z in the kernel would make x+z another solution, so the kernel is zero; the invertible-matrix theorem makes A invertible, and the determinant is nonzero. State n>=1.

items.title: A finite-dimensional linear operator over a field is invertible if and only if its determinant is nonzero
items.strategy: Choose a basis. The operator is invertible exactly when its representing matrix is invertible; over a field the unit-determinant criterion is the nonzero-determinant criterion. The unique endomorphism of the zero space is invertible and has determinant 1.

items.title: Determinant is a group homomorphism GL(V) to F^times, and det(T^{-1})=det(T)^{-1}
items.strategy: Multiplicativity and det(I)=1 put invertible operators in the unit group. Apply multiplicativity to TT^{-1}=I to obtain the inverse formula.

items.title: The adjugate of an operator on a positive-dimensional finite-dimensional vector space, defined by the adjugate matrix in any basis
For a positive-dimensional finite-dimensional operator, T adj(T)=adj(T)T=det(T) I
items.strategy: Choose a basis and take matrices. The two composites have matrices A adj(A) and adj(A)A, which equal det(A)I by the ring-level adjugate identity; basis independence identifies det(A) with det(T). Equality of representing matrices gives equality of operators.

pages.title: The Determinant of an Operator: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A nonidentity projection of the plane has determinant zero and is not invertible
items.strategy: For T(x,y)=(x,0), compute the diagonal matrix diag(1,0), its determinant, kernel and image, and compare with the operator invertibility criterion.

items.title: One operator has matrices diag(2,3) and [[2,0],[1,3]] in two bases, both with determinant 6
items.strategy: Take T(x,y)=(2x,3y), the standard basis E, and B=((1,1),(0,1)). Compute P_{E<-B}, P^{-1}AP, and both determinants explicitly, checking the abstract change-of-basis proof numerically.

items.title: Multiplication by 2 on Z is injective but not surjective: its determinant is the non-unit 2, its adjugate is integral, and its inverse exists only over Q
items.strategy: Represent n->2n by the 1 by 1 integer matrix [2]. Its determinant is 2 and its adjugate is [1]. Cancellation in Z proves injectivity, while 1 has no preimage proves nonsurjectivity; over Q the inverse matrix is [1/2].

items.title: FALSE: a square matrix over a commutative ring is invertible if and only if its determinant is nonzero
items.strategy: Refute the reverse implication with the preceding integer example: the one-by-one matrix [2] has nonzero determinant 2 in Z, but 2 is not a unit and multiplication by 2 is not surjective. The forward implication also needs a nonzero-ring hypothesis, since over the zero ring the one-by-one identity matrix is [0], is invertible, and has determinant 0. Contrast both failures with the proved unit criterion, which is the correct statement for every commutative ring.

items.title: A sparse 4 by 4 determinant is 30 by both cofactor expansion and row reduction
items.strategy: Use A=[[1,2,0,0],[0,3,0,0],[4,8,2,1],[0,0,0,5]]. Expand along the last row and then a sparse column to obtain 30. Separately replace row 3 by row 3 minus 4 row 1, producing a triangular matrix with diagonal 1,3,2,5 and no determinant-changing operation.

items.title: The adjugate gives the inverse of a three by three rational matrix with determinant 3
items.strategy: For A=[[1,2,0],[0,1,1],[1,0,1]], compute the cofactor matrix [[1,1,-1],[-2,1,2],[2,-1,1]], transpose it to adj(A)=[[1,-2,2],[1,1,-1],[-1,2,1]], and verify A adj(A)=3I. Since 3 is a unit in Q, conclude A^{-1}=(1/3)adj(A) and multiply once more to check.

items.title: Cramer's rule solves 2x+y=5 and x-y=1 as (x,y)=(2,1)
items.strategy: For A=[[2,1],[1,-1]] and b=(5,1), compute det(A)=-3, the two replacement determinants -6 and -3, divide in Q or R, and verify the resulting pair in both equations.

items.title: Determinant is additive in one selected column but not under simultaneous whole-matrix addition
items.strategy: Over Z, take u=(1,0)^T, v=(0,1)^T and w=(0,1)^T. The two-by-two formula gives det([u+v,w])=1=det([u,w])+det([v,w])=1+0, illustrating valid additivity in the first column while the second is fixed. Then directly compute with A=B=I_2 that det(A+B)=4 but det(A)+det(B)=2. The paired computations isolate exactly why columnwise multilinearity is not linearity in the whole matrix argument.

pages.title: Eigenvalues, Eigenvectors and the Characteristic Polynomial

items.title: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors, eigenspaces $E_\lambda(T)=\ker(T-\lambda I)$, and the spectrum $\sigma_F(T)$ of an endomorphism
For a finite-dimensional space, $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $T$ if and only if $T-\lambda I$ is not invertible
items.strategy: Unfold the eigenspace: an eigenvector is exactly a nonzero vector in the kernel of $T-\lambda I$. One direction follows because an invertible map has trivial kernel; for the other, rank-nullity makes an injective endomorphism of a finite-dimensional space surjective, hence invertible. The zero-dimensional case is explicit: its spectrum is empty and its unique endomorphism is invertible.

items.title: Eigenvectors belonging to pairwise distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent
items.strategy: Induct on the number of vectors. Apply $T-\lambda_m I$ to a vanishing relation; the last term disappears and the remaining eigenvectors acquire the nonzero coefficients $\lambda_i-\lambda_m$. Independence for the shorter list kills those coefficients, and then the original relation kills the last one.

items.title: An endomorphism of an $n$-dimensional space has at most $n$ distinct eigenvalues
items.strategy: Choose one eigenvector for each distinct eigenvalue. The distinct-eigenvalue theorem makes the chosen vectors independent, and an independent subset of an $n$-dimensional vector space has at most $n$ elements.

items.title: For $A\in M_n(F)$, the characteristic polynomial is $\chi_A(x)=\det(xI_n-A)$ when $n\geq1$, with $\chi_A(x)=1$ for the unique $0\times0$ matrix
$\chi_A(x)$ is monic of degree $n$; for $n\geq1$ its $x^{n-1}$ coefficient is $-\operatorname{tr}(A)$ and its constant coefficient is $(-1)^n\det(A)$, while $\chi_{0\times0}=1$
items.strategy: Handle $n=0$ directly from the convention $\chi_{0\times0}=1$. For $n\geq1$, expand $\det(xI-A)$ by the Leibniz formula. The identity permutation alone contributes degree $n$; its choices of one diagonal entry of $A$ give the $-\operatorname{tr}(A)$ coefficient, while every nonidentity permutation moves at least two indices and therefore has degree at most $n-2$. Evaluation at $x=0$ gives the constant coefficient.

items.title: The characteristic polynomial of a block upper- or lower-triangular matrix is the product of the characteristic polynomials of its diagonal blocks
items.strategy: Use the Leibniz formula for a block triangular matrix over the commutative ring $F[x]$: a nonzero permutation term cannot cross from one diagonal block without also crossing back through the zero block. The surviving permutations split uniquely into permutations of the two diagonal blocks, so the determinant factors; apply this to $xI-M$.

items.title: Similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial
items.strategy: If $B=P^{-1}AP$, then $xI-B=P^{-1}(xI-A)P$ as matrices over $F[x]$. Multiplicativity of determinant cancels the determinant factors of $P^{-1}$ and $P$, giving $\chi_B=\chi_A$ without evaluating at any scalar.

items.title: The basis-independent characteristic polynomial $\chi_T$ of an endomorphism of a finite-dimensional space, including $\chi_T=1$ in dimension zero
For every finite-dimensional space, $\sigma_F(T)$ is exactly the set of roots in $F$ of $\chi_T$
items.strategy: If the dimension is zero, the spectrum is empty and $\chi_T=1$ has no roots. In positive dimension and any basis, $\chi_T(\lambda)=\det(\lambda I-[T])=(-1)^n\det([T]-\lambda I)$. The determinant criterion says this vanishes exactly when $T-\lambda I$ is not invertible, and the shift proposition identifies that condition with $\lambda$ being an eigenvalue.

items.title: An algebraically closed field: every nonconstant polynomial has a root in the field
Every endomorphism of a nonzero finite-dimensional vector space over an algebraically closed field has an eigenvalue
items.strategy: The characteristic polynomial is monic of positive degree, hence nonconstant. Algebraic closedness supplies a root in the base field, and the spectrum-root theorem turns that root into an eigenvalue.

items.title: Algebraic multiplicity as the exponent of $x-\lambda$ in $\chi_T$, and geometric multiplicity as $\dim E_\lambda(T)$
If $\chi_T(x)=\prod_{i<n}(x-\lambda_i)$ in $F[x]$, then $\operatorname{tr}(T)=\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i$: trace is the sum of the eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity
items.strategy: For the zero space, compare the trace convention $0$ with the empty sum. In positive dimension, choose a basis and compare the coefficient of $x^{n-1}$ in the two expressions for $\chi_T$: the extreme-coefficient lemma gives $-\operatorname{tr}(T)$, while expanding the product of the linear factors gives $-\sum_{i<n}\lambda_i$. The root-spectrum theorem and the multiplicity definition identify the listed roots as precisely the eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity.

items.title: If $\chi_T(x)=\prod_{i<n}(x-\lambda_i)$ in $F[x]$, then $\det(T)=\prod_{i<n}\lambda_i$: determinant is the product of the eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity
items.strategy: For the zero space, compare the determinant convention $1$ with the empty product. In positive dimension, compare constant coefficients: the extreme-coefficient lemma gives $(-1)^n\det(T)$, while the displayed factorisation gives $(-1)^n\prod_{i<n}\lambda_i$. Cancel the unit $(-1)^n$. The root-spectrum theorem and the multiplicity definition identify the factors with the eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity.

items.title: The geometric multiplicity of an eigenvalue does not exceed its algebraic multiplicity
items.strategy: Start with a basis of the eigenspace and extend it to a basis of the whole finite-dimensional space. In that basis the matrix of $T$ is block upper triangular with leading block $\lambda I_g$, where $g$ is the eigenspace dimension. The block characteristic-polynomial lemma gives $\chi_T=(x-\lambda)^g q(x)$, so the maximal exponent defining algebraic multiplicity is at least $g$.

items.title: An eigenvalue of algebraic multiplicity one has a one-dimensional eigenspace
items.strategy: An eigenvalue has a nonzero eigenspace, so its geometric multiplicity is at least one. The multiplicity inequality bounds it above by the algebraic multiplicity one.

items.title: For $A,B\in M_n(F)$, the products $AB$ and $BA$ have the same characteristic polynomial
items.strategy: Work over $F[x]$ with the block matrix $\begin{pmatrix}xI&A\\-B&I\end{pmatrix}$. Multiply it by explicit block-unitriangular matrices of determinant one in two different orders; the resulting block triangular matrices have diagonal blocks $(xI+AB,I)$ and $(xI+BA,I)$. The block determinant calculation therefore gives $\det(xI+AB)=\det(xI+BA)$, and replacing $A$ by $-A$ yields the stated identity without dividing by $x$.

items.title: Polynomial evaluation at an endomorphism: $p(T)=\sum_k a_kT^k$

If $\chi_T(x)=\prod_{i<n}(x-\lambda_i)$ in $F[x]$, then $\chi_{p(T)}(y)=\prod_{i<n}(y-p(\lambda_i))$ for every $p\in F[x]$: the eigenvalues of $p(T)$ are $p(\lambda_i)$, counted with algebraic multiplicity
items.strategy: Induct on the finite dimension. The zero-dimensional identity is the empty product. For positive dimension, $\lambda_0$ is a root of $\chi_T$, so the root-spectrum theorem supplies an eigenvector. Extend its line to a basis without Choice; the matrix of $T$ is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks $\lambda_0$ and $B$, and cancellation in $F[x]$ shows $\chi_B=\prod_{0<i<n}(x-\lambda_i)$. Polynomial evaluation preserves the block form and changes its diagonal blocks to $p(\lambda_0)$ and $p(B)$. Apply the block characteristic-polynomial lemma and the induction hypothesis to obtain the displayed identity, which records multiplicities as well as the spectrum set.

items.title: If $\chi_T$ splits over $F$, every eigenvalue of $\chi_T(T)$ is $0$
items.strategy: Write $\chi_T(x)=\prod_{i<n}(x-\lambda_i)$ and apply spectral mapping with $p=\chi_T$. Every resulting eigenvalue is $\chi_T(\lambda_i)=0$ because each $\lambda_i$ is a root. In dimension zero the spectrum is empty, so the conclusion is vacuous.

items.title: Cayley-Hamilton: every finite-dimensional endomorphism satisfies its characteristic polynomial, $\chi_T(T)=0$
items.strategy: In dimension zero, $\chi_T=1$ and its value is the identity endomorphism, which equals the zero endomorphism on the zero space. Otherwise choose a basis and put $A=[T]$. In $M_n(F[x])$, expand $\operatorname{adj}(xI-A)=B_0+B_1x+\cdots+B_{n-1}x^{n-1}$ and use the published adjugate identity $(xI-A)\operatorname{adj}(xI-A)=\chi_A(x)I$. Compare matrix coefficients in the central indeterminate $x$ and combine the resulting recurrences after multiplying by powers of $A$; they telescope to $\chi_A(A)=0$. Translate back to $T$. This never treats substitution of $A$ into an arbitrary matrix-coefficient polynomial as a ring homomorphism.

items.title: The inverse of an invertible finite-dimensional endomorphism is a polynomial in that endomorphism
items.strategy: In dimension zero, the unique endomorphism, its identity, its inverse, and the zero polynomial in it all coincide. In positive dimension write $\chi_T(x)=x^n+c_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+c_0$. Cayley-Hamilton gives the corresponding operator identity, while $c_0=(-1)^n\det T$ is nonzero for invertible $T$. Move the constant term to the other side and multiply by $c_0^{-1}T^{-1}$ to express $T^{-1}$ using only $I,T,\ldots,T^{n-1}$.

pages.title: Eigenvalues and the Characteristic Polynomial: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ has characteristic polynomial $(x-2)(x-3)$ and two explicitly computed eigenspaces
items.strategy: Compute the triangular determinant and solve the two kernel equations. The eigenspaces are the spans of $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$, illustrating both the root criterion and independence for distinct eigenvalues.

items.title: A quarter-turn of $\mathbb R^2$ has characteristic polynomial $x^2+1$ and no real eigenvalue
items.strategy: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, calculate $\det(xI-A)=x^2+1$. Real square positivity shows this polynomial has no real root, so the real spectrum is empty even though the space is nonzero.

items.title: $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ over $\mathbb F_2$ has characteristic polynomial $x^2+x+1$ and no eigenvalue in its base field
items.strategy: Compute the determinant in $\mathbb F_2[x]$ and evaluate the polynomial at the only two scalars, $0$ and $1$; both values are $1$. The root-spectrum theorem then gives an empty spectrum over a finite non-algebraically-closed field.

items.title: $\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ has algebraic multiplicity two but geometric multiplicity one at $2$
items.strategy: The characteristic polynomial is $(x-2)^2$. Solving $(A-2I)v=0$ gives vectors $(a,0)$, a one-dimensional eigenspace, so the multiplicity inequality can be strict.

items.title: The scalar matrix $2I_2$ has algebraic and geometric multiplicity two at $2$
items.strategy: Its characteristic polynomial is $(x-2)^2$, while $A-2I=0$ has all of $F^2$ as its kernel. This contrasts the preceding repeated-root example without invoking diagonalisation theory.

items.title: Cayley-Hamilton reduces every power of $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ to a linear combination of $A$ and $I$
items.strategy: Compute $\chi_A(x)=x^2-x-1$. Cayley-Hamilton gives $A^2=A+I$, and induction then gives $A^m=F_mA+F_{m-1}I$ for $m\geq1$, with the recurrence itself established inline.

items.title: FALSE: substituting a fixed matrix $A$ for $x$ defines a ring homomorphism $M_n(F[x])\to M_n(F)$
items.strategy: Take $A=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ and the constant matrix $B=E_{12}$. In $M_2(F[x])$ the central matrix $xI$ commutes with $B$, but the proposed substitution sends the two equal products $(xI)B$ and $B(xI)$ to $AB=B$ and $BA=0$. Thus the map is not even well defined as a multiplicative evaluation rule, pinpointing the flaw in the naive Cayley-Hamilton pseudo-proof.

pages.title: Diagonalisation and the Minimal Polynomial
pages.note: frontier-13 D3.1 (2026-08-15): added the published order-54 page field-extensions-and-the-complex-numbers. thm-minimal-and-characteristic-polynomials-have-the-same-irreducible-factors proves the shared-factor claim by forming F[x]/(q) at an irreducible factor q of the characteristic polynomial and applying thm-evaluation-kernel-and-minimal-polynomial; neither that theorem nor thm-irreducible-quotient-adjoins-a-root was reachable from the two originally declared prerequisites. Verified published, order 54 < 88, not built in this run, and preserving the run's zero-cross-batch-seam property.

items.title: A diagonalisable endomorphism is one admitting a basis of eigenvectors, equivalently a diagonal matrix representation
The annihilator set $\operatorname{Ann}(T)=\{p\in F[x]:p(T)=0\}$; once existence is proved, its unique monic generator $\mu_T$ is the minimal polynomial
The annihilator ideal is nonzero and has a unique monic generator; $p(T)=0$ if and only if $\mu_T\mid p$
items.strategy: Verify the annihilators form an ideal; Cayley–Hamilton makes it nonzero; the PID theorem gives a generator, whose leading coefficient can be normalised uniquely. Unpack ideal membership and treat the zero space separately, where $\mu_T=1$.

items.title: The minimal polynomial is unchanged by choosing a matrix representation or replacing a matrix by a similar one
items.strategy: Prove the matrix of $p(T)$ is $p([T]_{\mathcal B})$, so operator and matrix annihilator ideals agree. If $B=P^{-1}AP$, show $p(B)=P^{-1}p(A)P$ and compare monic generators.

items.title: For a matrix over a field, extending the scalar field does not change its minimal polynomial
items.strategy: Let $A\in M_n(F)$ and let $K/F$ be a field extension. The polynomial $\mu_{A,F}$ still annihilates $A$ over $K$. Conversely, suppose a nonzero $q=\sum_{i=0}^r c_i x^i\in K[x]$ annihilates $A$. Choose a maximal $F$-linearly independent subfamily $d_1,\ldots,d_s$ of the finite coefficient family; it spans every $c_i$, so write $c_i=\sum_j a_{ij}d_j$ with $a_{ij}\in F$. Comparing each matrix entry in $0=q(A)=\sum_j d_j(\sum_i a_{ij}A^i)$ shows that every $\sum_i a_{ij}A^i$ vanishes. At least one corresponding $F$-polynomial is nonzero and has degree at most $r$. Thus $\deg\mu_{A,F}\leq\deg\mu_{A,K}$, while $\mu_{A,K}$ divides $\mu_{A,F}$ in $K[x]$; equal degrees and monicity give $\mu_{A,K}=\mu_{A,F}$. Include the $0\times0$ matrix, whose minimal polynomial is $1$.

items.title: The minimal polynomial divides the characteristic polynomial, $\mu_T\mid\chi_T$
items.strategy: Apply the annihilator criterion to the published Cayley–Hamilton identity. At dimension zero both polynomials are $1$.

items.title: Over every extension field, a scalar is an eigenvalue of the extended matrix exactly when it is a root of the minimal polynomial
items.strategy: Let $A$ be a matrix over $F$ and let $K/F$ be a field extension. Scalar-extension invariance identifies the minimal polynomial over $K$ with $\mu_A\in F[x]$. If $Av=\lambda v$ for nonzero $v$, then $p(A)v=p(\lambda)v$, so $\mu_A(\lambda)=0$. Conversely $\mu_A\mid\chi_A$, and the determinant formula leaves $\chi_A$ unchanged over $K$, so the root–spectrum theorem supplies an eigenvector. Include the zero space.

items.title: The minimal and characteristic polynomials have exactly the same monic irreducible factors
items.strategy: One direction follows from $\mu_T\mid\chi_T$. For a monic irreducible $q\mid\chi_T$, form $K=F[x]/(q)$ and let $a\in K$ be the distinguished root. The determinant formula leaves $\chi_T$ unchanged after scalar extension, so $a$ is an eigenvalue over $K$. Scalar-extension invariance identifies the extended minimal polynomial with $\mu_T$, and evaluation on an eigenvector gives $\mu_T(a)=0$. The evaluation-kernel theorem then forces $q\mid\mu_T$.

items.title: For every polynomial $p$, both $\ker p(T)$ and $\operatorname{im}p(T)$ are $T$-invariant
items.strategy: Polynomial evaluation commutes with $T$; apply this identity to kernel and image vectors.

items.title: The minimal polynomial of a restriction to an invariant subspace divides the original minimal polynomial
items.strategy: Every polynomial identity for $T$ restricts to $T|_W$, so $\mu_T(T|_W)=0$ and the restriction's annihilator criterion applies. Include $W=0$.

items.title: If $\gcd(f,g)=1$ and $(fg)(T)=0$, then $V=\ker f(T)\oplus\ker g(T)$
items.strategy: Use $af+bg=1$ to decompose each vector into the opposite kernels; apply the same identity to their intersection. Unit factors and the zero space remain valid.

items.title: Primary components $\ker q(T)^e$ and generalised eigenspaces $G_\lambda^{(e)}(T)=\ker(T-\lambda I)^e$
Primary decomposition: the irreducible-power factors of $\mu_T$ split $V$ into their invariant kernels
items.strategy: Factor $\mu_T=\prod q_i^{e_i}$ and iterate the coprime-kernel lemma. Prove invariance and prove each restriction has exactly the corresponding irreducible power as minimal polynomial; otherwise a smaller componentwise annihilator contradicts minimality. The empty factorisation is the zero space.

items.title: Each projection in the primary decomposition is a polynomial in the endomorphism
items.strategy: For $f_i=q_i^{e_i}$ and $g_i=\mu_T/f_i$, use Bézout to show $b_i(T)g_i(T)$ is identity on the $i$-th primary component and zero on the others.

items.title: If the minimal polynomial splits, $V$ is the direct sum of the stabilised generalised eigenspaces
items.strategy: Specialise primary decomposition to $q_i=x-\lambda_i$ and identify each primary kernel and its least stabilising exponent.

items.title: An endomorphism is diagonalisable exactly when $V=\bigoplus_{i<r}E_{\lambda_i}(T)$ for some finite list of distinct scalars $\lambda_i$
items.strategy: Partition an eigenbasis by its finitely many eigenvalues. Conversely concatenate bases of the finitely many eigenspaces in the displayed direct sum. The empty list and empty basis cover the zero space.

items.title: An endomorphism is diagonalisable if and only if its characteristic polynomial splits and every eigenvalue's geometric multiplicity equals its algebraic multiplicity
items.strategy: A diagonal matrix has a split characteristic polynomial, and for each eigenvalue the repeated diagonal entries count both its algebraic multiplicity and the dimension of its eigenspace. Conversely, when the characteristic polynomial splits, the algebraic multiplicities sum to $\dim V$. If they equal the geometric multiplicities, bases of the distinct eigenspaces together form a linearly independent list of $\dim V$ eigenvectors, hence a basis; apply the eigenspace direct-sum criterion. The empty factorisation handles $V=0$.

items.title: An endomorphism is diagonalisable if and only if its minimal polynomial is a product of distinct linear factors
items.strategy: An eigenbasis shows the product over distinct eigenvalues annihilates $T$, and every eigenvalue must be a root of $\mu_T$. Conversely primary decomposition with all exponents one is the eigenspace direct sum. The empty product handles the zero space.

items.title: A characteristic polynomial that splits into distinct linear factors forces diagonalisability
items.strategy: A divisor of a split squarefree polynomial is split and squarefree; combine $\mu_T\mid\chi_T$ with the criterion.

items.title: Every idempotent endomorphism is diagonalisable and is projection onto its image along its kernel
items.strategy: Since $T^2=T$, $\mu_T\mid x(x-1)$ and the criterion applies. Directly decompose $v=Tv+(v-Tv)$ and show image and kernel intersect trivially, including $0$ and $I$.

items.title: The restriction of a diagonalisable endomorphism to an invariant subspace is diagonalisable
items.strategy: The restriction minimal polynomial divides the ambient split squarefree polynomial, so it too is split and squarefree.

items.title: Simultaneous diagonalisability: one basis that diagonalises every endomorphism in a family
Commuting endomorphisms preserve each other's eigenspaces
items.strategy: If $ST=TS$ and $Tv=\lambda v$, compute $T(Sv)=S(Tv)=\lambda Sv$, allowing $Sv=0$.

items.title: A family of diagonalisable endomorphisms of a finite-dimensional space is simultaneously diagonalisable if and only if its members commute pairwise
items.strategy: For pairwise commuting families, induct in the finite case on eigenspaces of the last operator, using invariant diagonalisable restrictions. For an arbitrary family, its span is a subspace of the finite-dimensional space $\mathcal L(V,V)$; expand a finite basis of that span in the original family and take the union of the finite supports to obtain finitely many original members spanning it. Their common eigenbasis diagonalises every linear combination. Conversely, endomorphisms diagonal in one common basis commute because diagonal matrices commute. Include empty families and the zero space.

items.title: If two commuting endomorphisms are diagonalisable, then every finite linear combination of products of their powers is diagonalisable; in particular, their sum and product are diagonalisable
items.strategy: Choose the common eigenbasis supplied by simultaneous diagonalisation. Every power of either endomorphism is diagonal in that basis, so every product of powers and every finite linear combination of such products is diagonal in the same basis. The zero polynomial and empty space cause no exception.

items.title: The algebra $F[T]$ generated by an endomorphism is isomorphic to $F[x]/(\mu_T)$
items.strategy: Polynomial evaluation has image $F[T]$ and kernel $(\mu_T)$; apply the first isomorphism theorem, including the zero-space quotient by $(1)$.

pages.title: Diagonalisation and the Minimal Polynomial: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Minimal polynomials of scalar and diagonal endomorphisms, including the zero-dimensional case
items.strategy: Compute $1$ on the zero space, $x-\lambda$ for $\lambda I$ on a nonzero space, and the product of the distinct displayed diagonal factors for a diagonal matrix.

items.title: The identity and a nontrivial Jordan block have the same characteristic polynomial but different minimal polynomials
items.strategy: Compare $I_2$ with $J=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{psmallmatrix}$: both have $(x-1)^2$, while their minimal polynomials are $x-1$ and $(x-1)^2$.

items.title: Computing the minimal polynomial of an explicit $3\times3$ idempotent from its annihilating polynomials
items.strategy: For Conrad's matrix $\begin{psmallmatrix}0&-1&1\\1&2&-1\\1&1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$ compute $A^2=A$, $A\ne0,I$, $\mu_A=x(x-1)$, $\chi_A=x(x-1)^2$, and its image/kernel projection.

items.title: A nilpotent shift has minimal polynomial $x^n$ and one primary component
items.strategy: On $F^n$, send $e_i$ to $e_{i-1}$ for $i>0$ and $e_0$ to zero. Compute $T^n=0$ and $T^{n-1}e_{n-1}=e_0$ for $n>0$; at $n=0$, $\mu_T=1$.

items.title: Quarter-turn rotation is not diagonalisable over $\mathbb R$ but is diagonalisable over $\mathbb C$
items.strategy: For $R=\begin{psmallmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$ compute $\mu_R=\chi_R=x^2+1$; it is irreducible over $\mathbb R$ and has the distinct roots $\pm i$ over $\mathbb C$, where explicit eigenvectors form a basis.

items.title: Primary decomposition over $\mathbb Q$ with one linear and one irreducible quadratic factor
items.strategy: Take the direct sum of multiplication by $2$ and the companion matrix of $x^2+1$; compute $(x-2)(x^2+1)$ and its two Bézout projections without adjoining roots.

items.title: Lagrange polynomials give the three eigenspace projections of a diagonalisable endomorphism
items.strategy: For distinct $\lambda_i$, verify $e_i(x)=\prod_{j\ne i}(x-\lambda_j)/(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)$ has $e_i(\lambda_j)=\delta_{ij}$ and that $e_i(T)$ are orthogonal idempotent projections summing to $I$.

items.title: Two commuting non-scalar matrices simultaneously diagonalised in one explicit basis
items.strategy: Conjugate two non-scalar diagonal matrices by the same simple invertible matrix, verify the resulting matrices commute, and recover the common eigenbasis.

items.title: Commuting alone does not imply simultaneous diagonalisability
items.strategy: The family $\{I_2,\begin{psmallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{psmallmatrix}\}$ commutes, but the second matrix has minimal polynomial $(x-1)^2$.

items.title: FALSE: If the minimal polynomial splits, then the endomorphism is diagonalisable
items.strategy: The nontrivial $2\times2$ Jordan block has split minimal polynomial $(x-1)^2$; the missing condition is distinct roots.

items.title: FALSE: The characteristic polynomial determines whether an endomorphism is diagonalisable
items.strategy: Compute directly that the identity and the nontrivial $2\times2$ Jordan block share $(x-1)^2$, while their minimal polynomials are $x-1$ and $(x-1)^2$; apply the squarefree minimal-polynomial criterion.

items.title: FALSE: A diagonalisable endomorphism must have a characteristic polynomial with distinct roots
items.strategy: The identity on a nonzero two-dimensional space is diagonalisable but has characteristic polynomial $(x-1)^2$.
