pages.title: Dual Spaces, Bilinear and Quadratic Forms, and Sylvester's Law of Inertia

items.title: Linear functionals and the algebraic dual $V^*=\mathcal L(V,F)$
The dual family $(b^*)_{b\in B}$ associated to a Hamel basis $B$, defined by $b^*(c)=\delta_{bc}$
The dual family of a finite basis is a basis of the dual space, with the same dimension
items.strategy: Use unique coordinates in the original basis. A functional is determined by its finitely many values on the basis and equals their linear combination of the coordinate functionals; evaluation on each basis vector also proves independence. The empty basis handles the zero space.

items.title: For an infinite Hamel basis, its dual family is linearly independent but does not span the algebraic dual
items.strategy: Independence follows by evaluating a finite relation at its indexed basis vectors. Define a functional $\phi$ by assigning the value $1$ to every basis vector and extending through each vector's finite coordinate expansion. Every finite linear combination of coordinate functionals vanishes on all but finitely many basis vectors, whereas $\phi$ does not, so the dual family cannot span.

items.title: Assuming choice, if $v\notin U\leq V$, some $f\in V^*$ vanishes on $U$ and satisfies $f(v)=1$
items.strategy: Choose a basis of $U$, adjoin $v$ to it, and use the basis-extension theorem to obtain a basis of $V$. Prescribe value $1$ on $v$ and $0$ on every other basis vector, then extend by finite linear combinations. Independence guarantees the prescription is unambiguous.

items.title: The canonical evaluation map $J_V:V\to V^{**}$ given by $J_V(v)(f)=f(v)$
Assuming choice, the canonical map $J_V:V\to V^{**}$ is linear and injective
items.strategy: Linearity is pointwise. If $v\neq0$, apply the separation lemma to the zero subspace to obtain $f$ with $f(v)=1$; then $J_V(v)(f)=1$, so $J_V(v)$ is nonzero and the kernel is trivial.

items.title: Assuming choice, $J_V:V\to V^{**}$ is surjective if and only if $V$ is finite-dimensional
items.strategy: For a finite basis, the dual-basis expansion shows that every element of $V^{**}$ is evaluation at a unique vector. If a basis $B$ is infinite, let $\Phi$ be the proper span in $V^*$ of its coordinate functionals and choose the functional taking value $1$ on every $b\in B$ outside $\Phi$. Separate that functional from $\Phi$ inside $V^*$ to obtain $L\in V^{**}$ vanishing on every coordinate functional but not on it. Were $L=J_V(v)$, all coordinates of $v$ would vanish, forcing $v=0$ and contradicting the chosen nonzero value.

items.title: The annihilator $U^\circ\leq V^*$ of $U\leq V$ and the preannihilator ${}^\circ S\leq V$ of $S\leq V^*$
Assuming choice, ${}^\circ(U^\circ)=U$; in finite dimension, $\dim U^\circ=\dim V-\dim U$
items.strategy: The inclusion $U\subseteq{}^\circ(U^\circ)$ is immediate. If $v\notin U$, the separation lemma supplies a functional in $U^\circ$ not vanishing at $v$, proving the reverse inclusion. In finite dimension, restrict functionals from $V$ to $U$; its kernel is $U^\circ$, it is surjective by extending a basis of $U$, and rank-nullity plus the finite dual-dimension theorem gives the dimension formula.

items.title: The transpose or algebraic adjoint $T^*:W^*\to V^*$, $T^*(g)=g\circ T$, of a linear map $T:V\to W$
Transpose is linear, sends identities to identities, and reverses composition: $(S\circ T)^*=T^*\circ S^*$
items.strategy: Evaluate every claimed map at an arbitrary functional and then at an arbitrary vector. The identities reduce to pointwise linearity and associativity of function composition, including the reversed order.

items.title: Assuming choice, $\ker T^*=(\operatorname{im}T)^\circ$ and $\operatorname{im}T^*=(\ker T)^\circ$; in finite dimensions $\operatorname{rank}T^*=\operatorname{rank}T$
items.strategy: The kernel identity is immediate from $T^*(g)=g\circ T$. Every $T^*(g)$ vanishes on $\ker T$; conversely a functional vanishing there descends to $\operatorname{im}T$ and extends from that subspace to $W$ by a basis extension, proving the range identity. For finite-dimensional $V,W$, apply the annihilator dimension formula and rank-nullity to obtain equality of ranks.

items.title: In dual bases, the matrix of $T^*$ is the transpose of the matrix of $T$
items.strategy: If the $(i,j)$ entry of $[T]$ is the $i$th coordinate functional applied to $T(v_j)$, then the $(j,i)$ entry of $[T^*]$ is $T^*(w_i^*)(v_j)=w_i^*(T(v_j))$. These are the same scalar, including rectangular source and target dimensions.

items.title: Bilinear forms, and symmetric, skew-symmetric, and alternating bilinear forms
Alternating forms are skew-symmetric; the converse holds when $\operatorname{char}F\neq2$, while in characteristic $2$ alternating forms are symmetric
items.strategy: Expand $B(u+v,u+v)=0$ for an alternating form to obtain $B(u,v)+B(v,u)=0$. For a skew-symmetric form, $B(v,v)=-B(v,v)$ gives $2B(v,v)=0$, which forces alternation exactly when $2\neq0$. In characteristic two, the minus sign equals the plus sign, so skew-symmetry is symmetry.

items.title: Bilinear forms on $V$ correspond linearly and bijectively to linear maps $V\to V^*$
items.strategy: Send $B$ to $B^\flat$, where $B^\flat(v)$ is the functional $w\mapsto B(v,w)$. Bilinearity proves this is a linear map. Conversely send $L:V\to V^*$ to $(v,w)\mapsto L(v)(w)$; the two constructions are pointwise inverse and preserve addition and scalar multiplication.

items.title: The matrix, left and right radicals, rank, and nondegeneracy of a bilinear form on a finite-dimensional space
A basis change by $P$ changes the matrix of a bilinear form from $A$ to $P^{\mathsf T}AP$
items.strategy: Write both arguments in old coordinates: if the new-coordinate columns are $x,y$, their old-coordinate columns are $Px,Py$. Then $B(v,w)=x^{\mathsf T}P^{\mathsf T}APy$, so the new matrix is $P^{\mathsf T}AP$. Define matrix congruence by this relation and keep it distinct from similarity.

items.title: Congruent matrices have the same rank; hence rank and nondegeneracy of a bilinear form are basis-independent
items.strategy: Left and right multiplication by an invertible matrix do not change the dimension of the image of the represented map. Apply this to $P^{\mathsf T}AP$ and note that $P^{\mathsf T}$ is invertible whenever $P$ is. The radical interpretation then makes nondegeneracy basis-independent.

items.title: Sesquilinear and Hermitian forms over a field with an involution, using the convention linear in the first variable
For the linear-first convention, a basis change by $P$ sends a sesquilinear matrix $A$ to $P^{\mathsf T}A\,\sigma(P)$; Hermitian forms satisfy $A=\sigma(A)^{\mathsf T}$
items.strategy: Expand both vectors in the new basis and use linearity in the first variable and $\sigma$-linearity in the second. The coefficients collect as $x^{\mathsf T}P^{\mathsf T}A\sigma(P)\sigma(y)$. Evaluating Hermitian symmetry on pairs of basis vectors gives the conjugate-transpose identity, and conversely that identity gives the symmetry.

items.title: A quadratic form $q$ in arbitrary characteristic and its polar form $b_q(u,v)=q(u+v)-q(u)-q(v)$
If $\operatorname{char}F\neq2$, quadratic forms and symmetric bilinear forms correspond by $q(v)=B(v,v)$ and $B(u,v)=\tfrac12 b_q(u,v)$
items.strategy: For symmetric $B$, expand $q_B(u+v)$ to obtain $b_{q_B}=2B$. Conversely the quadratic homogeneity gives $b_q(v,v)=q(2v)-2q(v)=2q(v)$; dividing by two shows that $B_q=\tfrac12 b_q$ recovers $q$. The defining assumption that $b_q$ is bilinear supplies bilinearity, and its formula is symmetric.

items.title: Every symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional space over a field of characteristic not $2$ has an orthogonal basis
items.strategy: Induct on dimension, with the empty basis for the zero space. If the form is zero, any basis works. Otherwise polarization shows that some $v$ has $B(v,v)\neq0$; then $V=Fv\oplus v^\perp$, because subtracting $B(w,v)B(v,v)^{-1}v$ puts any $w$ in $v^\perp$ and the intersection is zero. Apply induction to the restricted symmetric form on $v^\perp$ and adjoin $v$.

items.title: Over a field of characteristic not $2$, every symmetric matrix is congruent to a diagonal matrix
items.strategy: Regard the matrix as the matrix of its associated symmetric bilinear form in the standard basis. An orthogonal basis makes all off-diagonal entries zero, and the change-of-basis formula says precisely that the two matrices are congruent.

items.title: Over a field of characteristic not $2$, every quadratic form has diagonal coordinates $q(x)=a_1x_1^2+\cdots+a_nx_n^2$
items.strategy: Use polarization to attach the symmetric bilinear form $B_q$. Choose an orthogonal basis for it; because $q(v)=B_q(v,v)$, expansion in that basis has no cross terms and gives the diagonal expression, including zero coefficients for the radical.

items.title: Every alternating form on a finite-dimensional space has a basis of symplectic pairs followed by a basis of its radical; in particular its rank is even
items.strategy: Induct on dimension. If the form is zero, the whole space is radical. Otherwise choose $e,f$ with $B(e,f)\neq0$, rescale to $B(e,f)=1$, and split off the nondegenerate plane they span by subtracting explicit $e$- and $f$-components from every vector. Its orthogonal complement carries the remaining alternating form; induction supplies the remaining pairs and radical basis. The displayed block matrix has one rank-two block per pair and zeros on the radical.

items.title: Positive and negative definiteness, the inertia $(p,q,r)$, rank $p+q$, and signature $p-q$ of a real symmetric bilinear or quadratic form
Sylvester's law of inertia: every real symmetric form is congruent to $\operatorname{diag}(I_p,-I_q,0_r)$, and $(p,q,r)$ is unique
items.strategy: Diagonalize the form and rescale each nonzero basis vector using the positive square root of the absolute value of its diagonal coefficient, obtaining the displayed normal form. In that form, the largest dimension of a subspace on which the form is positive definite is $p$: the positive coordinate space attains $p$, while any larger subspace meets the negative-plus-radical coordinate space nontrivially and cannot be positive definite. The analogous maximum is $q$ for negative definite subspaces, and $r$ follows from nullity. These intrinsic maxima prove uniqueness.

items.title: Two real symmetric bilinear forms are congruent if and only if they have the same inertia
items.strategy: Congruence preserves the intrinsic maximal positive and negative dimensions and the radical dimension, so it preserves inertia. Conversely, forms with the same inertia are each congruent to the same diagonal normal form; compose one basis change with the inverse of the other.

items.title: For symmetric $M=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\B^{\mathsf T}&C\end{pmatrix}$ with $A$ invertible, a block-unitriangular congruence gives $A\oplus(C-B^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}B)$ and factors $\det M$
items.strategy: Use the explicit invertible block-unitriangular matrix $P=\begin{pmatrix}I&-A^{-1}B\\0&I\end{pmatrix}$ and multiply out $P^{\mathsf T}MP$. It is block diagonal with the stated Schur complement. Multiplicativity and the unitriangular determinant $1$ give $\det M=\det A\det(C-B^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}B)$.

items.title: Sylvester's criterion: a real symmetric $n\times n$ matrix with $n\geq1$ is positive definite if and only if all leading principal minors are positive
items.strategy: If the form is positive definite, each restriction to the first $k$ coordinate subspace is positive definite; its inertia is $(k,0,0)$, so diagonal normalization makes its determinant positive. Conversely induct on $n$. The first minor gives $a_{11}>0$; Schur-complement factorization shows that every leading principal minor of the Schur complement is the next leading minor divided by $a_{11}$ and is positive. Induction makes the complement positive definite, and its congruent direct sum with the positive one-dimensional block makes the original matrix positive definite.

pages.title: Dual Spaces and Bilinear Forms: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: A dual basis and transpose computed for a linear map on $\mathbb F_3^2$
items.strategy: Use the standard basis and its coordinate functionals over $\mathbb F_3$. For the map with matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, evaluate the transpose on both coordinate functionals and recover the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$.

items.title: The annihilator of the coordinate plane $z=0$ in $\mathbb R^3$ is the line spanned by the third coordinate functional
items.strategy: Write a general functional as $a x^*+b y^*+c z^*$. Vanishing at $(1,0,0)$ and $(0,1,0)$ forces $a=b=0$, while every multiple of $z^*$ vanishes on the plane; the dimensions also verify the annihilator formula.

items.title: For the polynomial space $F[x]$, the canonical map to the algebraic double dual is injective but not surjective
items.strategy: Use the infinite Hamel basis $1,x,x^2,\ldots$. Its coordinate functionals span a proper subspace of $F[x]^*$; separate from that span the functional taking value $1$ on every basis monomial, producing a double-dual functional that vanishes on all coordinate functionals but not on that functional. No evaluation at a polynomial has those values, so the constructed double-dual element is outside the canonical image.

items.title: In infinite dimension, distinct subspaces of $V^*$ can have the same preannihilator
items.strategy: Fix an infinite Hamel basis $B$ and let $\Phi$ be the proper span of its coordinate functionals. Every nonzero vector has a nonzero coordinate, so ${}^\circ\Phi=\{0\}$. Functionals separate nonzero vectors, so ${}^\circ(V^*)=\{0\}$ as well, yet $\Phi\neq V^*$ by the infinite dual-family theorem. This shows why the finite-dimensional symmetric double-annihilator claim cannot be asserted for arbitrary subspaces of $V^*$.

items.title: The form on $\mathbb R^2$ with matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ is neither symmetric nor alternating
items.strategy: Evaluate on the standard basis: $B(e_1,e_2)=1$ but $B(e_2,e_1)=0$, so symmetry fails. Also $B(e_1+e_2,e_1+e_2)=1$, so alternation fails.

items.title: $q(x,y)=2x^2+4xy+5y^2=2(x+y)^2+3y^2$ has inertia $(2,0,0)$
items.strategy: Complete the square and record the invertible coordinate change $(u,v)=(x+y,y)$. Its matrix congruence changes $\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&5\end{pmatrix}$ to $\operatorname{diag}(2,3)$; positive rescaling then gives $I_2$, so the inertia is $(2,0,0)$.

items.title: A rank-two alternating form on $\mathbb R^3$ has one symplectic pair and a one-dimensional radical
items.strategy: Use the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\-1&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$. The first two standard vectors are a symplectic pair, the third spans the radical, and direct row inspection gives rank two, matching the normal-form theorem.

items.title: In characteristic $2$, a symmetric bilinear form need not have an orthogonal basis
items.strategy: On $\mathbb F_2^2$ take the nondegenerate alternating form with matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. It is symmetric in characteristic two and every vector has self-pairing zero. An orthogonal basis would therefore make every matrix entry zero, contradicting nondegeneracy.

items.title: In characteristic $2$, distinct quadratic forms can have the same polar form
items.strategy: On $\mathbb F_2^2$, compare $q_0(x,y)=0$ and $q_1(x,y)=x^2$. They are distinct, but direct expansion gives $b_{q_0}=0=b_{q_1}$ because $(x+u)^2=x^2+u^2$ in characteristic two. Thus polarization is not injective without the hypothesis that $2$ is invertible.

items.title: Positive determinant does not imply positive definiteness
items.strategy: The real diagonal matrix $\operatorname{diag}(-1,-1,1)$ has determinant $1>0$, but its quadratic form takes the negative value $-1$ at the first standard vector. Its inertia is $(1,2,0)$, showing why a single determinant cannot replace all leading principal minors.

items.title: Sylvester's criterion verifies positive definiteness for a concrete symmetric $3\times3$ matrix
items.strategy: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\1&2&1\\0&1&2\end{pmatrix}$, compute the leading principal minors $2$, $3$, and $4$. All are positive, so the criterion proves positive definiteness; an explicit completion of squares supplies an independent check.

items.title: Congruence need not preserve trace or determinant: the real $1\times1$ matrices $[1]$ and $[4]$ are congruent
items.strategy: With $P=[2]$, direct multiplication gives $P^{\mathsf T}[1]P=[4]$. Their traces and determinants are respectively $1$ and $4$, so neither quantity is a congruence invariant even though rank, nondegeneracy, and inertia are.

pages.title: Inner Product Spaces, Gram-Schmidt, Projections and Adjoints

items.title: Real and complex inner product spaces, with the inner product linear in the first argument
The norm $\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ induced by a real or complex inner product
The standard formulas $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{k<n}x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb R^n$ and $\sum_{k<n}x_k\overline{y_k}$ on $\mathbb C^n$ are inner products
items.strategy: Use finite additive-monoid sums and conjugation laws. The diagonal is a sum of squared moduli and vanishes only coordinatewise; at $n=0$ positive definiteness is vacuous.

items.title: Inner products separate vectors, and the induced norm is homogeneous: $\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert$
items.strategy: Pair a vector with itself for nondegeneracy. For norm homogeneity compute squared norms and use uniqueness of the nonnegative square root.

items.title: Cauchy–Schwarz: $|\langle u,v\rangle|\leq\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert$, with equality exactly for linearly dependent vectors
items.strategy: Separate $v=0$; otherwise expand the length of $u-\langle u,v\rangle\langle v,v\rangle^{-1}v$. Derive the squared inequality, take nonnegative roots, and prove both equality directions with symmetric dependence.

items.title: The inner-product norm is definite, homogeneous, and satisfies the triangle inequality
items.strategy: Use positive definiteness and homogeneity; expand the squared norm of $u+v$, bound the cross term by Cauchy–Schwarz, and compare nonnegative square roots. Do not cite the later generic norm definition.

items.title: Pythagoras, the parallelogram identity, and the real and complex polarisation identities
items.strategy: Expand squared lengths. Orthogonality removes cross terms; add or combine the expansions to obtain the parallelogram and the separate real and complex polarisation formulas compatible with linearity in the first variable.

items.title: On $\mathbb R^n$, abstract Cauchy–Schwarz is exactly the published finite-sum Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
items.strategy: Substitute the standard coordinate formulas and match the inequality and symmetric equality condition term for term, including the empty list.

items.title: Orthogonal vectors and subspaces, orthogonal and orthonormal sets, and orthonormal bases
The orthogonal complement $W^\perp=\{v:\langle v,w\rangle=0\text{ for all }w\in W\}$
Every finite orthogonal list of nonzero vectors is linearly independent
items.strategy: Pair a vanishing linear combination with each listed vector; orthogonality removes every other term. Include the empty and singleton lists.

items.title: Gram–Schmidt turns every finite independent list into an orthonormal list with the same successive spans
items.strategy: Induct, subtract projections onto earlier orthonormal vectors, prove the residual orthogonal and nonzero, then normalise. Prove both inclusions of every successive-span equality, starting with the empty list.

items.title: Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis
items.strategy: Choose a finite basis and apply Gram–Schmidt; dimension zero uses the empty basis.

items.title: Bessel's inequality for a finite orthonormal list and Parseval's identity for an orthonormal basis
items.strategy: Set $p=\sum_i\langle v,e_i\rangle e_i$, show $v-p$ is orthogonal to the list, and apply Pythagoras. Equality means $v$ lies in the span; for a basis obtain coordinate, inner-product, and squared-length Parseval formulas. Include the empty list.

items.title: For a subspace $W$ of a finite-dimensional inner product space, $V=W\oplus W^\perp$
items.strategy: Choose a basis of $W$, extend it to $V$, and apply Gram–Schmidt with the flag clause. The remaining orthonormal vectors span a subspace of $W^\perp$; positive definiteness makes the intersection zero. Include $W=0,V$.

items.title: In finite dimension, $W^{\perp\perp}=W$ and $\dim W+\dim W^\perp=\dim V$
items.strategy: Use conjugate symmetry for inclusion, orthogonal decomposition for dimensions, and equal finite dimensions for equality. Include $W=0,V$.

items.title: The orthogonal projection $P_Wv$ is the $W$-component in $V=W\oplus W^\perp$
Orthogonal projection is linear, and an orthonormal basis $(e_i)$ of $W$ gives $P_Wv=\sum_i\langle v,e_i\rangle e_i$
items.strategy: The displayed vector lies in $W$ and leaves an orthogonal error, so direct-sum uniqueness identifies it. Prove linearity and record range, kernel, idempotence, and $I-P_W=P_{W^\perp}$.

items.title: The orthogonal projection is the unique nearest point in the subspace
items.strategy: For $w\in W$, decompose $v-w=(v-P_Wv)+(P_Wv-w)$ orthogonally and apply Pythagoras; equality forces $w=P_Wv$.

items.title: The Gram matrix $G(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})=(\langle v_i,v_j\rangle)_{i,j<r}$ and Gram determinant, with empty value $1$
A Gram determinant is nonnegative and is positive exactly when the vector list is linearly independent
items.strategy: Dependence gives a kernel vector. For an independent list, Gram–Schmidt and the linear-first convention give $G=R^{\mathsf T}\overline R$ with nonzero triangular diagonal, so $\det G=|\det R|^2>0$. The empty Gram determinant is $1$.

items.title: Every invertible real or complex square matrix has a unique factorisation $A=QR$ with $Q$ orthogonal or unitary and $R$ upper triangular with positive real diagonal
items.strategy: Apply flag-preserving Gram–Schmidt to the columns. For uniqueness, $Q_1^*Q_2=R_1R_2^{-1}$ is unitary and upper triangular with positive diagonal, hence identity by induction. Include $0\times0$.

items.title: Finite-dimensional Riesz representation: every functional is uniquely $v\mapsto\langle v,w\rangle$
items.strategy: In an orthonormal basis set $w=\sum_i\overline{f(e_i)}e_i$ and verify the formula. Nondegeneracy gives uniqueness; $w\mapsto\langle\,\cdot\,,w\rangle$ is a conjugate-linear bijection, including dimension zero.

items.title: The adjoint $T^*:W\to V$ is characterised by $\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$
Every linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces has a unique adjoint
items.strategy: For fixed $w$, apply finite Riesz to $v\mapsto\langle Tv,w\rangle$. Uniqueness of representatives proves linearity in $w$ and uniqueness of the map.

items.title: Adjoints satisfy $(S+T)^*=S^*+T^*$, $(\lambda T)^*=\overline\lambda T^*$, $(ST)^*=T^*S^*$, and $T^{**}=T$
items.strategy: Pair candidate sides with arbitrary vectors, use the defining identity and linear-first convention, and invoke uniqueness. Track conjugation in the scalar clause.

items.title: In orthonormal bases, the matrix of the adjoint is the conjugate transpose of the matrix
items.strategy: If $a_{ij}=\langle Te_j,f_i\rangle$, the adjoint identity gives the reverse entry $\overline{a_{ij}}$. Include zero-sized bases.

items.title: $\ker T^*=(\operatorname{im}T)^\perp$ and $\operatorname{im}T^*=(\ker T)^\perp$ in finite dimension
items.strategy: Unpack the adjoint identity for the first equality. Apply it to $T^*$, use $T^{**}=T$, and take finite-dimensional double orthogonal complements for the second.

items.title: For a linear map $T:V\to W$ between finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, $x$ minimises $\lVert Tx-b\rVert$ if and only if $T^*(Tx-b)=0$, equivalently $T^*Tx=T^*b$; minimisers exist and any two differ by an element of $\ker T$
items.strategy: The unique nearest point to $b$ in $\operatorname{im}T$ is $P_{\operatorname{im}T}b$, and it has a preimage, so minimisers exist. A vector $x$ is a minimiser exactly when $b-Tx\perp\operatorname{im}T$. The adjoint kernel–range identity converts this condition into $T^*(b-Tx)=0$, which is the normal equation. Finally two minimisers have the same image under $T$, so their difference lies in $\ker T$, and adding a kernel vector preserves the residual.

items.title: If $W$ is $T$-invariant, then $W^\perp$ is $T^*$-invariant
items.strategy: For $v\in W^\perp,w\in W$, use conjugate symmetry and the adjoint identity to rewrite $\langle T^*v,w\rangle$ in terms of $Tw\in W$.

items.title: An endomorphism is an orthogonal projection exactly when it is idempotent and self-adjoint
items.strategy: Projection formulas give both properties. Conversely decompose $v=Pv+(I-P)v$; idempotence places the terms in image and kernel, and self-adjointness makes those subspaces orthogonal. Include $0,I$.

items.title: Linear isometries, and orthogonal or unitary operators on finite-dimensional inner product spaces
For an endomorphism in finite dimension, preserving lengths, preserving inner products, carrying orthonormal bases to orthonormal bases, and $T^*T=I$ are equivalent
items.strategy: Use polarisation, test orthonormal bases, and expand in one. From $T^*T=I$, multiplicativity gives $\det(T^*)\det(T)=1$, so $T$ is invertible, $T^{-1}=T^*$, and $TT^*=I$. Include dimension zero.

items.title: Orthogonal and unitary operators form groups, and their determinants have modulus one
items.strategy: Adjoint identities give the group laws. Take determinants in $T^*T=I$ and use the conjugate-transpose matrix formula to get $\overline{\det T}\det T=1$; over $\mathbb R$, $\det T=\pm1$. Include dimension zero.

pages.title: Inner Product Spaces and Orthogonality: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Positive coordinate weights define an inner product and change lengths and projections
items.strategy: For positive weights, verify the weighted coordinate form, including the empty space; in $\mathbb R^2$ use unequal weights to compare a length and projection with the standard form.

items.title: The Frobenius inner product on a real or complex matrix space
items.strategy: Define the pairing as the finite sum of entrywise products, conjugating the second matrix over the complex field. Verify the inner-product axioms and identify the associated squared length with the sum of squared entry moduli, including zero-sized shapes.

items.title: Evaluation at four distinct real points gives an inner product on polynomials of degree at most three
items.strategy: A zero diagonal sum forces four roots; the root bound makes the degree-at-most-three polynomial zero. This is a finite algebraic substitute for an integral example.

items.title: Gram–Schmidt on an explicit basis of $\mathbb R^3$
items.strategy: Apply the algorithm to $(1,1,1),(0,1,2),(1,0,2)$; display residuals, normalisations, and each successive-span equality.

items.title: Gram–Schmidt on an explicit basis of $\mathbb C^2$ with conjugation visible
items.strategy: Use vectors with a nonreal cross inner product; compute the linear-first projection coefficient, residual, normalisation, and both off-diagonal pairings.

items.title: A worked QR factorisation of an invertible real matrix
items.strategy: Apply Gram–Schmidt directly to the chosen matrix columns, assemble $Q,R$, and check $A=QR$ with positive diagonal.

items.title: Bessel's inequality is strict for a vector outside the span of a proper orthonormal set
items.strategy: In $\mathbb R^3$ use $(e_0,e_1)$ and a vector with nonzero $e_2$ component; compute the positive gap as the squared orthogonal remainder.

items.title: Projection onto a plane in $\mathbb R^3$ and the nearest-point calculation
items.strategy: Compute $P_Wv$ from an orthonormal plane basis, verify the residual is orthogonal, and write the Pythagorean comparison with every other point.

items.title: The Riesz representative of an explicit functional on $\mathbb C^3$
items.strategy: For $f(z)=\sum a_kz_k$, compute the representative $(\overline{a_0},\overline{a_1},\overline{a_2})$ and check the conjugate-linear dependence.

items.title: The adjoint of an explicit map $\mathbb C^2\to\mathbb C^3$ is its conjugate-transpose matrix
items.strategy: Choose nonreal entries, form the $2\times3$ conjugate transpose, and verify the adjoint identity on generic coordinates.

items.title: The Gram determinant of two vectors detects dependence and measures the squared planar area
items.strategy: Compute $\lVert u\rVert^2\lVert v\rVert^2-|\langle u,v\rangle|^2$, give independent and dependent examples, and identify vanishing with equality in Cauchy–Schwarz.

items.title: A nondegenerate indefinite symmetric form can have $W\cap W^\perp\ne0$
items.strategy: For $B(x,y)=x_0y_0-x_1y_1$ and $v=(1,1)$, the matrix is invertible but $B(v,v)=0$, so the nonzero line $W=\mathbb Rv$ lies in $W^\perp$.

items.title: FALSE: Every complex inner product satisfies $\langle u,v\rangle=\langle v,u\rangle$
items.strategy: In standard $\mathbb C$, $\langle i,1\rangle=i$ while $\langle1,i\rangle=-i$; conjugate symmetry is the correct law.

items.title: FALSE: Every orthogonal set is an orthonormal basis
items.strategy: The singleton $(2,0)$ in $\mathbb R^2$ is orthogonal but neither normalised nor spanning; the empty set also exposes the spanning boundary.

items.title: FALSE: Every idempotent endomorphism of an inner product space is an orthogonal projection
items.strategy: For $P=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{psmallmatrix}$, $P^2=P$ but $P^{\mathsf T}\ne P$ and its kernel is not orthogonal to its image.

items.title: FALSE: On a complex inner product space, $(\lambda T)^*=\lambda T^*$ for every scalar
items.strategy: Take $T=I$ and $\lambda=i$: $(iI)^*=-iI$, exposing the conjugate scalar forced by the convention.

pages.title: Algebraic Extensions, the Degree of an Extension, and Finite Fields

items.title: The degree $[K:F]=\dim_F K$ of a finite field extension
A finite extension has degree one if and only if the two fields are equal
items.strategy: If the degree is one, the nonzero vector $1$ is a basis, so every element of $K$ is a scalar multiple of $1$ and lies in $F$. Conversely $F/F$ has basis $\{1\}$.

items.title: Products of bases form a basis in a tower of finite extensions
items.strategy: For bases $u_1,\ldots,u_m$ of $K/F$ and $v_1,\ldots,v_n$ of $L/K$, expand first in the $v_j$ and then each coefficient in the $u_i$ to prove spanning by $u_iv_j$. Reverse coefficient comparison to prove independence.

items.title: Tower law for finite extensions: $[L:F]=[L:K][K:F]$
items.strategy: Choose finite bases for $K/F$ and $L/K$. Their products form a basis of $L/F$ indexed by the Cartesian product, so its size is the product of the two sizes. All displayed degrees are finite-dimensional degrees.

items.title: The degree of an intermediate field divides the degree of a finite extension
items.strategy: For $F\subseteq K\subseteq L$ with $L/F$ finite, obtain finite bases for the subextensions from finite spanning sets and apply $[L:F]=[L:K][K:F]$.

items.title: Every finite field extension is algebraic
items.strategy: If $[K:F]=n$, then $1,a,\ldots,a^n$ are $n+1$ vectors in a space spanned by an $n$-element basis and are dependent. The resulting nontrivial relation is a nonzero polynomial over $F$ vanishing at $a$.

items.title: An element is algebraic over $F$ if and only if its simple extension $F(a)/F$ is finite
items.strategy: The forward implication is the published quotient-and-power-basis theorem. The reverse implication applies finite-implies-algebraic to $F(a)/F$ and selects $a$.

items.title: Finitely generated field extensions $F(a_1,\ldots,a_r)$
An extension generated by finitely many algebraic elements is finite
items.strategy: Build the tower obtained by adjoining one generator at a time. Each step is finite because its generator stays algebraic over the larger base. Repeatedly apply the tower law; the empty generating list has degree one.

items.title: The elements of an extension algebraic over the base field form a subfield
items.strategy: For algebraic $a,b$, the field $F(a,b)$ is finite over $F$. Its elements, including $a-b$, $ab$, and $a^{-1}$ when $a\ne0$, are algebraic. Verify zero and one and apply the subfield criterion.

items.title: The relative algebraic closure of $F$ in an extension $K$
Algebraicity is transitive in towers of field extensions
items.strategy: For $a$ algebraic over $K$, take one polynomial over $K$ that it satisfies. Its finitely many coefficients generate a finite extension $M/F$; adjoining $a$ is finite over $M$. The tower law makes $M(a)/F$ finite, hence $a$ algebraic over $F$.

items.title: The relative algebraic closure of $F$ in $K$ has no further algebraic elements inside $K$
items.strategy: If $A$ is the subfield of elements algebraic over $F$ and $b\in K$ is algebraic over $A$, then $A(b)/A$ and $A/F$ are algebraic. Transitivity makes $b$ algebraic over $F$, so $b\in A$.

items.title: For finite subextensions in a common field, $[EE':F]\le [E:F][E':F]$
items.strategy: Products of bases of $E/F$ and $E'/F$ span the generated ring. Algebraicity reduces inverses by minimal polynomials, so this ring is the compositum. Extract a basis from the product spanning set to obtain the bound.

items.title: The prime subfield as the intersection of all subfields
The characteristic of a field is zero or a prime number
items.strategy: The characteristic is not one. If a positive characteristic $n$ were composite, write $n=ab$ with $1<a,b<n$. Minimality makes $a1_F$ and $b1_F$ nonzero, while their product is $n1_F=0$, contradicting the domain property.

items.title: A field's prime subfield is isomorphic to $\mathbb Q$ in characteristic zero and to $\mathbb F_p$ in characteristic $p$
items.strategy: In characteristic $p$, map $[n]$ in $\mathbb Z/p$ to $n1_F$. In characteristic zero, extend the injective integer map by $a/b\mapsto(a1_F)(b1_F)^{-1}$. Each image is a subfield contained in every subfield.

items.title: The binomial theorem over an arbitrary commutative ring
items.strategy: Induct on $n$. Multiply the previous expansion by $x+y$, reindex the two finite sums, and use Pascal's identity. Coefficients are repeated additions, never quotients, so positive characteristic is included.

items.title: A prime $p$ divides $\binom pk$ for $0<k<p$
items.strategy: Use $k\binom pk=p\binom{p-1}{k-1}$. Since $p$ does not divide $k$, Euclid's lemma forces $p$ to divide the binomial coefficient. Keep the endpoint coefficients outside the claim.

items.title: Frobenius $x\mapsto x^p$ is an injective endomorphism in characteristic $p$, and an automorphism for finite fields
items.strategy: The ring binomial theorem gives $(x+y)^p=x^p+y^p$ because the intermediate coefficients vanish. Powers give multiplicativity. The kernel is zero in a field; on a finite field injectivity gives bijectivity. The $n$-fold iterate is $x\mapsto x^{p^n}$.

items.title: Finite fields and their order
Every finite field has order $p^n$ for a unique prime characteristic $p$ and positive integer $n$
items.strategy: The prime subfield has $p$ elements. The finite underlying set spans the field over it and contains a basis of size $n\ge1$. Coordinates identify the field with the functions from an $n$-set to a $p$-set, hence it has $p^n$ elements. Record uniqueness.

items.title: The multiplicative group $\mathbb F_q^\times$ of a finite field is cyclic
items.strategy: A field is an integral domain and its nonzero elements are its units. Apply the published theorem that every finite subgroup of a domain's unit group is cyclic to the whole finite unit group. Its proof already supplies the root-bound and finite-abelian-structure argument.

items.title: In characteristic $p$, the roots of $x^{p^n}-x$ form a subfield and are all simple
items.strategy: Iterated Frobenius proves closure under subtraction and multiplication; zero and one are roots, and inverses follow from $a^q=a$. The derivative is $qx^{q-1}-1=-1$, so the roots are simple. Require $n\ge1$.

items.title: For every prime $p$ and $n\ge1$, a field with $p^n$ elements exists
items.strategy: Take a splitting field of $x^{p^n}-x$ over $\mathbb F_p$. Its roots form a subfield and generate the splitting field, hence are the whole field. Simplicity and the degree show that there are exactly $p^n$ roots.

items.title: A field with $q$ elements is the splitting field of $x^q-x$ over its prime subfield
items.strategy: Cyclicity gives $a^{q-1}=1$ for every nonzero $a$, and zero also satisfies $a^q=a$. Thus all $q$ elements are roots of the degree-$q$ polynomial, and they generate the field.

items.title: Finite fields of the same order are isomorphic
items.strategy: Two fields of order $q=p^n$ have isomorphic prime subfields and are splitting fields of $x^q-x$ over them. Transport the base copy and apply splitting-field uniqueness. Do not claim the isomorphism is unique.

items.title: The subfields of $\mathbb F_{p^n}$ are the unique fields $\mathbb F_{p^d}$ for positive divisors $d$ of $n$
items.strategy: A subfield has order $p^d$ and the tower law forces $d\mid n$. Conversely the roots of $x^{p^d}-x$ inside $\mathbb F_{p^n}$ form a subfield with $p^d$ elements when $d\mid n$. Any subfield of that order has the same root set.

items.title: Over $\mathbb F_q$, $x^{q^n}-x$ is the product of all monic irreducibles whose degrees divide $n$
items.strategy: In the splitting field, an irreducible of degree $d$ contributes roots exactly when their simple extension is the subfield with $q^d$ elements, equivalent to $d\mid n$. The derivative is $-1$, so factors occur once. Normalize them to be monic.

items.title: For every finite field $\mathbb F_q$ and every $n\ge1$, a monic irreducible polynomial of degree $n$ exists
items.strategy: Choose a generator of $\mathbb F_{q^n}^{\times}$. If its minimal polynomial had degree $d<n$, the element would lie in a subfield with at most $q^d-1$ nonzero elements, contradicting its order $q^n-1$.

items.title: Every finite extension of a finite field is simple
items.strategy: Coordinates make the extension finite as a set. A generator of its cyclic multiplicative group, together with zero, lies in and exhausts the subfield it generates.

items.title: Algebraically constructible real numbers as the smallest real subfield closed under positive square roots
A real number is algebraically constructible exactly when it lies in a finite tower of real quadratic adjunctions
items.strategy: The union of all finite towers from $\mathbb Q$ obtained by adjoining positive square roots is a subfield: combine two towers by appending their generators. It is square-root closed, and minimality gives equality with the constructible field.

items.title: An algebraically constructible real algebraic number has degree over $\mathbb Q$ equal to a power of two
items.strategy: Place the number in a finite quadratic tower. The top degree is a power of two by the tower law, and the simple subextension degree divides it. Unique prime factorization makes that divisor a power of two.

items.title: The real cube root of two is algebraic but not algebraically constructible
items.strategy: Eisenstein at $2$ makes $x^3-2$ irreducible, so the simple extension has degree three. Since three is not a power of two, the constructible-degree obstruction applies.

pages.title: Algebraic Extensions and Finite Fields: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)/\mathbb Q$ has degree two
items.strategy: Prove $x^2-2$ irreducible and apply the simple-extension theorem for basis $1,\sqrt2$ and degree two. Display two-coordinate arithmetic.

items.title: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]{2})/\mathbb Q$ has degree three
items.strategy: Eisenstein at $2$ proves irreducibility of $x^3-2$. The quotient-and-power-basis theorem gives basis $1,a,a^2$.

items.title: $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt3)$ has degree four and equals $\mathbb Q(\sqrt2+\sqrt3)$
items.strategy: Use the tower law and compare coordinates to get degree four. For $a=\sqrt2+\sqrt3$, compute $a^{-1}=\sqrt3-\sqrt2$ and recover both roots. Verify the four-element product basis.

items.title: The relative algebraic closure of $\mathbb R$ in $\mathbb C$ is all of $\mathbb C$
items.strategy: Every $a+bi$ satisfies the nonzero real polynomial $(x-a)^2+b^2$, so every complex number is algebraic over the reals.

items.title: $\mathbb F_4=\mathbb F_2[t]/(t^2+t+1)$ with complete addition and multiplication tables
items.strategy: Check the quadratic has no root in $\mathbb F_2$, list $0,1,a,a+1$, reduce by $a^2=a+1$, compute both tables, and verify the three nonzero elements form a cyclic group.

items.title: $\mathbb F_8=\mathbb F_2[t]/(t^3+t+1)$ and its power table
items.strategy: Test zero and one to prove the cubic irreducible, list the eight power-basis elements, reduce by $a^3=a+1$, and compute powers through $a^7=1$.

items.title: $\mathbb F_9=\mathbb F_3[t]/(t^2+1)$ and a generator of its multiplicative group
items.strategy: Check that $-1$ is not a square in $\mathbb F_3$, list the nine elements, and find an element of order eight. Contrast it with the residue class of $t$, which has order four.

items.title: Frobenius on $\mathbb F_4$ swaps the two non-prime-field elements
items.strategy: Rebuild $\mathbb F_4$ as $\mathbb F_2[t]/(t^2+t+1)$ and write $a$ for the residue class of $t$. Using $a^2=a+1$, compute the squares of all four elements. Frobenius fixes $\mathbb F_2$, exchanges $a$ and $a+1$, and its square is the identity.

items.title: The subfields of $\mathbb F_{64}$ have orders $2,4,8,64$
items.strategy: Since $64=2^6$, apply the lattice theorem to divisors $1,2,3,6$ and identify each unique subfield as a Frobenius root set.

items.title: The residue class of $t$ generates $\mathbb F_8^\times$
items.strategy: Rebuild $\mathbb F_8$ as $\mathbb F_2[t]/(t^3+t+1)$ and write $a$ for the residue class of $t$. Reduce powers by $a^3=a+1$ to show $1,a,\ldots,a^6$ are the seven distinct nonzero elements and $a^7=1$. No primitive-root definition from the other run batch is used.

items.title: An algebraic extension need not be finite
items.strategy: Inside $\mathbb R$, take the union of $\mathbb Q(2^{1/2^m})$. Every element lies in a finite algebraic stage, but the stage degrees $2^m$ are unbounded; a finite total degree would be divisible by all of them.

items.title: There is no field with six elements
items.strategy: A finite-field order is a prime power, and six is no positive power of any prime. A six-element ring may exist, but not a field.

items.title: FALSE: $\mathbb F_{p^n}$ is the ring $\mathbb Z/p^n\mathbb Z$
items.strategy: For $p=2,n=2$, the finite-field existence theorem supplies a field with four elements, while $\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$ has the nonzero nilpotent class $[2]$ and is not a field. Equal cardinality does not determine ring structure.

items.title: FALSE: degrees add in a tower of finite field extensions
items.strategy: Use $\mathbb F_2\subset\mathbb F_4\subset\mathbb F_{64}$. The step degrees are two and three, while the total degree is six, not five; the tower law gives the product.

items.title: Unital left and right modules over a ring; unqualified module means left module
In a module, $0_Rm=0_M$, $r0_M=0_M$, $(-r)m=-(rm)$ and $r(-m)=-(rm)$
items.strategy: direct

The one-step submodule criterion; intersections and sums of submodules are submodules

Annihilators, torsion elements and the torsion subset of a module
Quotient module $M/N$ with scalar multiplication on additive cosets
Module homomorphism and isomorphism, kernel, image and cokernel

items.title: The canonical map $M\to M/N$ is a surjective module homomorphism with kernel $N$; thus every submodule is a kernel

items.title: A module homomorphism vanishing on $N$ factors uniquely through $M/N$

items.strategy: direct

items.strategy: direct

items.strategy: direct

pages.title: Free Modules, Exact Sequences, Projective and Injective Modules

items.title: The direct sum of an indexed family of modules
Universal property of a direct sum of modules
items.strategy: For M=⊕_{i∈I}M_i with coordinate inclusions, send a finitely supported tuple to the finite sum of its prescribed component maps. Prove linearity, uniqueness from the coordinate decomposition, and the empty-family case M=0. No choice is used because each input has finite support.

items.title: The free module on a set and its standard basis
Universal property of the free module on a set
items.strategy: Identify R^(X) with the direct sum of copies of the regular module indexed by X. For a set map f:X→M, apply the direct-sum universal property to the maps r↦rf(x). Give the resulting finite-sum formula, prove uniqueness, and include X=∅ explicitly.

items.title: Every module is a quotient of a free module
items.strategy: Apply the free universal property to the identity set map on the underlying set of M. The induced map R^(M)→M sends e_m to m and is surjective because every m is in its image. This construction is canonical and choice-free.

items.title: Invariant basis number and the rank of a free module
Every nonzero commutative ring has invariant basis number for finite bases
items.strategy: An isomorphism R^m≅R^n and its inverse give rectangular matrices A,B with AB=I_n and BA=I_m. If n>m, expand det(AB) using multilinearity in the n columns: every term selects n columns of A from only m positions, so a column repeats and every term vanishes, contradicting det(I_n)=1≠0. Symmetry excludes m>n. This finite determinant proof is choice-free and does not use maximal ideals.

items.title: Exact sequences and short exact sequences of modules
The endpoints of a short exact sequence encode injectivity and surjectivity
items.strategy: Prove exactness of 0→A→B is equivalent to injectivity of A→B by identifying the kernel with zero; dually prove exactness of B→C→0 is equivalent to surjectivity by identifying the image with C. Combine these into the usual characterization of a short exact sequence.

items.title: Split short exact sequences, sections, and retractions
The splitting lemma for short exact sequences of modules
items.strategy: For 0→A--i→B--p→C→0, show a section s of p gives B=i(A)⊕s(C), construct a retraction r of i by decomposing b-s(p(b)), and obtain an isomorphism A⊕C→B, (a,c)↦i(a)+s(c). Conversely extract section and retraction from a direct-sum isomorphism. Prove every implication and uniqueness of the decomposition.

items.title: The abelian group $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N)$ and maps induced by pre- and postcomposition
Covariant and contravariant $\operatorname{Hom}$ are left exact
items.strategy: For 0→A→B→C exact, prove 0→Hom(X,A)→Hom(X,B)→Hom(X,C) exact by image/kernel factorization; for A→B→C→0 exact, prove 0→Hom(C,X)→Hom(B,X)→Hom(A,X) exact by factorization through the quotient. Carry out the elementwise well-definedness checks rather than invoking category theory.

items.title: The injective and surjective Four Lemmas
items.strategy: For a commutative diagram with exact rows A→B→C→D and A'→B'→C'→D', chase an element of ker(B→B') using surjectivity on A and injectivity on C to prove the injective version; reverse the chase using surjectivity on B and injectivity on D to prove the surjective version. State hypotheses adjacent to the relevant conclusion.

items.title: The Five Lemma for modules
items.strategy: In a commutative diagram of two exact five-term rows, apply the injective Four Lemma to the middle map using the left outer epimorphism and its neighboring isomorphisms, and the surjective Four Lemma using the right outer monomorphism and neighboring isomorphisms. State the standard weaker outer hypotheses as well as the all-four-isomorphisms corollary.

items.title: The Snake Lemma for modules
items.strategy: For a commutative diagram of short exact rows, define δ:ker(c)→coker(a) by lifting z through the top epimorphism, applying the middle vertical map, and lifting back through the bottom monomorphism. Prove independence of both lifts, linearity, and exactness at each of the six kernel/cokernel terms by a complete element chase; include the initial and terminal zero terms.

items.title: Projective modules and the lifting property
Free modules are projective, with the exact choice boundary
items.strategy: Given a surjection E→M and a map from a free module R^(X) to M, choose one preimage in E for each basis value and extend by the free universal property. For finite X, finite choice (provable in ZF) suffices; for arbitrary X, this is an application of full AC to the family of nonempty fibers. No countable-choice or dependent-choice principle is invoked as a separate hypothesis.

items.title: Equivalent characterizations of projective modules
items.strategy: Assuming AC where arbitrary free modules are used, prove equivalence of: the lifting property; every short exact sequence ending in P splits; P is a direct summand of a free module; and Hom_R(P,-) is exact. The first, second, and Hom-exactness equivalences are choice-free; P projective implies a free summand choice-free via the canonical free cover, while the reverse direction imports the arbitrary-free projectivity choice boundary.

items.title: Direct sums of projectives are projective, and module categories have enough projectives
items.strategy: Under AC, lift each component map from P_i through a fixed epimorphism and combine the lifts by the direct-sum universal property; this proves ⊕P_i projective. The canonical free cover R^(M)→M then gives enough projectives. Note that a finite direct sum needs only finite choice, while arbitrary families and arbitrary bases use full AC.

items.title: Injective modules and the extension property
Equivalent characterizations of injective modules
items.strategy: Prove equivalence of the extension property, splitting of every short exact sequence beginning in I, and exactness of Hom_R(-,I). Extend the identity along an embedding to obtain a retraction; use a split sequence to extend an arbitrary map; combine with contravariant Hom left exactness. These equivalences are choice-free.

items.title: Baer's criterion for injective modules
items.strategy: The forward implication is immediate by extending maps from left ideals R to R. Conversely, assume every map from a left ideal extends to R; partially order extensions of a given map N→I across submodules of M, use Zorn's lemma to obtain a maximal extension, and if its domain is not M use the left ideal {r:rx lies in the domain} to extend across one more generator, contradiction. This converse uses full AC through Zorn, not merely countable or dependent choice.

items.title: Divisible modules over an integral domain
Over a PID, injective modules are exactly divisible modules
items.strategy: For a PID R, injectivity extends the map rR→D sending r to d and produces x with rx=d, so injective implies divisible without choice. Conversely every ideal is rR and a map rR→D is determined by d=f(r); divisibility supplies x with rx=d, so Baer's criterion gives injectivity. Include R=Z as the abelian-group specialization. The converse inherits Baer's full-AC/Zorn boundary.

items.title: Every abelian group embeds in a divisible abelian group
items.strategy: Let F=Z^(A) map canonically onto A with kernel K. Embed F coordinatewise into the divisible group Q^(A), and map F/K into Q^(A)/K. The kernel is (F∩K)/K=0, while a quotient of a divisible group is divisible. Division of a finite-support tuple uses only finitely many explicit rational divisions, so this construction is choice-free; it also corrects Kleshchev's source typo calling the containing group free.

items.title: Products of injective modules are injective, with the exact choice boundary
items.strategy: For an embedding A→B and map A→∏_{i∈I}I_i, extend every coordinate map A→I_i to B→I_i and combine the extensions into a product map. Finite I needs only finite choice; an arbitrary index set uses full AC to choose one extension from each nonempty set of extensions. Conversely each factor is a direct summand of the product and injectivity passes to direct summands.

items.title: Coinduction sends injective abelian groups to injective modules
items.strategy: For a unital ring R and injective abelian group D, give Hom_Z(R,D) the left R-action (r·φ)(s)=φ(sr). Establish the natural bijection Hom_R(M,Hom_Z(R,D))≅Hom_Z(M,D) by evaluation at 1, with inverse g↦(m↦[r↦g(rm)]). Since the right side extends across subgroup inclusions, the left side does too, proving injectivity.

items.title: Module categories have enough injectives
items.strategy: First give the arbitrary-unital-ring coinduction proof: embed the underlying abelian group of M in a divisible (hence, under Baer, injective) group D, then send m to [r↦j(rm)] in Hom_Z(R,D), with evaluation at 1 proving injectivity. For commutative R, also record Stacks' functorial version: character dual (-)^∨=Hom_Z(-,Q/Z) is exact, evaluation M→M^∨∨ is injective, and dualizing the canonical free cover of M^∨ embeds it in J(M)≅∏R^∨; coinduction and the product theorem make J(M) injective. Full AC enters through Baer and arbitrary products, while the divisible-hull embedding itself is choice-free; countable or dependent choice is not separately used.

pages.title: Free Modules and Exact Sequences: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The standard basis and a universal map from $R^3$
items.strategy: Write e_1,e_2,e_3 explicitly and, for chosen m_1,m_2,m_3 in M, compute the unique linear map R^3→M as (r_1,r_2,r_3)↦r_1m_1+r_2m_2+r_3m_3. Verify uniqueness on the three basis vectors.

items.title: $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$ is generated but not free as a $\mathbb Z$-module for $n>1$
items.strategy: The residue of 1 generates. Every nonzero free abelian group has a basis element of infinite additive order, whereas every element of Z/nZ is killed by n. Thus generated does not imply free; include the n=1 zero-module boundary separately.

items.title: A regular module with bases of sizes one and two
items.strategy: Let V have countable basis e_0,e_1,… over a field and R=End(V). Define α_0,α_1 by embedding into even and odd coordinates and β_0,β_1 by the inverse projections, so β_iα_j=δ_ij and α_0β_0+α_1β_1=1. The left R-linear maps f↦(fα_0,fα_1) and (g,h)↦gβ_0+hβ_1 are inverse, proving _RR≅_RR^2 and rank failure.

items.title: $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ is projective but not free over $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$
items.strategy: Use the idempotent 3 in R=Z/6Z: R=3R⊕(1-3)R and 3R≅Z/2Z, so the module is a direct summand of the free module R and hence projective. It is not free because its cardinality 2 is not 6^n for any finite n, while an infinite-rank free module is infinite.

items.title: $0\to\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{\times2}\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z\to0$ does not split
items.strategy: Verify exactness directly. If the quotient map had a section, the image of the nonzero residue class would be an integer x with 2x=0 but x odd, impossible. Equivalently, any retraction r of multiplication by 2 would satisfy 2r(1)=1.

items.title: $0\to A\to A\oplus C\to C\to0$ is canonically split
items.strategy: Use inclusion a↦(a,0), projection (a,c)↦c, section c↦(0,c), and retraction (a,c)↦a. Verify exactness and both splitting identities, then identify the splitting-lemma isomorphism with the identity on A⊕C.

items.title: $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(-,\mathbb Z)$ need not preserve surjections on the right
items.strategy: Apply Hom_Z(-,Z) to the nonsplit sequence 0→Z--2→Z→Z/2→0. Since Hom(Z/2,Z)=0 and precomposition by ×2 acts as multiplication by 2 on Hom(Z,Z)≅Z, the resulting map Z→Z is not surjective. This pinpoints why Hom is left exact but not generally exact.

items.title: Every short exact sequence of modules splits
items.strategy: Refute with 0→Z--2→Z→Z/2→0, reproducing the one-line section obstruction inside this item rather than depending on another B-page item. Contrast with the exact projective-ending and injective-beginning criteria.

items.title: Every projective module is free
items.strategy: Reuse the construction—not the B-page item—of the ideal 3R in R=Z/6Z. The idempotent decomposition makes 3R projective, while cardinality rules out every possible free rank. This distinguishes direct summands of free modules from free modules themselves.

items.title: Every injective module is projective
items.strategy: Use Q/Z as a Z-module. It is divisible and hence injective. If it were projective, it would be a direct summand of a free abelian group; free abelian groups are torsion-free, as are their subgroups and direct summands, but Q/Z is nonzero torsion. Thus it is not projective.

Both verified published, strictly below order 106, absent from the prior closure (37 -> 39), and seam-free against all 11 run pairs.

items.title: Balanced maps from a right module and a left module, and bilinear maps over a commutative ring
The tensor product $M\otimes_R N$ from the additive group underlying the free $\mathbb Z$-module on $M\times N$, elementary tensors, and finite tensor sums
Universal property of the tensor product for balanced maps into abelian groups
items.strategy: Let $F=\mathbb Z^{(M\times N)}$ be the free $\mathbb Z$-module on $M\times N$, and regard its underlying additive group explicitly as the free abelian group on that set. View the target abelian group as a $\mathbb Z$-module, extend a balanced map uniquely to a $\mathbb Z$-linear map from $F$, check that it kills every generator of the relation subgroup $H$, and factor through $F/H$. Conversely compose a homomorphism out of $F/H$ with the elementary-tensor map. Prove the two assignments inverse and retain the empty and zero-module cases.

items.title: Tensor products are unique up to a unique isomorphism carrying elementary tensors to elementary tensors
items.strategy: Given two representing pairs, apply each universal property to the other's universal balanced map. Each composite fixes every elementary tensor, so uniqueness makes the composites identities. State uniqueness relative to the specified universal maps, which licenses the phrase 'the tensor product'.

items.title: Module homomorphisms induce tensor-product homomorphisms functorially
items.strategy: For a right-linear map $f:M\to M'$ and a left-linear map $g:N\to N'$, verify that $(m,n)\mapsto f(m)\otimes g(n)$ is balanced and invoke the universal property. Check identity and composition on elementary tensors, then use uniqueness; over a commutative ring record that the induced map is linear for the separately constructed module structure.

items.title: A formula on elementary tensors defines a homomorphism exactly when its underlying pairing is balanced
items.strategy: Restate the universal-property bijection as a descent test: a prescription $m\otimes n\mapsto b(m,n)$ extends precisely when $b$ is additive in each variable and balanced. Then give the mandatory failure: on $\mathbb Z\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z$, the prescription $q(m\otimes n)=m$ would send $2\otimes1=1\otimes2$ to both $2$ and $1$, so it is not well defined. Emphasize that checking a formula only on symbols is never enough.

items.title: $(S,R)$-bimodules and commuting left and right scalar actions
A commuting outer scalar action descends to a tensor product
items.strategy: If $M$ is a right $R$-module and $N$ an $(R,S)$-bimodule, use the universal property to define $(m\otimes n)s=m\otimes(ns)$ and check the right $S$-module axioms on elementary tensors. Prove the left-handed analogue and the compatibility needed for iterated tensor products. Each equality is forced by a balanced pairing, not by an unchecked symbol rule.

items.title: Associativity of tensor products for compatible bimodules
items.strategy: For a right $R$-module $M$, an $(R,S)$-bimodule $N$, and a left $S$-module $P$, construct $(M\otimes_RN)\otimes_SP\to M\otimes_R(N\otimes_SP)$ from $(m,n,p)\mapsto m\otimes(n\otimes p)$. Build the reverse map similarly. Prove both maps are defined through successive universal properties and check the composites on elementary tensors.

items.title: Over a commutative ring, $M\otimes_RN$ is an $R$-module with $r(m\otimes n)=(rm)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn)$
items.strategy: Keep this separate from the arbitrary-ring construction. For fixed $r$, descend $(m,n)\mapsto(rm)\otimes n$ through the universal property, use commutativity to verify balance, and check the module axioms on elementary tensors. The defining balance relation proves equality with $m\otimes(rn)$. Note explicitly that no such single $R$-action is asserted for an arbitrary noncommutative ring.

items.title: Symmetry and associativity isomorphisms for tensor products over a commutative ring
items.strategy: Descend $(m,n)\mapsto n\otimes m$ to obtain the symmetry isomorphism and make its square the identity by checking elementary tensors. Specialize balanced associativity to commutative-ring modules, verify $R$-linearity using the constructed module action, and state naturality of both isomorphisms.

items.title: The regular module is a tensor unit: $R\otimes_RN\cong N$ and $M\otimes_RR\cong M$
items.strategy: Send $r\otimes n$ to $rn$ and $m\otimes r$ to $mr$; balance makes both maps well defined. Their inverses send $n$ to $1\otimes n$ and $m$ to $m\otimes1$. Check both composites on elementary tensors and use the unit laws, including the zero ring and zero modules.

items.title: Finite iterated tensor products represent multilinear maps independently of parenthesization
items.strategy: Induct on the number of factors using the binary universal property and associativity. Take the empty tensor product to be $R$ and the one-factor tensor product to be the module itself; verify those two boundaries separately. Use the associativity isomorphisms to transport the representing map between parenthesizations and uniqueness to prove coherence for the comparison used here.

items.title: Tensor products commute with arbitrary direct sums
items.strategy: For an arbitrary family $(M_i)_{i\in I}$ over a commutative ring, construct the map from $(\bigoplus_iM_i)\otimes_RN$ by summing the coordinate tensor maps; finite support makes the sum legitimate. Construct the inverse from the family of maps $M_i\otimes_RN\to(\bigoplus_iM_i)\otimes_RN$. Use the two universal properties and check both composites on summands and elementary tensors. Include $I=\varnothing$.

items.title: The elementary tensors of two bases form the product basis of the tensor product
items.strategy: Identify free modules on basis sets $I$ and $J$ with direct sums of copies of $R$. Apply arbitrary direct-sum distributivity twice and the tensor-unit isomorphism to obtain $R^{(I)}\otimes_RR^{(J)}\cong R^{(I\times J)}$. Track the canonical generators to show that the resulting basis is exactly $(e_i\otimes f_j)_{(i,j)\in I\times J}$, including either empty basis.

items.title: $R^m\otimes_RR^n\cong R^{mn}$ with the product basis, and $\dim_F(V\otimes_FW)=\dim_FV\,\dim_FW$
items.strategy: Apply the product-basis theorem to the standard bases indexed by $m$ and $n$, and identify the product index set with $mn$. Over a field, apply this to finite bases of $V$ and $W$ and the published definition of dimension. Check $m=0$ or $n=0$ explicitly: both sides are the zero module and the product basis is empty.

items.title: The $R$-module $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,N)$ over a commutative ring
For finite-dimensional $V$, the canonical map $V^*\otimes_FW\to\operatorname{Hom}_F(V,W)$ is an isomorphism
items.strategy: Use evaluation to descend $(\phi,w)\mapsto[v\mapsto\phi(v)w]$. Choose a finite basis of $V$ with dual basis and send $T$ to the finite sum of dual-basis tensors with $T$ of the corresponding basis vectors. Check the two composites on basis vectors and elementary tensors; treat $V=0$ by the empty sum.

items.title: Under $\operatorname{End}_F(V)\cong V^*\otimes_FV$, tensor contraction is the trace
items.strategy: For a finite basis and its dual, identify a rank-one tensor $\phi\otimes v$ with the endomorphism $x\mapsto\phi(x)v$. Its matrix has trace $\phi(v)$. Extend linearly and use the finite-dimensional Hom-tensor isomorphism; verify the zero-dimensional case gives the zero map and trace zero.

items.title: Algebras over a commutative ring, central structure maps, and algebra homomorphisms
The tensor product of $R$-algebras has multiplication $(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')=aa'\otimes bb'$
items.strategy: For algebras whose commutative base ring acts centrally, use the finite multilinear universal property to descend the four-variable multiplication formula, and separately descend $r\mapsto r(1\otimes1)$ for the structure map. Verify associativity, distributivity, and the identity $1\otimes1$ on elementary tensors; if both factors are commutative, so is the result. The descent guard supplies well-definedness before any ring-law computation.

items.title: Universal mapping property of the tensor product of commutative algebras
items.strategy: For $R$-algebra maps $f:A\to C$ and $g:B\to C$ with $C$ commutative, the pairing $(a,b)\mapsto f(a)g(b)$ is bilinear, so it induces $A\otimes_RB\to C$. Check multiplicativity and the identity on elementary tensors. Conversely any algebra map compatible with $a\mapsto a\otimes1$ and $b\mapsto1\otimes b$ is forced on $a\otimes b=(a\otimes1)(1\otimes b)$, proving uniqueness.

items.title: Hom-tensor adjunction: $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M\otimes_RN,P)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,P))$
items.strategy: Send $F$ to the curried map $m\mapsto[n\mapsto F(m\otimes n)]$ and reverse the construction by uncurrying an $R$-linear map into Hom. Verify additivity, balance, and $R$-linearity explicitly before applying the tensor universal property. Check the two constructions inverse on evaluations and state naturality in all three modules.

items.title: Tensoring is right exact
items.strategy: For an exact sequence $A\to B\to C\to0$ and a module $N$ over a commutative ring, prove surjectivity on elementary tensors by lifting their first factors. Quotient $B\otimes_RN$ by the image from $A\otimes_RN$ and construct the inverse map from $C\otimes_RN$ using a lift of $c$; exactness makes the value independent of the lift. The descent guard and universal property establish the map rigorously. Conclude equality of image and kernel without claiming injectivity at the left.

items.title: The submodule $IM$ generated by products of elements of an ideal $I$ with elements of a module $M$
$M\otimes_RR/I\cong M/IM$ naturally
items.strategy: Tensor the exact sequence $I\to R\to R/I\to0$ with $M$ and use the tensor-unit isomorphism to identify the middle term with $M$. Track $i\otimes m$ to $im$ so that the incoming image is exactly $IM$, then apply the quotient universal property. Record both the $R$-module and induced $R/I$-module interpretations and include $I=0$ and $I=R$.

items.title: Flat and faithfully flat modules and ring homomorphisms
Flatness is equivalent to preserving injections and to the ideal and finitely generated ideal tests
items.strategy: Show exactness implies preservation of injections by adjoining cokernels, and that injection preservation implies both ideal tests. For the finitely generated-ideal converse, reduce a kernel element, represented by a finite tensor sum, to finitely generated submodules and then to an inclusion into a finite free module. Prove injectivity for submodules of $R^n$ by induction on $n$, with the ideal test as the base case. Track $n=0$ and the zero ideal explicitly.

items.title: Every projective module over a commutative ring is flat
items.strategy: First use arbitrary direct-sum distributivity and the tensor-unit isomorphism to show every free module is flat. A projective module is a direct summand of its canonical free cover; tensoring preserves the splitting maps, so its tensor functor is a direct summand of an exact free-module tensor functor and therefore preserves injections. No choice is needed for projective implies flat.

items.title: Under the stated choice boundary, free modules are projective and hence flat
items.strategy: Invoke the published theorem that arbitrary free modules are projective under AC, with finite bases needing only finite choice and the empty basis needing none, then apply projective implies flat. Also note that flatness of a free module follows directly from tensor-unit and arbitrary direct-sum distributivity without AC; keep the two logical routes distinct.

items.title: For flat $M$, one has $IM\cap JM=(I\cap J)M$
items.strategy: Apply flatness to the injection $I\cap J\to R$ inside the exact sequence $0\to I\cap J\to R\to R/I\oplus R/J$. Identify the tensor of $R$ with $M$, use the quotient-tensor isomorphisms to identify the two quotient components, and compute the resulting kernel as $IM\cap JM$. Check $I=R$, $J=R$, and the zero ideal.

items.title: A short exact sequence with flat quotient remains short exact after tensoring
items.strategy: For $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ with $C$ flat, resolve the other tensor factor by a free cover and form the resulting three-by-three diagram. Right exactness supplies the rows and columns, tensoring with the free module gives an exact middle row, and flatness of $C$ gives the required injective outer map. Perform the elementary diagram chase explicitly rather than naming an unbuilt snake lemma.

items.title: Restriction of scalars and extension of scalars $S\otimes_RM$ along a ring homomorphism $R\to S$
Extension of scalars is left adjoint to restriction of scalars
items.strategy: For a ring map $R\to S$, an $R$-module $M$, and an $S$-module $N$, send an $S$-linear map $S\otimes_RM\to N$ to $m\mapsto F(1\otimes m)$. Conversely send an $R$-linear map $f:M\to N$ to $s\otimes m\mapsto sf(m)$, verify balance, and invoke the universal property. Check the two maps inverse and natural in both modules.

items.title: Change of rings: $N\otimes_RM\cong N\otimes_S(S\otimes_RM)$
items.strategy: For $R\to S$, a right $S$-module $N$, and a left $R$-module $M$, specialize bimodule associativity to the $(S,R)$-bimodule $S$ and use $N\otimes_SS\cong N$. Track the isomorphism on elementary tensors as $n\otimes m\mapsto n\otimes(1\otimes m)$ and its inverse $n\otimes(s\otimes m)\mapsto ns\otimes m$.

items.title: Extension of scalars carries flat modules to flat modules
items.strategy: For $R\to S$ and flat $M$ over $R$, rewrite $N\otimes_S(S\otimes_RM)$ as $N\otimes_RM$ by change of rings for every injection of right $S$-modules. Restriction of scalars preserves injectivity, so flatness over $R$ gives injectivity after tensoring; conclude $S\otimes_RM$ is flat over $S$.

items.title: Flatness is transitive under a flat change of rings
items.strategy: Let $R\to S$ be flat and let $N$ be flat over $S$. For an exact sequence of $R$-modules, first tensor with $S$ to retain exactness, then tensor the resulting $S$-sequence with $N$. Use change-of-rings associativity and the tensor-unit map to identify the composite with tensoring directly by the restricted $R$-module $N$. State the corresponding composition result for flat ring maps.

items.title: The character dual of a flat module is injective
items.strategy: Let $R$ be commutative, let $P$ be flat, and let $D$ be an injective abelian group. Give $P^+=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(P,D)$ the action $(r\phi)(p)=\phi(rp)$. Establish the natural bijection $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M,P^+)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(M\otimes_RP,D)$. Flatness turns a module injection into an injection after tensoring, and injectivity of $D$ extends the corresponding group homomorphism; transpose back to prove $P^+$ injective.

pages.title: Tensor Products of Modules — Examples

items.title: False: $\mathbb Z/m\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z/n$ is nonzero for all positive $m,n$
items.strategy: Use the quotient-tensor theorem to identify the tensor product with $(\mathbb Z/m)/n(\mathbb Z/m)$, then use Bezout to identify this quotient with $\mathbb Z/\gcd(m,n)$. The concrete choice $(m,n)=(2,3)$ gives the zero group and refutes the claim. Treat the convention $\mathbb Z/1=0$ explicitly.

items.title: $\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z/n=0$ for every positive $n$
items.strategy: Apply the quotient-tensor theorem with $M=\mathbb Q$ and $I=n\mathbb Z$. Multiplication by positive $n$ is surjective on $\mathbb Q$, so $n\mathbb Q=\mathbb Q$ and the quotient is zero. Do not use this statement at $n=0$.

items.title: $(R/I)\otimes_R(R/J)\cong R/(I+J)$ for ideals of a commutative ring
items.strategy: Apply the quotient-tensor theorem to $M=R/I$ and the ideal $J$. Identify $J(R/I)$ with $(I+J)/I$, and use the quotient-of-a-quotient isomorphism to obtain $R/(I+J)$. Include $I=R$, $J=R$, and both zero ideals.

items.title: $S\otimes_RR[x]\cong S[x]$ as $S$-algebras
items.strategy: For a homomorphism of commutative rings $R\to S$, send $s\otimes\sum_i r_ix^i$ to $\sum_i s f(r_i)x^i$. Descend the formula by the tensor universal property and verify multiplication using the tensor-product algebra law. Construct the inverse by sending each monomial coefficient $s x^i$ to $s\otimes x^i$ and use finite coefficient support to prove the composites are identities.

items.title: For a field extension $K/F$, one has $K\otimes_FM_n(F)\cong M_n(K)$ as $K$-algebras
items.strategy: Send $k\otimes(a_{ij})$ to $(k a_{ij})$ entrywise. The matrix units form an $F$-basis, so the tensor-basis theorem proves this is a $K$-module isomorphism; multiplication of matrix units proves it is a $K$-algebra isomorphism. Include $n=0$ under the library's empty-matrix convention and $n=1$ as the tensor-unit case.

items.title: For a field extension $K/F$, one has $K\otimes_FF^n\cong K^n$
items.strategy: Use extension of scalars together with the standard basis of $F^n$: the elements $1\otimes e_j$ form a $K$-basis by the product-basis theorem. Send $k\otimes(a_0,\ldots,a_{n-1})$ to $(ka_0,\ldots,ka_{n-1})$ and verify the inverse on the basis. Include $n=0$.

items.title: $\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C\cong\mathbb C\times\mathbb C$ as $\mathbb R$-algebras
items.strategy: Use the published real embedding and real basis $1,i$ of $\mathbb C$. Descend the bilinear map $z\otimes w\mapsto(zw,\overline z\,w)$, verify multiplicativity from the tensor-product algebra law, and compare the four real basis elements $1\otimes1$, $i\otimes1$, $1\otimes i$, $i\otimes i$ with their images to prove bijectivity. Exhibit the product idempotents as halves of $1\otimes1\mp i\otimes i$.

items.title: Tensoring the injection $k[x]\xrightarrow{\cdot x}k[x]$ with $k[x]/(x)$ gives the zero map
items.strategy: Multiplication by $x$ is injective because $k[x]$ is a domain. Identify each tensor product with $k[x]/(x)$ by the tensor-unit and quotient-tensor results. The induced map is multiplication by the class of $x$, hence zero, while the source is nonzero. This is the polynomial analogue of the integer counterexample.

items.title: False: $m\otimes n=0$ implies $m=0$ or $n=0$
items.strategy: In $\mathbb Z\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Z/2$, the nonzero factors $2$ and $\overline1$ satisfy $2\otimes\overline1=1\otimes2\overline1=0$. Use the unit isomorphism to confirm that $\mathbb Z\otimes\mathbb Z/2$ itself is nonzero, so the witness is not caused by a zero tensor-product group.

items.title: False: every element of $M\otimes_RN$ is an elementary tensor
items.strategy: For any field $F$, take bases $e_1,e_2$ of $F^2$ and $f_1,f_2$ of another copy. The tensor $e_1\otimes f_1+e_2\otimes f_2$ has coefficient matrix of rank two. If it were $(ae_1+be_2)\otimes(cf_1+df_2)$, coefficient comparison would give $ac=bd=1$ and $ad=bc=0$, an immediate contradiction in a field.

items.title: False: tensoring preserves injections
items.strategy: Start with the injection $\mathbb Z\xrightarrow{\cdot2}\mathbb Z$. Tensor with $\mathbb Z/2$ and identify both sides with $\mathbb Z/2$ using the unit isomorphism. The induced map is multiplication by $2$, hence zero and not injective. Place it beside right exactness to show precisely why tensoring is not left exact in general.

items.title: Nondecreasing, increasing (strictly increasing), nonincreasing, decreasing, monotone and strictly monotone real functions on a subset of $\mathbb{R}$, with the dictionary to monotone sequences

One-sided limits of a monotone function always exist: for $f$ nondecreasing on an interval $I$ and $c \in I$, $\lim_{x \to c^{-}} f(x) = \sup\{f(x) : x \in I,\ x < c\}$ whenever $I$ has points below $c$, $\lim_{x \to c^{+}} f(x) = \inf\{f(x) : x \in I,\ x > c\}$ whenever it has points above $c$, and these satisfy $\lim_{x \to c^{-}} f(x) \le f(c) \le \lim_{x \to c^{+}} f(x)$
items.strategy: direct

items.title: The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set

Carath\'eodory's characterisation: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ if and only if there is $\varphi : A \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, with $f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)$ for every $x \in A$, and then $\varphi(c) = f'(c)$

items.title: The linear-approximation form of the derivative: $f$ is differentiable at $c$ with $f'(c) = L$ if and only if the remainder $r(x) = f(x) - f(c) - L(x-c)$ satisfies $\lim_{x \to c} r(x)/(x-c) = 0$, so $L$ is the unique real for which the affine map $x \mapsto f(c) + L(x-c)$ approximates $f$ to first order

items.title: Sums, scalar multiples, products and quotients: $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$, $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$, $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$, and $(f/g)'(c) = \bigl(f'(c)g(c) - f(c)g'(c)\bigr)/g(c)^{2}$ when $g(c) \ne 0$

items.title: The chain rule, in one line from Carath\'eodory: if $g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $f$ is differentiable at $g(c)$, then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ with $(f \circ g)'(c) = f'(g(c))\,g'(c)$

items.title: Derivative of an inverse: if $f$ is continuous and injective on an interval $I$ and differentiable at $c \in I$ with $f'(c) \ne 0$, then the inverse $g$ is differentiable at $f(c)$ with $g'(f(c)) = 1/f'(c)$; and if $f'(c) = 0$ then $g$ is not differentiable at $f(c)$
