pages.title: The Riemann Integral in R^m and Jordan Content

items.title: Axis-parallel rectangles in $\mathbb R^m$ and their volume
items.strategy: Fix $m\geq1$. For vectors $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\leq b_j$, define $[a,b]=\{x:a_j\leq x_j\leq b_j\text{ for }j<m\}$ and $\operatorname{vol}([a,b])=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j)$. Call the rectangle nondegenerate when every inequality is strict. The finite product is the published recursive product, so volume exists; prove nonnegativity and the effect of a coordinate cut. State that at $m=1$ this is the published interval and its length.

items.title: Grid partitions of a rectangle in $\mathbb R^m$, their cells, refinements and mesh
items.strategy: A grid partition is a list of one-dimensional partitions indexed by $j<m$. Its cells are indexed by the multi-indices $i\in\mathbb N^m$ satisfying $i_j<n_j$, and each cell is the product of the corresponding subintervals. Define every sum over cells as an iterated finite sum, recursively in the $m$ coordinate index ranges; this avoids importing the finite-index-set sum from a page outside the fixed prerequisite closure. Define the mesh as the maximum coordinate subinterval length; by the norm/metric dictionary this is the $d_\infty$ diameter of the largest cell. Define coordinatewise refinement and common refinement, prove the cells cover the rectangle with disjoint interiors, and prove by induction on $m$ that the iterated sum of cell volumes is the rectangle volume. No multidimensional partition or sum may be left as an informal picture.

items.title: Lower and upper Darboux sums over a grid partition in $\mathbb R^m$
items.strategy: For bounded $f$ on a nondegenerate rectangle and each grid cell $Q_i$, take $m_i=\inf f[Q_i]$ and $M_i=\sup f[Q_i]$, then form the iterated finite sums of $m_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)$ and $M_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)$ fixed in the grid definition. Prove the extrema exist, the sums are finite reals, and lower sum $\leq$ upper sum. Record that the gap is the corresponding iterated sum of cell oscillations times cell volumes.

items.title: Refinement raises multidimensional lower sums and lowers upper sums, with a quantitative boundary-slab estimate
items.strategy: For one inserted coordinate hyperplane, split the relevant coordinate sum and group the resulting iterated finite sums inside each old cell to prove monotonicity. Iterate coordinatewise for a general refinement. Add the quantitative clause needed for mesh-based Riemann sums: after refining an arbitrary fine grid by one fixed grid, only cells meeting the fixed interior hyperplanes can change the coarse Darboux bounds; their total volume is bounded by a fixed cross-sectional constant times the fine mesh. Prove that slab bound by induction and finite-product distributivity rather than appealing to measure or to sums over abstract finite sets.

items.title: The lower and upper Darboux integrals over a nondegenerate rectangle in $\mathbb R^m$
items.strategy: On a nondegenerate rectangle, take the supremum of all lower grid sums and infimum of all upper grid sums, and call $f$ integrable when they agree. The endpoint grids are nonempty, refinement bounds the two sum families, and completeness plus the infimum theorem supplies the extrema. Do not define an integral on degenerate rectangles, because the grid definition requires strict coordinate partitions.

items.title: Riemann's criterion on a nondegenerate rectangle in $\mathbb R^m$: integrability is equivalent to arbitrarily small Darboux gaps
items.strategy: On a nondegenerate rectangle, repeat the published supremum/infimum argument with grid partitions: equality of the lower and upper integrals gives grids good for the two sides and their common refinement is good for both. Conversely one small Darboux gap bounds the integral gap.

items.title: Tagged grid partitions and Riemann sums in $\mathbb R^m$
items.strategy: A tagging assigns one point to each multi-indexed grid cell. A canonical lower-corner tagging proves existence without choice; when arbitrary cellwise selections are needed, enumerate the finitely nested coordinate ranges and apply finite choice inductively. Define $S(f,P,\xi)$ by the iterated finite-sum convention of the grid definition. Define mesh convergence to $I$ by requiring every tagged grid of sufficiently small mesh to have sum near $I$. Prove each Riemann sum lies between the Darboux sums of the same grid.

items.title: The multidimensional Darboux and tagged-mesh definitions of the Riemann integral agree
items.strategy: The easy direction traps every tagged sum between the Darboux sums of one grid. For the converse, choose a fixed grid with small Darboux gap, refine an arbitrary sufficiently fine grid by it, and use the quantitative boundary-slab estimate to control the change in upper and lower sums. Choose near-extremal tags cellwise by finite choice, exactly as the published one-dimensional proof does. This is a long proof already decomposed by the refinement lemma; do not rebuild that estimate inside the theorem.

items.title: At $m=1$, nondegenerate multidimensional rectangles, grid sums and the integral are exactly the published one-dimensional notions
items.strategy: Identify $\mathbb R^1$ with $\mathbb R$. Nondegeneracy is exactly $a<b$; a coordinate grid is one ordinary partition, its cells are the published subintervals, volume is length, and both Darboux and tagged sums agree term for term. Conclude that the integrability classes and values coincide.

items.title: Linearity, monotonicity, the absolute-value estimate and coordinate-slice additivity for the Riemann integral in $\mathbb R^m$
items.strategy: On a nondegenerate rectangle prove linearity and monotonicity from Darboux gaps and identify values through tagged-sum convergence; derive $|\int f|\le\int|f|$. For a strictly interior coordinate cut, splice coordinate partitions and split the nested finite sum to obtain additivity and the converse integrability statement. Endpoint cuts are excluded because they create degenerate subrectangles, for which this integral is not defined.

items.title: Every continuous function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle in $\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable
items.strategy: A closed nondegenerate rectangle is compact by Heine-Borel. Metric Heine-Cantor makes a continuous scalar function uniformly continuous, and the extreme-value theorem makes it bounded. A grid below the uniform-continuity threshold has small oscillation on every cell, so the multidimensional Riemann criterion applies.

items.title: Measure zero and content zero in $\mathbb R^m$ by countable and finite cube covers
items.strategy: For $m\geq1$, define a closed axis-parallel cube and its volume. A set is null when for every $\varepsilon>0$ it has a countable cube cover whose volume series is at most $\varepsilon$; it has content zero when a finite such cover exists. Cube covers are chosen because Lipschitz images are controlled by cubes without aspect-ratio defects. Prove inheritance by subsets and finite-cover padding. Do not define Lebesgue measure or outer measure.

items.title: At $m=1$, cube-nullity and cube-content-zero are exactly the published interval-cover notions
items.strategy: Under the isometry $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$, a closed cube is a closed interval and its volume is its length. The countable and finite cover quantifiers, including their finite-sum and series bounds, are therefore word for word those of the published definition. Record both directions explicitly so later items may move between the vocabularies.

items.title: Subsets and countable unions of null subsets of $\mathbb R^m$ are null
items.strategy: Subset closure is immediate. For a sequence of null sets, assign the $j$-th set a geometric fraction of the $\varepsilon$ budget, use countable choice to select one cube cover for each set, and enumerate the doubly indexed cubes through the published bijection $\mathbb N^2\to\mathbb N$. Bound finite partial sums by finite rectangles of indices, as the published one-dimensional theorem does. State the countable-choice cost in the theorem.

items.title: For compact subsets of $\mathbb R^m$, measure zero and content zero coincide
items.strategy: Content zero implies nullity by padding. Conversely enlarge every closed covering cube slightly to an open cube, spending a geometric fraction of the remaining volume budget; compactness gives a finite subcover, and bounding its finitely many indices controls the total enlarged volume. Use Heine–Borel only to identify compact sets when needed, not as a substitute for the finite-subcover definition.

items.title: Oscillation of a real function on subsets of $\mathbb R^m$ and at a point
items.strategy: For $f:A\to\mathbb R$ define $\omega_f(S)=\sup\{|f(x)-f(y)|:x,y\in S\}$ in the extended reals and $\omega_f(c)=\inf_{r>0}\omega_f(A\cap B(c,r))$, using Euclidean balls. Prove well-posedness and monotonicity under inclusion as in the published real-domain definition. Include the dictionary clause that under $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ this is exactly `def-oscillation`.

items.title: A function on a subset of $\mathbb R^m$ is continuous at $x$ iff its oscillation there is $0$, and every oscillation superlevel set is closed
items.strategy: Translate the epsilon definition of metric continuity into small oscillation on a ball for one direction; for the other, use one point fixed at $x$ in the oscillation bound. To prove $\{x:\omega_f(x)\geq\varepsilon\}$ closed relative to the domain, show its complement is open: one ball with oscillation below $\varepsilon$ works for every sufficiently nearby centre after shrinking the radius. State the result for bounded $f$ when real-valued oscillations are needed by integration.

items.title: A finite rectangle cover admits grid control with arbitrarily small volume excess
items.strategy: Enlarge each cube in a given finite cover by a positive margin so that the sum of the enlarged volumes increases by less than a prescribed $\eta$; continuity of the finitely many integer-power volume functions at margin $0$ supplies the choice. Take the minimum of the finitely many positive margins, insert every enlarged-cube endpoint into the corresponding coordinate partition, and pass to a common refinement of mesh below that minimum. Every refined cell meeting the originally covered set then lies inside one of the enlarged cubes. Split the iterated cell sum along the aligned endpoints to bound the total volume of those cells by the sum of the enlarged-cube volumes. Treat closed-cell boundary overlap explicitly. This is the cover-to-grid lemma used twice in the multidimensional Lebesgue criterion.

items.title: Lebesgue's criterion in $\mathbb R^m$: a bounded function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle is Riemann integrable iff its discontinuity set is null
items.strategy: On a closed nondegenerate rectangle, prove sufficiency using compact oscillation superlevels, finite cube covers, grid control, and one uniform mesh on the compact complement. For necessity, a small Darboux gap bounds the total volume of high-oscillation cells. Prove directly that every finite family of axis-parallel rectangles, degenerate ones included, has finite cube covers with total volume arbitrarily close to its rectangle-volume sum, using one common cube side, the integer-part theorem, and polynomial continuity. This converts both the high cells and grid-hyperplane pieces to content-zero covers; countable-union closure then handles the full discontinuity set.

items.title: Jordan inner and outer content and Jordan measurable bounded sets in $\mathbb R^m$
items.strategy: For metric-bounded $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, derive a nondegenerate coordinate bounding box from a Euclidean ball. Define outer content by finite rectangle covers and inner content by finite interior-disjoint inscribed families. The box makes the extrema finite; refining endpoints proves every inner sum is at most every outer sum. Define Jordan measurability by equality and handle empty and degenerate sets explicitly.

items.title: A bounded set is Jordan measurable iff its indicator is Riemann integrable, and the integral is its Jordan content
items.strategy: Choose a nondegenerate bounding rectangle. Indicator lower and upper grid sums are the inner and outer grid approximations. Compare arbitrary finite rectangle approximations with grid approximations by small enlargement or shrinking. Coordinate additivity in a larger rectangle proves that integrability and value are independent of the chosen nondegenerate bound.

items.title: A bounded set in $\mathbb R^m$ is Jordan measurable iff its boundary is null, equivalently of content zero
items.strategy: The indicator of $E$ is discontinuous exactly at $\partial E$. Apply the multidimensional Lebesgue criterion on a nondegenerate bounding rectangle. Metric boundedness supplies a closed bounding box containing $\overline E$; the boundary is closed and therefore compact by Heine-Borel. Compact nullity is equivalent to content zero.

items.title: The Riemann integral of a bounded function over a bounded Jordan measurable set
items.strategy: Let $E$ be metric-bounded and Jordan measurable and $f:E\to\mathbb R$ bounded. Choose a nondegenerate bounding rectangle, extend $f$ by $0$, and define integrability and the integral through that extension. Record bounding-rectangle independence in `justified_by`; for $f=1$ recover Jordan content.

items.title: The Riemann integral over a Jordan set is independent of the bounding rectangle
items.strategy: Place two nondegenerate bounding rectangles strictly inside a larger nondegenerate rectangle. Strict coordinate cuts decompose the larger rectangle into the chosen box and nondegenerate added pieces. Coordinate-slice additivity shows that extending by zero preserves integrability and value, and comparison through the common larger box proves independence.

items.title: A continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set is Riemann integrable over that set
items.strategy: Treat the empty set separately; otherwise the metric extreme-value theorem makes $f$ bounded. In a nondegenerate bounding rectangle the zero extension can be discontinuous only on $\partial E$, which is null by the Jordan criterion. The multidimensional Lebesgue criterion makes the extension integrable.

items.title: Jordan content is finitely additive when the overlap has content zero
items.strategy: For Jordan measurable bounded $E,F$ with $E\cap F$ of content zero, use $1_{E\cup F}=1_E+1_F-1_{E\cap F}$ and multidimensional linearity. The indicator of a content-zero set has integral $0$ by the indicator theorem. State the disjoint case explicitly and obtain finite families by induction, not by a count in prose.

items.title: A Lipschitz map $\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m$ sends null sets to null sets
items.strategy: Cover the null set by cubes. A cube of side $\ell$ has Euclidean diameter at most $\iota(m)\ell$ using the norm comparisons. An $L$-Lipschitz image of it lies in a cube of side $2L\iota(m)\ell$, whose volume is the fixed factor $(2L\iota(m))^m$ times the original volume. Allocate the input cover the corresponding scaled $\varepsilon$ budget and sum. Treat $L=0$ separately. Restrict to equal domain and codomain dimensions; the statement is false across arbitrary dimensions.

items.title: The graph of a continuous function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle in $\mathbb R^m$ has content zero in $\mathbb R^{m+1}$
items.strategy: Uniform continuity gives a sufficiently fine coordinate grid on the domain for which the vertical oscillation of $f$ on each cell is small. Above each domain cell, stack finitely many $(m+1)$-dimensional cubes whose side is the grid scale; the integer-part lemma bounds the number of cubes by the vertical oscillation divided by that scale plus a fixed endpoint allowance. Summed over the domain grid, their total volume is bounded by a fixed rectangle-dependent constant times the oscillation bound plus the grid scale, and therefore can be made arbitrarily small. This produces the cube covers required by `def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn`, not merely skinny rectangle covers. State $m\geq1$; no metric on $\mathbb R^0$ is needed.

items.title: If every finite interval cover of $A\subseteq\mathbb R$ has total length at least $c$, then every rectangle cover of $A\times[0,d]$ has total area at least $cd$
items.strategy: List a finite rectangle cover and clip it to a bounding rectangle, then partition $[0,d]$ at all listed vertical endpoints. On each resulting horizontal strip, choose an interior height; the horizontal projections of the covering rectangles active there cover $A$, so their widths total at least $c$. Multiply by the strip height and sum. Reindex the resulting nested finite sums using splitting and distributivity. This elementary product estimate supplies the positive-content claim in the compact and open counterexamples without using Fubini or abstract finite-index-set sums.

items.title: Conventions and proved scope for the Riemann integral in $\mathbb R^m$ and Jordan content
items.strategy: Record $m\geq1$, axis-parallel grids, cube covers for nullity, arbitrary finite rectangle covers for Jordan outer content, and both one-dimensional agreement results. State that `thm-lebesgue-criterion-in-rn` uses only cover-nullity and no Lebesgue measure. Record the proved Lipschitz-image theorem. Say only that a continuously differentiable image theorem is not asserted on this page; do not mention an unbuilt total derivative as though it were a dependency.

pages.title: The Riemann Integral in R^m and Jordan Content: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The unit box in $\mathbb R^m$ has volume $1$, and the integral of a constant $c$ over it is $c$
items.strategy: Every side length is $1$, so the finite product volume is $1$, including the indexing check over $j<m$. On every grid, the lower and upper sums of the constant function coincide with $c$ times the sum of cell volumes, hence with $c$. This is a direct computation from the definitions, not an appeal to iterated integration.

items.title: The rational points of $[0,1]^2$ form a bounded null set that is not Jordan measurable
items.strategy: The set $(\mathbb Q\cap[0,1])^2$ is countable, using countability of $\mathbb Q$ and the published pairing of naturals, hence null by the countable-union lemma applied to singleton cubes. Density of the rationals and irrationals in each coordinate makes both the set and its complement dense in the square, so its boundary is the whole square. The unit square is not null, and the Jordan boundary criterion gives non-measurability. This is the bounded plane set without area.

items.title: The Smith–Volterra–Cantor slab $S\times[0,1]$ is compact and not Jordan measurable
items.strategy: The fat Cantor set $S$ is compact, nowhere dense, and every interval cover has total length at least $1/2$. The product slab is closed and bounded in $\mathbb R^2$, hence compact, and has empty interior, so it equals its boundary. The product lower-bound lemma gives Jordan outer content at least $1/2$ for that boundary. The boundary criterion therefore rules out Jordan measurability. No product measure or Fubini theorem is used.

items.title: $((0,1)\setminus S)\times(0,1)$ is bounded and open, but its boundary has positive Jordan outer content
items.strategy: The complement of the closed fat Cantor set inside $(0,1)$ is open, so the product is open and bounded. Its boundary contains $S\times[0,1]$ (verify neighbourhood intersections with the open set using nowhere density and with its complement using membership in $S$). Outer-content monotonicity and the slab lower bound give a positive lower bound for the boundary, so the open set is not Jordan measurable.

items.title: The parabola segment $\{(x,x^2):0\leq x\leq1\}$ has content zero in $\mathbb R^2$
items.strategy: Apply the graph theorem to the continuous polynomial $x\mapsto x^2$ on $[0,1]$. Also give the direct uniform-grid estimate: on an interval of width $1/\iota(N)$ the vertical oscillation is at most $2/\iota(N)$, so rectangles covering the graph have total area tending to $0$. Write every reciprocal of a natural through $\iota$.

items.title: The right triangle $\{(x,y)\in[0,1]^2:x+y\leq1\}$ has Jordan content $1/2$
items.strategy: Use uniform $N$-by-$N$ grids. Count cells wholly inside and cells meeting the triangle; the two staircase areas differ by at most $1/\iota(N)$ and bracket $1/2$. Prove the finite identity $\sum_{k<N}\iota(k)=\iota(N)\iota(N-1)/2$ by induction or cite a published equivalent only after reading it. The Riemann criterion for the indicator gives Jordan measurability and the common limit $1/2$. The sloping boundary also follows as a graph-content-zero check.

items.title: The Cantor slab $C\times[0,1]$ has content zero in $\mathbb R^2$
items.strategy: Cover the Cantor set by finitely many small intervals. Above an interval of width $\ell>0$, stack finitely many squares of side $\ell$; the integer-part theorem bounds their total area by $\ell+2\ell^2$. Summing gives arbitrarily small finite rectangle covers, so Jordan outer content is zero and the nonnegative inner content is squeezed to zero. Contrast with the fat-Cantor slab.

items.title: The term “rectifiable” for Jordan measurable sets is unrelated to rectifiable curves
items.strategy: Record with a checked Munkres reference that some multivariable-analysis texts call bounded sets with null boundary rectifiable. State the proposition itself: in this page's terminology these are the Jordan measurable bounded sets by the boundary criterion. Warn that this usage does not mean finite curve length and creates no dependency on the arc-length page. Keep the remark terminological and source-backed.

pages.title: Fubini and Change of Variables

items.title: Sections, lower and upper section integrals, and iterated Riemann integrals on product rectangles and Jordan sets
A product grid bounds the Darboux sums of the lower and upper section-integral functions
items.strategy: Regroup the finite Darboux sums over product cells, compare each cell infimum and supremum with the corresponding section sums, and obtain both outer Darboux inequalities without assuming that individual sections are integrable.

items.title: Riemann--Fubini on product rectangles, with lower and upper section integrals and content-zero exceptional sections
items.strategy: Use arbitrarily small product-grid Darboux gaps and the preceding bounds to prove that both lower and upper section-integral functions are integrable with the multiple integral as value; repeat after swapping the coordinate blocks, then identify the two functions off any content-zero exceptional set of integrable sections.

items.title: A continuous function on a closed rectangle has repeated Riemann integrals in every coordinate order, all equal to its multiple integral
items.strategy: Continuity passes to every coordinate section, the published compact-rectangle theorem gives integrability at every stage, and repeated applications of Riemann--Fubini permit an arbitrary permutation of the coordinate order.

items.title: The integral of a product function on a product rectangle is the product of the two integrals
items.strategy: For continuous functions on the two factor rectangles, apply Riemann--Fubini to the continuous product and pull the constant factor through the inner and outer integrals; include the coordinate-independent case by taking one factor constant one.

items.title: An integrable function whose sections vanish outside finite sets has multiple integral zero
items.strategy: Cover each finite section support by finitely many cubes of arbitrarily small total volume to show that its section integral is zero, then apply Riemann--Fubini in the section direction.

items.title: Fubini over a bounded Jordan set when all but a content-zero family of sections are integrable
items.strategy: Extend the integrand by zero to a product bounding rectangle, identify almost every extended section with the integral over the corresponding Jordan section, and apply the exceptional-section clause of rectangular Riemann--Fubini; verify independence of both bounding rectangles.

items.title: Cavalieri: Jordan content is the integral of sectional contents, and equal sections give equal content
items.strategy: Apply Jordan--Fubini to the constant-one function. For the comparison clause, integrate the common sectional-content function after discarding the stated content-zero exceptional parameter set.

items.title: A region between two continuous graphs is Jordan measurable, and a continuous integrand extending to its closure integrates by vertical sections
items.strategy: Describe the boundary by the two graphs and the endpoint segments, use the published graph-nullity and boundary criteria for Jordan measurability, then apply Jordan--Fubini to the continuous extension; boundary sections and the boundary of the region contribute zero.

items.title: The Jacobian determinant of a square-dimensional $C^1$ map is the determinant of its Jacobian matrix
Finite Jordan covers bound upper integrals, while interior-disjoint Jordan subfamilies bound lower integrals
items.strategy: Compare the relevant indicator functions, use finite additivity after isolating content-zero overlaps, and apply monotonicity to the positive and negative parts so that signed integrands are handled without an illicit supremum inequality.

items.title: A linear endomorphism of $\mathbb R^n$ sends bounded Jordan sets to bounded Jordan sets and scales their content by the absolute determinant
items.strategy: Treat singular matrices by row reduction and a thin-slab cover of a proper coordinate subspace, and use the real determinant criterion to identify the determinant factor as zero. Factor an invertible matrix into elementary matrices, verify coordinate swaps and scalings directly and shears by Cavalieri, multiply the scale factors using the determinant laws, and extend from rectangles to arbitrary bounded Jordan sets by finite inner and outer approximation.

items.title: The Jordan content of the parallelepiped spanned by the columns of a square real matrix is the absolute value of its determinant
items.strategy: Realize the parallelepiped as the linear image of the unit cube and apply the linear content-scaling theorem, including singular matrices and the zero-content conclusion.

items.title: A $C^1$ map uniformly close to the identity derivative sandwiches a cube between contracted and expanded cubes
items.strategy: The total-derivative mean-value inequality gives the outer containment. For a target in the contracted cube, turn its preimage equation into a self-map of the complete cube and apply Banach's fixed-point theorem; track the strict error bound and the zero-radius exclusion explicitly.

items.title: On a small cube, a $C^1$ diffeomorphism distorts Jordan content by factors arbitrarily close to its linearized absolute determinant
items.strategy: Normalize by translation and the inverse derivative at the cube centre, apply the near-identity cube sandwich, and then apply linear content scaling; use continuity of the derivative to make the error uniform on the cube and record both lower and upper factors.

items.title: An injective $C^1$ map with invertible derivative sends compact Jordan sets to compact Jordan sets
items.strategy: Compactness and continuity give a compact bounded image. The inverse function theorem makes the map locally open and locally bi-Lipschitz near the compact set; show the image boundary is contained in the image of the source boundary, then use Lipschitz preservation of null sets and the Jordan boundary criterion.

items.title: A compact subset of an open Euclidean set has a compact Jordan neighborhood inside that open set
items.strategy: Cover the compact set by finitely many sufficiently small closed grid rectangles whose slightly enlarged rectangles remain in the open set. Their finite union is compact, contains the set in its interior, lies in the open set, and is Jordan because its boundary is contained in finitely many coordinate hyperplanes.

items.title: A bounded open Jordan set has an increasing exhaustion by compact finite unions of grid rectangles with vanishing content remainder
items.strategy: Choose successively finer grids and retain the closed cells contained in the open set. Compact subsets eventually lie in the retained union, while every omitted cell meeting the set lies near its content-zero boundary; grid-control makes the omitted content tend to zero and a common-refinement construction makes the exhaustion increasing.

items.title: Change of variables for an injective $C^1$ map on a compact Jordan set
items.strategy: Use the Leibniz polynomial formula and continuity of the Jacobian-matrix entries to prove that the absolute Jacobian determinant is continuous and Riemann integrable on the compact Jordan set. Reduce by a finite interior-disjoint rectangle cover inside the open domain, estimate nonnegative upper sums on each small cube with the local volume-distortion lemma, and let the distortion tend to one. Apply the same one-sided inequality to the $C^1$ inverse and use the chain rule and determinant multiplication for equality; split a signed integrand into positive and negative parts and prove the transformed integrability simultaneously.

items.title: The content of a compact Jordan image is the integral of the absolute Jacobian determinant
items.strategy: Apply change of variables to the constant-one function on the image and identify its integral with Jordan content.

items.title: The support of a function on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its compactly supported Riemann integral
The Riemann integral of a compactly supported function is independent of its bounding rectangle
items.strategy: Given two bounding rectangles containing the support, place both in a third rectangle. Outside the support the function is zero, so both restrictions have the same zero extension to the common rectangle; apply the published well-definedness of Jordan-set integration twice, including the empty-support case.

items.title: A compactly supported Riemann integrand admits the global change-of-variables formula from a diffeomorphism near the relevant compact preimage
items.strategy: Choose a compact Jordan neighborhood inside the region on which the map is injective and $C^1$, extend both integrands by zero, and apply compact-Jordan change of variables; verify that points outside the chosen preimage contribute zero.

items.title: Change of variables on bounded open Jordan sets when both integrands are bounded and Riemann integrable
items.strategy: Apply compact-Jordan change of variables to the compact grid exhaustion. Bound the omitted source and image contributions by the two integrand suprema times the corresponding vanishing remainder contents, and pass to the limit; the statement must assume the Riemann integrability of both sides rather than smuggle in an improper-integral convention.

items.title: In one dimension the compact-Jordan formula is substitution over the unoriented image interval with the absolute derivative
items.strategy: For an injective $C^1$ map with nonzero derivative on a compact interval, use monotonicity to identify the image interval and its orientation. Compare the absolute-derivative formula with the published oriented substitution theorem in the increasing and decreasing cases.

pages.title: Fubini and Change of Variables: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: An integrable function on the unit square with one Dirichlet section and only one defined order of ordinary iteration
items.strategy: Use the function supported on the rational points of the vertical line $x=1/2$; squeeze its two-dimensional upper sum into an arbitrarily thin strip, compute every horizontal section, and identify the exceptional vertical section as the Dirichlet function.

items.title: One existing iterated integral does not imply multiple Riemann integrability
items.strategy: For $f(x,y)=x$ when $y$ is rational and zero otherwise on $[-1,1]\times[0,1]$, compute the $x$-first integral as zero, show the other inner sections fail except at $x=0$, compute their lower and upper integrals, and invoke Fubini contrapositively to refute multiple integrability.

items.title: A Riemann-integrable Thomae-type function whose $x$-sections are nonintegrable at every rational height
items.strategy: Use the rational-denominator height from Lebl's exercise, dominate the exceptional horizontal layers by finitely many small-denominator rationals plus a uniformly small tail, and compute the two directions of lower, upper, and ordinary iteration explicitly.

items.title: Fubini computes $\int_0^1\int_{-1}^1 x\exp(xy)\,dx\,dy$ by reversing the order
items.strategy: Use continuity and Fubini to integrate with respect to $y$ first, recognize $x\exp(xy)$ as the derivative of $\exp(xy)$ in $y$, then use the fundamental theorem once more in $x$ and simplify the endpoints.

items.title: A coordinate shear preserves Jordan content by translating every section
items.strategy: For $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\mapsto(x_1,\ldots,x_j+c x_i,\ldots,x_n)$, identify every affected section as a translate of the old one and apply Cavalieri; check directly that the shear determinant is one.

items.title: The content of a concrete three-dimensional parallelepiped computed from its spanning matrix
items.strategy: Write the three spanning vectors as matrix columns, evaluate the determinant by the published finite formula, take its absolute value, and compare with a direct base-times-height check in this triangular example.

items.title: Polar change of variables on a compact annular sector gives the Jacobian factor $r$ and its area
items.strategy: On a sector with positive inner radius and angular width below one full turn, compute the derivative matrix and determinant, verify injectivity from the chosen angular interval, apply change of variables to the constant-one function, and evaluate the repeated integral.

items.title: Cylindrical coordinates have absolute Jacobian determinant $r$ on an injective compact box
items.strategy: Differentiate $(r,\theta,z)\mapsto(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,z)$, expand its determinant, and verify the change-of-variables hypotheses on a box with positive inner radius and a seam-free angular interval.

items.title: Spherical coordinates have absolute Jacobian determinant $r^2\sin\phi$ away from the axis and angular seam
items.strategy: Differentiate the standard spherical-coordinate map, evaluate the determinant using the trigonometric identities, and state a compact parameter box on which the radius is positive, the polar angle stays strictly between the poles, and the map is injective.

items.title: The hyperspherical-coordinate Jacobian is the standard product of a radial power and sine powers
items.strategy: Use induction on dimension: split off the final polar angle, arrange the derivative columns into radial, angular, and lower-dimensional blocks, expand the determinant, and obtain $r^{n-1}\sin^{n-2}\phi_1\cdots\sin\phi_{n-2}$ on a seam-free compact parameter box.

items.title: Polar coordinates on a full closed angular period are not injective and are singular at radius zero
items.strategy: Exhibit the two seam points $(r,0)$ and $(r,2\pi)$ with the same image for $r>0$, then show that every angle maps to the origin at $r=0$ and that the Jacobian determinant vanishes there.

items.title: Omitting the absolute value from the Jacobian gives negative length under the reflection $x\mapsto1-x$
items.strategy: Take the constant-one integrand on $[0,1]$, compute the image integral as one, and compute the un-absolute transformed integral as minus one because the derivative is constantly negative one.

items.title: Dropping injectivity double-counts under $x\mapsto x^2$ on two disjoint intervals
items.strategy: Use the compact Jordan domain $[-2,-1]\cup[1,2]$ and the constant-one integrand on $[1,4]$; the derivative is nonzero throughout the domain, but the absolute-Jacobian integral is six whereas the image length is three.

pages.title: The Fundamental Theorems of Calculus

items.title: Roadmap through the three strengths of FTC I and the five Riemann strengths of FTC II
items.strategy: Locate the two named fundamental theorems on the published working-FTC page at order 161. Organize FTC I into its continuous-integrand consequence, its sharp pointwise Riemann form, and the deferred Lebesgue form. Organize FTC II into the C1 working form, the published closed-interval differentiable form with integrable derivative, this page's interior-derivative form, its finite-exception form, and Botsko's countable-exception form, then point onward to the deferred absolutely-continuous/Lebesgue characterization. Mark every stage as published, proved here, or deferred so none of this orientation is load-bearing.

items.title: Assuming Countable Choice, the integral function of a Riemann-integrable function is Lipschitz and differentiable almost everywhere, with derivative equal to the integrand there
items.strategy: Use the published Lipschitz estimate for the integral function. Lebesgue's criterion makes the discontinuity set of the integrand null under Countable Choice, and the pointwise first FTC gives the derivative at every point outside that set, including the appropriate one-sided endpoint statement.

items.title: Newton–Leibniz needs only continuity on $[a,b]$, differentiability on $(a,b)$, and a Riemann-integrable extension of the interior derivative
items.strategy: For an arbitrary partition, apply the mean value theorem only on its open subintervals. Each endpoint increment lies between the lower and upper Darboux contributions of the given integrable extension; sum, telescope, and squeeze between the lower and upper integrals. The extension's endpoint values are never used.

items.title: Newton–Leibniz remains valid across finitely many exceptional interior points when the primitive is continuous
items.strategy: Order the finite exceptional set, split the interval at those points, apply the interior-derivative Newton–Leibniz theorem on every resulting closed subinterval, and telescope the endpoint differences. Empty exceptional sets and exceptions at the written endpoints reduce to the preceding theorem.

items.title: Botsko's theorem: if $F$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, $F'(x)=f(x)$ off a countable subset of $(a,b)$, and $f$ is Riemann integrable, then $\int_a^b f=F(b)-F(a)$
items.strategy: Prove inline the countable-exception monotonicity lemma by enumerating a nonempty exceptional set with repetitions, assigning its points an epsilon-times-$2^{-n}$ error budget, and using continuity at exceptional points, the derivative inequality elsewhere, and a least-upper-bound first-crossing argument; treat the empty exceptional set separately. On each subinterval of an arbitrary partition, apply that lemma to $F(x)-M_i x$ and $m_i x-F(x)$, where $m_i$ and $M_i$ are the infimum and supremum of $f$ there. Sum the resulting increment bounds, telescope, and squeeze between the lower and upper Darboux integrals. No gauge integral or choice principle enters.

items.title: Integration by parts for continuous factors with Riemann-integrable extensions of their interior derivatives
items.strategy: The product is continuous on the closed interval and differentiable in the interior. The product rule identifies its interior derivative, the algebra of Riemann-integrable functions makes both product terms integrable, and the strengthened Newton–Leibniz theorem evaluates the integral of the product derivative.

items.title: Substitution for a continuous inner map with a Riemann-integrable extension of its interior derivative, without monotonicity or injectivity
items.strategy: Let $F$ be the integral function of the continuous outer integrand. The first FTC and the chain rule identify the interior derivative of $F\circ\varphi$ as $(f\circ\varphi)h$, where $h$ is the integrable derivative extension. Prove that product integrable, apply interior Newton–Leibniz, and retain oriented limits when the two endpoint images reverse or coincide.

items.title: For an integrable $f$, the one-sided derivatives of $F(x)=\int_a^x f$ equal the corresponding one-sided limits of $f$; at a jump they are unequal
items.strategy: Write each one-sided difference quotient as the average of $f$ over the interval between the base point and the varying point. Subtract the relevant one-sided limit and bound the average error by the local supremum error. At an interior point the ordinary derivative exists exactly when the two one-sided limits agree; the value $f(c)$ itself is immaterial unless continuity is asserted.

items.title: Leibniz's rule on a compact rectangle: an interior parameter derivative with a continuous extension may be passed through a Riemann integral
items.strategy: Assume the integrand is continuous on the compact rectangle and, for each fixed integration variable, its ordinary one-variable derivative in the parameter exists on the interior parameter range and is represented by a function extending continuously to the rectangle. For an interior parameter increment, apply the one-variable mean value theorem at each fixed integration variable. Uniform continuity of the extension makes the resulting difference quotient converge uniformly to it. The published uniform integral-error bound passes the limit through the Riemann integral; the same estimate gives the relative one-sided endpoint derivatives and continuity of the derivative extension. No total-derivative or multivariable partial-derivative notion is used.

items.title: The two FTC forms for a Riemann–Stieltjes integral with a $C^1$ integrator
items.strategy: Reduce every Stieltjes integral on a subinterval to the ordinary integral of $f\alpha'$. The pointwise first FTC gives the derivative of the accumulation function wherever $f$ is continuous. For Newton–Leibniz, apply the interior-derivative theorem to a continuous $G$ whose interior derivative is $f\alpha'$, yielding $\int_a^b f\,d\alpha=G(b)-G(a)$ without endpoint derivatives.

pages.title: The Fundamental Theorems of Calculus: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: $G(x)=x^2\sin(1/x)$ has a bounded derivative discontinuous at $0$ that is nevertheless Riemann integrable, and Newton–Leibniz evaluates its integral
items.strategy: Define $G(0)=0$, calculate $G'(0)=0$ from the difference quotient and $G'(x)=2x\sin(1/x)-\cos(1/x)$ away from zero. Bound the derivative, note that its sole discontinuity is at zero, invoke the finite-discontinuity integrability criterion, and apply Newton–Leibniz on $[0,1]$.

items.title: Volterra's function is differentiable everywhere with bounded derivative, but its derivative is not Riemann integrable
items.strategy: Use the published Smith–Volterra–Cantor set. On each complementary interval insert a truncated mirrored copy of $x^2\sin(1/x)$ whose derivative is zero at the joins, and set the function to zero on the fat Cantor set. Prove differentiability with derivative zero on that set and a uniform derivative bound. Every neighborhood of every fat-Cantor point contains derivative values separated by a fixed amount; combine the quantitative positive-measure cover bound with Darboux oscillation to force every upper-minus-lower sum above a positive constant.

items.title: A bounded increasing integrand discontinuous at every rational has an integral function nondifferentiable at every rational in $(0,1)$
items.strategy: Use countability of the rationals to specialize the A-page prescribed-discontinuity theorem to $E=\mathbb{Q}$, then restrict the resulting bounded nondecreasing function to $[0,1]$. The theorem supplies continuity at every irrational and a jump at every rational; monotonicity gives Riemann integrability. At each rational interior point the one-sided FTC gives unequal one-sided derivatives of the integral function, while the pointwise FTC gives differentiability at every irrational.

items.title: Thomae's integrand is discontinuous at every rational, yet its integral function is identically zero and differentiable everywhere
items.strategy: Start from the A-page definition and continuity-set theorem for Thomae's function. It is bounded and its discontinuities on $[0,1]$ form a subset of the countable rationals, so the A-page countable-discontinuity criterion makes it Riemann integrable. Every partition subinterval contains an irrational, hence every lower Darboux sum is zero; integrability then forces the integral to be zero. Positivity, monotonicity, and additivity squeeze every initial integral to zero, so the integral function is identically zero and has derivative zero everywhere, agreeing with the integrand at irrationals and differing at every rational.

items.title: The indicator of $\{1,1/2,1/4,1/8,\ldots\}$ is discontinuous at $0$, but its integral function has derivative $0=f(0)$ there
items.strategy: Define the value at zero to be zero. Prove integrability and integral zero by isolating finitely many large spikes in short partition intervals and confining all remaining spikes to a short interval at zero. The integral function is constant zero, while the sequence of spikes proves discontinuity at zero; nevertheless its derivative there equals the chosen value zero.

items.title: The Cantor function is continuous, has derivative $0$ off a null set, and still rises from $0$ to $1$
items.strategy: Use the published facts that the Cantor function is continuous, has endpoint values zero and one, and is locally constant on every component of the complement of the null Cantor set. It follows directly that its derivative is zero at every complementary point, while its endpoint change is one. This isolates why an almost-everywhere derivative hypothesis alone is not the Riemann Newton–Leibniz theorem.

pages.title: Line Integrals and the Gradient Theorem

items.title: Reversal, concatenation, closed paths, and oriented piecewise-C1 reparametrizations
items.strategy: For piecewise-C1 paths define the reversed path, the normalized concatenation on [0,1], a closed path by equality of endpoints, and a piecewise-C1 reparametrization gamma composed with a bijection whose derivative has a fixed nonzero sign on its smooth pieces. Call it orientation-preserving or orientation-reversing according to that sign. Include constant paths even though they are not regular, since their line integrals must be zero.

items.title: Scalar line integrals with respect to arc length and vector-field line integrals
items.strategy: For a continuous scalar field f and continuous vector field F on a set containing the image of a piecewise-C1 path gamma, define integral_gamma f ds as the sum of integral f(gamma(t))||gamma'(t)|| over smooth pieces and integral_gamma F dot dr as the corresponding sum of integral <F(gamma(t)),gamma'(t)>. The next lemma proves independence of the chosen admissible partition and must be named in justified_by when authored.

items.title: The piecewise-C1 line-integral sums do not depend on the admissible partition
items.strategy: Take the common refinement of two finite admissible partitions. Additivity of the one-variable Riemann integral shows that subdividing a smooth piece leaves each scalar or vector sum unchanged; hence both original sums equal the common-refinement sum. Treat the constant path and a partition with no interior breakpoints explicitly. This is the well-definedness discharge for the preceding definition.

items.title: Scalar line integrals are parametrization-independent; vector line integrals retain orientation and change sign when it reverses
items.strategy: On each smooth piece apply one-variable substitution and the chain rule to gamma composed with h. The absolute value in ||(gamma composed h)'|| removes the sign for scalar integrals; the vector integrand retains h', so an orientation-reversing bijection swaps limits and introduces a minus sign. Refine the partitions to handle piecewise-C1 paths, and state bijectivity/nonvanishing-derivative hypotheses exactly so multiple coverings are excluded.

items.title: Line integrals under reversal and concatenation
items.strategy: Use the affine reversal t maps to a+b-t and the two affine halves of the normalized concatenation. Scalar integrals are unchanged by reversal, vector integrals are negated, and both kinds add under concatenation when endpoints match. Check constant paths and the join point, whose derivative need not exist but is an allowed piecewise breakpoint.

items.title: Line-integral estimates by arc length and the supremum of the field
items.strategy: For a path of finite length prove |integral_gamma f ds|<=M L(gamma) when |f|<=M on the trace, and |integral_gamma F dot dr|<=M L(gamma) when ||F||<=M there. Apply the ordinary integral bound and, in the vector case, Cauchy-Schwarz pointwise; sum over pieces and use the published piecewise-C1 length formula. Include length zero and M=0.

items.title: The scalar line integral of one is the arc length
items.strategy: Put f=1 in the scalar line-integral definition and compare the resulting sum of speed integrals with the published piecewise-C1 arc-length theorem. The identity includes constant paths and degenerate parameter intervals, for which both sides are zero.

items.title: For a C1 path the arc-length accumulation function has derivative equal to speed
items.strategy: For s(t)=L(gamma restricted to [a,t]), use the C1 speed formula to write s(t)=integral_a^t ||gamma'(u)||du. Continuity of the speed and the first FTC give s'(t)=||gamma'(t)||, with relative one-sided endpoint derivatives. Do not claim unit speed unless the path is parametrized by arc length.

items.title: Piecewise-C1 path-connected domains, potential functions, conservative fields, and path independence
items.strategy: Call U piecewise-C1 path-connected when every ordered pair of points is joined in U by such a path; this is the exact connectivity notion used on this page and does not import the later general-topology path definition. For continuous F on open U, define a C1 potential phi by F=grad phi, call F conservative when a potential exists, and define path independence only among piecewise-C1 paths with the same ordered endpoints.

items.title: The gradient theorem: the line integral of a gradient is the endpoint increment
items.strategy: Let phi be C1 on an open set containing a piecewise-C1 path gamma. On every smooth piece the total-derivative chain rule gives (phi composed gamma)'=<grad phi(gamma),gamma'>. Apply Newton-Leibniz on each closed subinterval and telescope across all joins to obtain integral_gamma grad phi dot dr=phi(gamma(b))-phi(gamma(a)). Include constant paths and coincident endpoints.

items.title: Conservative fields are path-independent and have zero integral around every closed path
items.strategy: If F=grad phi, apply the gradient theorem to any two paths with the same endpoints and to a closed path. Both conclusions are endpoint statements; no connectedness is needed for the closed-loop clause, while path independence is asserted within every component in which the relevant paths exist.

items.title: Path independence is equivalent to zero integral around every closed piecewise-C1 path
items.strategy: On a piecewise-C1 path-connected domain, one direction applies path independence to a closed path and the constant path. For the reverse direction concatenate alpha with the reversal of beta; additivity and the reversal sign make its zero loop integral equal integral_alpha F dot dr minus integral_beta F dot dr. State the path-connectedness hypothesis because otherwise endpoint pairs in different components have no comparison paths.

items.title: A continuous path-independent field has a potential constructed by line integrals
items.strategy: Let U be nonempty, open, and piecewise-C1 path-connected; fix a in U and define phi(x)=integral_a^x F dot dr, which is well-defined by path independence. For small h use a comparison path ending with the coordinate segment from x to x+h e_j. The difference quotient is an average of F_j on that segment and tends to F_j(x) by continuity. Thus all partials are the continuous components F_j, and the published continuous-partials theorem makes phi C1 with grad phi=F. Record the basepoint choice and phi(a)=0.

items.title: Conservative, path-independent, and zero-closed-loop conditions are equivalent
items.strategy: For a continuous field on a nonempty open piecewise-C1 path-connected domain, combine the gradient theorem, the closed-loop equivalence, and the line-integral construction of a potential. State all three clauses in one theorem and identify the constructed normalized potential. Do not replace piecewise-C1 path-connectedness by the bare word connected.

items.title: Two potentials of the same field differ by a constant on each piecewise-C1 path component
items.strategy: Apply the gradient theorem to grad(phi-psi)=0 along a path joining arbitrary points of one piecewise-C1 path component. The endpoint increment vanishes. State componentwise constancy rather than global constancy when the domain is disconnected.

items.title: Potentials glue after a constant adjustment over a nonempty path-connected overlap
items.strategy: Let phi_1 and phi_2 be potentials for the same field on open U_1 and U_2, with nonempty piecewise-C1 path-connected intersection. Their difference is constant on the overlap by potential uniqueness. Subtract that constant from phi_2, define the common function on U_1 union U_2, and verify it is C1 and has the required gradient. The overlap hypotheses are essential for a single adjustment to work.

items.title: Exact and closed C1 vector fields
items.strategy: For an open U in R^n and a C1 vector field F=(F_1,...,F_n), call F exact when F=grad phi for some C2 scalar potential phi, and closed when partial_j F_i=partial_i F_j for every i,j. Explain the C2/C1 regularity pairing and identify these as the vector-field forms of exact and closed one-forms, without importing differential-form machinery.

items.title: Continuous second partials of a scalar potential commute
items.strategy: For a C2 phi and distinct coordinate directions i,j, form the rectangular second difference at x with small nonzero side lengths h,k lying in an open ball inside the domain. Apply the one-variable mean value theorem first in direction i then j to identify it with partial_j partial_i phi at an interior point; reverse the order to identify the same quotient with partial_i partial_j phi at another interior point. Let h,k tend to zero and use continuity. The i=j case is tautological.

items.title: Every exact C1 vector field is closed
items.strategy: Write F_i=partial_i phi for a C2 potential. The preceding mixed-partial lemma gives partial_j F_i=partial_j partial_i phi=partial_i partial_j phi=partial_i F_j for every i,j. Keep the C1/C2 hypotheses in the statement; exactness with a merely C1 potential does not make these second partials available.

items.title: Star-shaped open subsets of Euclidean space
items.strategy: Define a nonempty open U to be star-shaped with respect to a in U when a+t(x-a) belongs to U for every x in U and 0<=t<=1. Record that convex open sets are star-shaped about every point, while the definition itself requires a specified centre and therefore excludes the empty set.

items.title: Poincare's lemma on a star-shaped domain: every closed C1 field is exact
items.strategy: Let a be a star centre and define phi(x)=integral_0^1 <F(a+t(x-a)),x-a> dt. Differentiate under the integral. Closedness converts partial_j F_i into partial_i F_j, so the jth partial integrand becomes d/dt of t F_j(a+t(x-a)); Newton-Leibniz gives partial_j phi=F_j(x). Verify continuity on the compact parameter interval, the t=0 boundary term, and C2 regularity from F being C1.

items.title: On a star-shaped open domain, closed, exact, conservative, path-independent, and zero-loop are equivalent
items.strategy: A star-shaped domain is piecewise-C1 path-connected by its two radial line segments. Combine exact-implies-closed, the star-shaped Poincare lemma, and the conservative/path-independence/zero-loop theorem. Align regularity: F is C1, exact means a C2 potential, and conservative uses the same potential viewed as C1.

items.title: Type I, Type II, and elementary regions for Green's theorem
items.strategy: Define a compact Type I region as the set between continuous piecewise-C1 lower and upper graphs on [a,b], with strict separation in the interior and the possible vertical endpoint arcs included; define Type II by continuous piecewise-C1 left and right graphs over [c,d]. Call a region elementary for Green's theorem when it admits both descriptions. Define a finite elementary Green region as a nonempty finite union of elementary pieces with pairwise disjoint interiors, whose pairwise intersections are finite unions of complete shared boundary arcs and endpoints, and require every positive-length internal arc to belong to exactly two pieces with opposite induced orientations. This is explicit geometric data, not the interior supplied by an arbitrary Jordan curve.

items.title: Positive orientation of elementary-region boundaries
items.strategy: For a Type I piece orient the lower graph from left to right, the right endpoint arc upward, the upper graph from right to left, and the left endpoint arc downward; equivalently the region remains locally on the left. Give the analogous Type II traversal. For a finite elementary union, delete every shared arc together with its oppositely oriented copy and orient each surviving boundary arc as inherited from its piece. Zero-length arcs are omitted. This defines the positive boundary combinatorially without invoking the Jordan curve theorem.

items.title: The Type I boundary identity for the P dx term
items.strategy: Let D be a Type I region between piecewise-C1 graphs alpha and beta and let P be C1 on an open neighbourhood of D. Parametrize the positively oriented lower, right, upper, and left arcs. The vertical arcs contribute zero to P dx, and reversal gives the upper arc the opposite sign. Fubini over the graph-bounded region followed by one-variable Newton-Leibniz in y proves integral over partial D of P dx equals minus the double integral over D of partial_y P. Treat coincident endpoint arcs and piecewise breakpoints explicitly.

items.title: The Type II boundary identity for the Q dy term
items.strategy: Let D be a Type II region between piecewise-C1 left and right graphs and let Q be C1 on an open neighbourhood of D. Parametrize the positive boundary so the horizontal arcs contribute zero to Q dy, while the right and left graph arcs carry opposite directions. Apply the symmetric-coordinate form of Jordan-Fubini and Newton-Leibniz in x to obtain integral over partial D of Q dy equals the double integral over D of partial_x Q. Check coincident endpoint arcs and all piecewise-C1 joins.

items.title: Shared boundary arcs cancel when finitely many elementary regions are glued
items.strategy: For a nonempty finite elementary decomposition, sum the positively oriented boundary integrals of a continuous planar field over all pieces. Every shared arc occurs twice with opposite orientations, so reversal cancels those two line integrals; endpoints contribute nothing, leaving exactly the induced positively oriented boundary of the union. For a continuous scalar integrand, use zero extensions to one bounding rectangle, linearity of the multidimensional integral, and the content-zero shared graph arcs to prove that the piece integrals sum to the integral over the union. Include the one-piece case and exclude overlapping interiors by hypothesis.

items.title: Green's theorem for finite unions of elementary regions
items.strategy: Let D be a finite elementary Green region with its boundary positively oriented by the preceding definition, and let P,Q be C1 on an open neighbourhood of D. On each elementary piece, add the Type I identity for P dx to the Type II identity for Q dy. Sum over the finite decomposition, use the gluing lemma for cancellation of internal arcs and additivity of the region integral, and conclude that the boundary integral of P dx+Q dy equals the double integral of partial_x Q minus partial_y P. State the supplied elementary decomposition as part of the hypothesis; make no claim for an arbitrary Jordan domain.

items.title: Area of an elementary Green region as a boundary line integral
items.strategy: Apply Green's theorem to P=-y/2 and Q=x/2, whose scalar curl partial_x Q-partial_y P equals one, to obtain cont(D)=one half of the positively oriented boundary integral of x dy-y dx. Also record the equivalent formulas cont(D)=integral x dy=-integral y dx by choosing (P,Q)=(0,x) and (-y,0). The one-piece case is included by the same formula.

items.title: Limitation: arbitrary Jordan domains are not covered by the elementary Green theorem
items.strategy: Record explicitly that the theorem proved here applies only when a Type I-and-Type II elementary decomposition and the stated finite gluing data are supplied. It does not infer an interior or such a decomposition from an arbitrary Jordan curve. The general Jordan-domain form would require the Jordan curve theorem and additional decomposition geometry; the library records the former only as not proved here, so neither is used as a hidden premise.

items.title: Closedness is local, exactness is global, and a domain hypothesis cannot be omitted
items.strategy: Record the precise logical boundary established here: exact C1 fields are closed on every open domain, and closed C1 fields are exact on star-shaped open domains. Do not state the converse on arbitrary connected domains. Mention that simple connectedness is the standard broader sufficient hypothesis, but its homotopy machinery occurs later in the library and is not silently imported here; the companion gives the punctured-plane obstruction.

pages.title: Line Integrals and the Gradient Theorem: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The scalar line integral of x over the right unit semicircle equals two
items.strategy: Parametrize the right semicircle by gamma(t)=(cos t,sin t) for -pi/2<=t<=pi/2. Its speed is one and x=cos t, so the scalar line integral is integral cos t=2. Reverse the path to check orientation independence.

items.title: Scalar and vector line integrals along an affine line segment
items.strategy: For gamma(t)=(1-t)p+tq on [0,1], compute speed ||q-p|| and write both formulas explicitly: integral_gamma f ds=||q-p|| integral_0^1 f((1-t)p+tq)dt and integral_gamma F dot dr=integral_0^1 <F((1-t)p+tq),q-p>dt. Include p=q, where both integrals vanish.

items.title: A polynomial potential evaluates work along every path by endpoints
items.strategy: Take phi(x,y,z)=x^2 y+yz^2 and F=grad phi. Verify the three components and evaluate the integral from a stated point p to q by phi(q)-phi(p), then check the value directly along the affine segment. This exercises both the gradient theorem and the line-segment formula.

items.title: Constructing a potential on a rectangle by coordinate-segment integrals
items.strategy: For a concrete closed C1 planar field on an open rectangle, fix (a,b) and define phi(x,y)=integral_a^x F_1(t,b)dt+integral_b^y F_2(x,t)dt. Differentiate, use closedness to recover F_1 and F_2, and compare with the radial Poincare formula. This makes the construction algorithm visible rather than merely asserting existence.

items.title: The vector field (y,0) gives different integrals along two paths with the same endpoints
items.strategy: From (0,0) to (1,0), integrate along the x-axis to get zero and along beta(t)=(t,t(1-t)) to get integral_0^1 t(1-t)dt=1/6. Concatenating one path with the reverse of the other yields a closed loop with nonzero integral, displaying both failures in the equivalence theorem.

items.title: The vortex field is closed but not exact on the punctured plane
items.strategy: On U=R^2 minus {(0,0)} take F(x,y)=(-y/(x^2+y^2),x/(x^2+y^2)). Compute the cross partials and show they agree. On the counterclockwise unit circle the vector integrand is identically one, so the integral is 2pi. The gradient theorem would force zero for an exact field; hence F is closed but not exact, not conservative, and not path-independent. Note that U is path-connected but not star-shaped or simply connected.

items.title: FALSE: every closed C1 field on a connected open set is exact
items.strategy: Use the vortex field on the punctured plane. The domain is connected by explicit polygonal paths, the field is closed, and its unit-circle integral is 2pi, contradicting exactness by the gradient theorem. Correct the statement with the star-shaped hypothesis proved on the A page; mention simple connectedness only as the standard broader condition, not as a theorem proved here.

items.title: FALSE: vector line integrals are invariant under reversing a path
items.strategy: Take the constant field F=(1,0) and the segment from (0,0) to (1,0). The forward integral is one and the reversed integral is minus one. Contrast this with scalar ds integrals, where the speed's absolute value makes reversal invariant.

items.title: A vector line integral around the vortex counts repeated traversals
items.strategy: Parametrize the unit circle once by gamma(t)=(cos t,sin t) and twice by beta(t)=(cos(2t),sin(2t)) on [0,2pi]. For the vortex field the integrals are respectively 2pi and 4pi. The images and orientations agree, but beta is not a bijective reparametrization of gamma, so the parametrization-invariance theorem is not contradicted.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, the deleted Tychonoff plank is a regular nonnormal open subspace of a compact Hausdorff normal space
items.strategy: Use ordinal $T_3$-ness and productive regularity for the deleted plank, Tychonoff compactness plus compact Hausdorff normality for the full plank, and separate the two edge sets only far enough to derive the standard boundedness contradiction below $\omega_1$.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, normality is not hereditary, even to open regular subspaces
items.strategy: Use the full Tychonoff plank and its deleted open subspace from the preceding lemma.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, refuted: every regular space is normal
items.strategy: The deleted Tychonoff plank is the licensed regular nonnormal witness.

items.title: A worked preservation table for subspaces and products of the standard, cofinite, and ordinal topologies

items.title: Closed subspaces inherit normality: compact intervals, ordinal endpoints, and finite closed pieces
items.strategy: Identify each subset as closed and apply closed-heredity, noting that no conclusion is available for an arbitrary subspace.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, the deleted Tychonoff plank worked as $T_3$ but not normal inside its compact Hausdorff normal parent
items.strategy: Compute the edge sets and the tail rectangles explicitly, isolating the one use of countable boundedness below $\omega_1$.

items.title: Assuming choice, the lower-limit line is normal while its square is regular and nonnormal
items.strategy: Display the clopen interval base, the finite-support product base, and the Jones antidiagonal obstruction side by side.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, normality is not open-hereditary: deleting one corner of the Tychonoff plank
items.strategy: The deleted corner is closed, so its complement is open; the A-page lemma supplies normality of the parent and nonnormality of the complement.

items.title: Assuming choice, normality is not even finitely productive: two copies of the lower-limit line
items.strategy: Package the square theorem as the sharp binary counterexample.

items.title: Regular and normal do not imply $T_1$ under the library's conventions
items.strategy: Use a small indiscrete space, where the relevant point-versus-closed-set and closed-set-versus-closed-set obligations are vacuous but $T_1$ fails.

items.title: The dyadic rationals of $[0,1]$, their finite levels $D_n$, and their density in $[0,1]$

If $(U_r)_{r \in D}$ are open with $\overline{U_r} \subseteq U_s$ whenever $r < s$ and $U_1 = X$, then $x \mapsto \inf\{ r \in D : x \in U_r \}$ is a continuous map $X \to [0,1]$, and no choice principle is used
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Urysohn's lemma, under the axiom of dependent choice: in a normal space two disjoint closed sets are separated by a continuous function into $[0,1]$, and conversely such a space is normal
items.strategy: constructive

items.title: Under dependent choice a normal $T_1$ space is completely regular, so $T_4 \Rightarrow T_{3\frac{1}{2}}$, and together with the implications already proved this is the whole classical chain

items.title: If for every $\varepsilon > 0$ some continuous $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfies $\lvert f(x) - g(x)\rvert < \varepsilon$ for all $x$, then $f$ is continuous; in particular a uniformly convergent series of continuous real functions has a continuous sum
items.strategy: direct

items.title: Under dependent choice a space is perfectly normal if and only if it is normal and every closed set is a zero set

items.title: Tietze's extension theorem, under dependent choice: a continuous map from a closed subspace of a normal space into $[a,b]$ extends continuously to the whole space, and this property characterises normality

items.title: A continuous real-valued map on a closed subspace of a normal space extends to the whole space, and a map into an open interval extends into that same open interval

The sets $U_0, U_1, U_{1/2}, U_{1/4}, U_{3/4}$ of the Urysohn construction computed for two disjoint closed subsets of $\mathbb{R}$
In a metric space the function $d(x,A)/(d(x,A) + d(x,B))$ separates two disjoint closed sets outright, so the metric case spends no choice principle
Every closed subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is a zero set and a $G_\delta$, as the perfect-normality criterion predicts

pages.title: Partitions of Unity and Paracompactness

items.title: Refinements, locally finite families, point-finite families, and star refinements
Locally finite families remain locally finite after taking closures, closure commutes with their union, and a locally finite union of closed sets is closed
items.strategy: At a point choose one neighbourhood meeting only finitely many members; the same neighbourhood misses the closures of every other member.

items.title: Paracompactness: every open cover has a locally finite open refinement, with no separation axiom built into the word
Every compact space is paracompact
items.strategy: A finite subcover is itself a finite, hence locally finite, open refinement.

items.title: Every closed subspace of a paracompact space is paracompact
items.strategy: Extend a subspace cover to the ambient space by adjoining the complement of the closed subspace, refine there, and take traces.

items.title: Every paracompact Hausdorff space is regular
items.strategy: For a point outside a closed set, take all Hausdorff neighbourhoods of closed-set points whose closures miss the point, refine this cover locally finitely, and unite the refinement members that meet the closed set; local finiteness lets closure commute with that union and keeps the point out, with no simultaneous choice of neighbourhoods.

items.title: Every paracompact Hausdorff space is normal
items.strategy: Use the preceding regularity result to take the family of all neighbourhoods of one closed set whose closures miss the other, refine the resulting cover locally finitely, and unite just the refinement members meeting that closed set.

items.title: Locally finite partitions of unity and subordination to an open cover
Sums, products, absolute values, finite maxima and minima, and quotients of continuous real-valued maps on a topological space are continuous where defined
items.strategy: Pair the maps into $\mathbb R^2$ by the product universal property and prove the elementary real operations continuous by epsilon estimates; compose, restricting a quotient to the open cozero set of its denominator.

items.title: A locally finite family of continuous nonnegative functions has a continuous pointwise sum
items.strategy: Near each point all but finitely many functions vanish, so the pointwise sum agrees locally with a finite continuous sum.

items.title: A locally finite nonnegative family with positive pointwise sum normalizes to a partition of unity
items.strategy: Apply the locally finite sum lemma and divide every function by the everywhere-positive sum; supports and local finiteness are unchanged.

items.title: Under choice, every open cover of a paracompact Hausdorff space has locally finite open refinements $\{V_s\}$ and $\{W_s\}$ with $\overline{V_s}\subseteq W_s\subseteq U_s$
items.strategy: Use regularity to shrink one neighbourhood at each point inside an assigned refinement member, then invoke paracompactness a second time; local finiteness makes the closures of the second refinement stay inside the first assigned members.

items.title: Under choice and dependent choice, every open cover of a paracompact Hausdorff space admits a locally finite subordinate partition of unity
items.strategy: Shrink the cover twice, apply Urysohn's lemma to each pair $\overline{V_s}\subseteq W_s$, and normalize the resulting locally finite positive family.

items.title: For a Hausdorff space, paracompactness is equivalent, under choice and dependent choice, to the existence of a locally finite subordinate partition of unity for every open cover
items.strategy: Use the existence theorem forward; conversely the positive cozero sets of a subordinate partition form a locally finite open refinement.

items.title: Under choice and dependent choice, every open cover of a compact Hausdorff space admits a finite subordinate partition of unity
items.strategy: Use compactness for a finite subcover and the partition theorem, then group all functions assigned to the same member of that finite subcover; local finiteness makes each grouped sum continuous.

items.title: Under choice, every open cover of a metric space has a point-finite open refinement
items.strategy: Following Ornstein's first stage, stratify points by a dyadic ball small enough to lie in a cover member, well-order each stratum, and retain only the first eligible balls; verify point-finiteness scale by scale.

items.title: Under choice, Ornstein's point-finite refinement of a metric cover admits a locally finite open refinement
items.strategy: Apply Ornstein's part (B) to the point-finite refinement from part (A): use maximal admissible ball radii and first containing cover members, then combine the radius comparison with point-finiteness of the input cover to prove local finiteness.

items.title: Stone's theorem, under choice: every metric space is paracompact
items.strategy: Apply Ornstein's point-finite refinement construction and then its locally finite refinement to an arbitrary metric open cover.

items.title: Under choice and dependent choice, metric open covers admit locally finite subordinate partitions of unity
items.strategy: Metric spaces are Hausdorff, then apply Stone and the partition theorem.

items.title: Assuming countable choice, every countably compact paracompact Hausdorff space is compact
items.strategy: A locally finite open refinement of an open cover cannot have infinitely many essential members in a countably compact space; a finite selection of their assigned cover members is then a subcover.

items.title: Under countable choice, every regular Lindelöf space is paracompact
items.strategy: Shrink an all-eligible-neighbourhood refinement and thin it to a countable cover; replacing its enumeration by successive differences of accumulated closed cores yields a locally finite open refinement.

items.title: Refuted: every paracompact space is normal
items.strategy: Use a finite compact topology with two disjoint closed sets that have no disjoint open neighbourhoods; compactness gives paracompactness, while the failure shows why Hausdorffness is load-bearing.

items.title: Refuted: paracompactness is hereditary
items.strategy: The compact ordinal $\omega_1+1$ is paracompact, while its open subspace $\omega_1$ is countably compact and noncompact and hence not paracompact by the preceding lemma.

items.title: Assuming choice, refuted: paracompactness is productive
items.strategy: The lower-limit line is regular Lindelöf and therefore paracompact. Its square is Hausdorff but nonnormal by the earlier preservation page, so paracompact Hausdorff implies normal rules out paracompactness.
