items.title: Covering maps, evenly covered neighbourhoods, fibres, sheets, and trivial coverings
Maps and isomorphisms of covering spaces over a fixed base
Lifts of maps, paths, and homotopies through a covering map
Covering maps are surjective local homeomorphisms with discrete fibres
items.strategy: An evenly covered neighbourhood restricts the projection to a homeomorphism on each sheet, which gives the local-homeomorphism property. Intersect a sheet with a fibre to isolate its unique point. Keep surjectivity as part of the covering-map definition rather than infer it from local data.

items.title: The cardinality of a covering fibre is locally constant and is constant on a connected base
items.strategy: Over an evenly covered neighbourhood every fibre meets each sheet in exactly one point, so all fibres there are in bijection with the sheet index set. The subsets on which a fixed fibre cardinal occurs are open; connectedness permits only one nonempty such subset. Do not assert global constancy for a disconnected base.

items.title: Existence and uniqueness of path lifts through a covering map
items.strategy: Pull back evenly covered neighbourhoods along the path to obtain an open cover of the compact interval, choose a Lebesgue subdivision, and lift successively sheet by sheet from the prescribed initial point. Agreement at subdivision endpoints gives a continuous pasted path; sheet uniqueness proves uniqueness, including constant paths.

items.title: Existence and uniqueness of homotopy lifts through a covering map
items.strategy: For a homotopy $H:Y\times I\to X$ and a lift at time zero, use evenly covered neighbourhoods and compactness of the interval to extend the lift over successive time strips locally in $Y$. Pasting gives a global lift, and the set of points where two lifts agree is open and closed on each vertical interval, yielding uniqueness. Record the endpoint-fixed consequence when the original homotopy is relative to endpoints.

items.title: The endpoint of a lifted path depends only on its endpoint-fixed homotopy class
items.strategy: Lift an endpoint-fixed homotopy starting from the chosen lift of one path. Along each endpoint edge the lifted map takes values in a discrete fibre; connectedness of the interval makes it constant, so the terminal endpoints agree.

items.title: A covering map induces an injective homomorphism on fundamental groups
items.strategy: If a loop upstairs maps to a nullhomotopic loop downstairs, lift a nullhomotopy with the given loop as its initial edge. Uniqueness forces the opposite edge to be constant, yielding a nullhomotopy upstairs. Preserve the chosen basepoints and the exact published definition of the induced map.

items.title: Two lifts from a connected space that agree at one point agree everywhere
items.strategy: The equaliser of two lifts is open because a common image point has an evenly covered neighbourhood and both lifts must lie in the same sheet near an agreement point. Its complement is open by choosing disjoint sheets near a disagreement point. Connectedness and the named agreement point force the equaliser to be the whole domain.

items.title: Lifting criterion for maps from path-connected locally path-connected spaces
items.strategy: For a based map $f:(Y,y_0)\to(X,x_0)$ with $Y$ path-connected and locally path-connected, necessity follows by functoriality. For sufficiency, define the candidate lift at $y$ by lifting $f$ along any path from $y_0$; the subgroup inclusion makes the endpoint independent of the chosen path. Local path-connectedness and an evenly covered neighbourhood make the candidate continuous. Uniqueness follows from connectedness.

items.title: The pullback of a covering space along a continuous map
Covering spaces are stable under restriction, finite products, and pullback
items.strategy: Restrict an evenly covered neighbourhood for restriction, take products of evenly covered neighbourhoods for finite products, and identify each pullback sheet with the corresponding open subset of the new base. State surjectivity in every construction and the empty-product convention separately. Do not claim unrestricted closure under composition: an infinite family of intermediate sheets need not admit one common refinement.

items.title: A composite of covering maps is a covering when the outer covering is finite-sheeted
items.strategy: For coverings $p:E\to B$ and $q:B\to X$, evenly cover a neighbourhood of $x$ for $q$. There are only finitely many resulting $q$-sheets. Around the unique point of each such sheet over $x$, choose a smaller neighbourhood evenly covered by $p$; intersect their finitely many images downstairs and restrict all sheets to that common neighbourhood. The resulting two-level sheets evenly cover the composite. Separate the empty base case, and record that the finite-sheet hypothesis is what permits the common intersection.

items.title: The monodromy right action on a covering fibre and its equivalent left-action convention
Monodromy acts by fibre bijections, and its orbits are the intersections of path components with the fibre
items.strategy: Path reversal gives the inverse endpoint permutation and concatenation gives the right-action law under the library's convention that $[\alpha][\beta]$ traverses $\alpha$ first. A lifted loop is a path upstairs joining its starting and endpoint fibre points. Conversely, project any path upstairs between fibre points to a loop downstairs. Thus transitivity is equivalent to path-connectedness of the relevant covering component.

items.title: Deck transformations and the deck-transformation group of a covering
On a connected covering space, a deck transformation is determined by one point and the deck action is free
items.strategy: Two deck transformations are lifts of the same projection. If they agree at one point, uniqueness of lifts from the connected total space makes them equal. Applying this to a deck transformation and the identity shows that a fixed point forces the transformation to be the identity.

items.title: Covering-space actions by disjoint translates of neighbourhoods
The orbit map of a covering-space action is a covering, with the acting group equal to the deck group when the total space is path-connected
items.strategy: For a neighbourhood whose nonidentity translates are disjoint, its orbit image is open in the quotient and its full preimage is the disjoint union of all translates. Each translate maps homeomorphically onto that quotient neighbourhood. The action is free automatically and embeds the acting group in the deck group. If the total space is path-connected, compare any deck transformation at one point with the unique group translate taking that point to its image; one-point determination then proves equality with that translate.

items.title: Local path-connectedness lifts and descends along covering maps
items.strategy: Every point has a sheet homeomorphic to an open neighbourhood of its image. Local path-connectedness passes to open subspaces and across homeomorphisms, which proves both directions using surjectivity to choose a point over each basepoint.

items.title: Semilocally simply connected spaces with explicit basepoint convention
Universal covering spaces
A space admitting a universal covering is semilocally simply connected
items.strategy: At a basepoint choose an evenly covered neighbourhood and a lift of that point. Any loop in the neighbourhood lifts to a loop in its sheet. The induced fundamental-group map of the universal cover is injective and its domain group is trivial, so the inclusion-induced class downstairs is trivial. No local path-connectedness is needed for this necessity direction.

items.title: The based path-class model and basic sets for a universal cover
For a path-connected locally path-connected semilocally simply connected space, the path-class projection is a covering map
items.strategy: Refine each semilocally simply connected neighbourhood to an open path-connected one. For a path class ending at its centre, append paths in that neighbourhood to obtain a basic sheet. Triviality of the inclusion-induced fundamental group makes the endpoint description independent of the appended path, and distinct initial classes give disjoint sheets. Verify that these basic sets form a topology and map homeomorphically onto the chosen neighbourhood.

items.title: Every path-connected locally path-connected semilocally simply connected space has a universal cover
items.strategy: Use the path-class projection, already proved to be a covering. The path-class space is nonempty and path-connected by truncating representatives. A loop upstairs projects to a loop whose path-class endpoint is the starting class, hence to the trivial element downstairs; injectivity of the fundamental-group map then makes every upstairs loop nullhomotopic. Thus the total space is simply connected.

items.title: For a path-connected locally path-connected base, universal covers are uniquely isomorphic over the base and lift to every connected covering
items.strategy: Let the base be path-connected and locally path-connected and fix points over a common basepoint. The lifting criterion applies to a universal cover because its fundamental group is trivial, giving a unique covering map to any connected covering. Applying this in both directions between two universal covers and using uniqueness of lifts makes the composites identities.

items.title: A connected covering of a locally path-connected simply connected space is one-sheeted and trivial
items.strategy: Local path-connectedness lifts to the connected total space, making it path-connected. If two points lie in one fibre, join them upstairs; the projected loop is null-homotopic because the base is simply connected, while endpoint homotopy invariance forces its lift to have the same initial and final point. Thus every fibre is a singleton, and a one-sheeted covering is a homeomorphism by its local sheet descriptions.

items.title: For a nonempty path-connected total space, a covering fibre is in bijection with the cosets of the induced fundamental-group subgroup
items.strategy: Fix a point in the fibre. Send a loop class to the endpoint of its lifted path. Endpoint homotopy invariance makes this well defined; two classes have the same endpoint exactly when their quotient lies in the image of the upstairs fundamental group. Path-connectedness of the total space gives surjectivity onto the fibre. State left-versus-right cosets consistently with the published path-product order, then translate the bijection into the published index convention: the finite cardinalities agree, and one side is infinite exactly when the other is recorded as $\infty$.

items.title: For a finite-sheeted covering, the total space is compact exactly when the base is compact
items.strategy: The forward direction is the continuous image theorem and uses surjectivity. For the reverse direction, over each basepoint choose an evenly covered neighbourhood; because its fibre is finite, shrink once so that every sheet above the smaller neighbourhood lies in a selected member of a given open cover upstairs. Compactness supplies finitely many such base neighbourhoods and hence finitely many cover members upstairs.

items.title: For a path-connected locally path-connected semilocally simply connected base, the deck group of a universal cover is isomorphic to the fundamental group with the inverse-path convention
items.strategy: For a path-connected locally path-connected semilocally simply connected base and a chosen point upstairs, each loop class determines the endpoint of its lift. The universal-cover lifting criterion gives the unique deck transformation taking the chosen point to that endpoint. Because the library multiplies loops in traversal order, insert path reversal in the assignment so composition is a homomorphism rather than an antihomomorphism. Freeness gives injectivity and path-connectedness gives surjectivity.

pages.title: Covering Spaces and Lifting — Examples

items.title: Trivial coverings are products with a discrete fibre
items.strategy: For any space $X$ and discrete set $F$, verify that the projection $X\times F\to X$ is a covering, with every open subset of the base evenly covered. Identify its sheets and fibre, including $F=\varnothing$: the projection then fails surjectivity unless $X=\varnothing$, so state the nonempty-fibre convention explicitly.

items.title: A surjective local homeomorphism need not be a covering map
items.strategy: Let the domain be the disjoint union of $(0,2)$ and $(1,2)$ and map both components by inclusion onto the base $(0,2)$. The first component makes the map surjective and each inclusion is a local homeomorphism. The fibre has one point at $1$ and two immediately to its right, so local constancy of sheet number rules out a covering; equivalently, the second component supplies only a one-sided partial sheet above every neighbourhood of $1$.

items.title: A covering over a disconnected base can have different sheet numbers on different components
items.strategy: Map a three-point discrete space onto a two-point discrete space with one point over the first basepoint and two over the second. Each singleton base neighbourhood is evenly covered, while the fibre cardinal is not globally constant. This isolates exactly why connectedness appears in the sheet-number theorem.

items.title: The quotient $\mathbb R\to\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ is a covering with integer translations as deck transformations
items.strategy: Use the equivalence relation $x\sim y$ iff $x-y$ is an integer and the quotient topology. Intervals of length less than one have pairwise disjoint integer translates whose quotient images are evenly covered. Verify directly that translations are deck transformations and that every deck transformation is the unique integer translation determined by the image of zero, without computing the fundamental group of the quotient.

items.title: The projected unit interval is not nullhomotopic in $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$
items.strategy: The loop $t\mapsto[t]$ lifts from zero to the path $t\mapsto t$, whose endpoint is one. If it had an endpoint-fixed nullhomotopy, homotopy lifting would keep the terminal lift in the discrete fibre while deforming the initial lift to the constant path at zero, forcing endpoints one and zero to agree. This proves essentiality without asserting $\pi_1(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z$.

items.title: The maps $[x]\mapsto[mx]$ on $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ are $m$-sheeted coverings for $m\ge1$
items.strategy: Check well-definedness modulo integer translation. Around a class choose an interval short enough that its $m$ inverse branches are disjoint; these branches give the evenly covered neighbourhood and exactly $m$ fibre points. At $m=1$ the map is the identity, so no zero-sheet or division-by-zero case is hidden.

items.title: Pulling a covering back to an evenly covered open set gives a trivial covering
items.strategy: For the inclusion $U\hookrightarrow X$ of an evenly covered open set, identify the pullback with the disjoint union of the sheets over $U$. Write the explicit mutually inverse maps over $U$ and verify their continuity from the pullback subspace topology.

items.title: The Hawaiian earring is locally path-connected but has no universal cover
items.strategy: Model the earring as countably many copies of $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with diameters tending to zero and all zero classes identified, using the standard shrinking-wedge metric. Away from the wedge point, sufficiently short open arcs are path-connected neighbourhoods. At the wedge point, every open neighbourhood contains a smaller metric ball whose intersection with each circle is an arc through the wedge point and which contains every sufficiently small circle, so that ball is path-connected. Retraction to one such small circle and the essential unit loop show its inclusion carries a nontrivial loop, so semilocal simple connectedness fails at the wedge point. The necessity theorem then rules out a universal cover.

items.title: $\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ as the Euclidean plane and as a normed real algebra: what the identification preserves
items.strategy: Start with the published quotient construction, not an unproved pair model. Under $\Phi(a+bi)=(a,b)$, record that addition and real scalar multiplication are coordinatewise, complex multiplication has the published bilinear coordinate formula, conjugation is reflection in the real axis, and $|z|=\|\Phi(z)\|_2$, so the metric, convergence, continuity, and topology agree with those of $\mathbb R^2$. State equally explicitly what is not being identified: a general real-linear map need not be complex-linear, multiplication is extra structure beyond the real vector space, and the Euclidean identification supplies no compatible field order. Treat the last clause as an inline reminder from $i^2=-1$, not as a second false-statement item.

items.title: A complex domain is a nonempty connected open subset of $\mathbb C$
Complex differentiability at a point, the complex derivative, holomorphic functions, and entire functions
The complex derivative at a point is unique
items.strategy: If two numbers $L$ and $M$ are limits of the same difference quotient, assume $L\ne M$ and apply both limit estimates with tolerance $|L-M|/3$. The triangle inequality then gives $|L-M|<2|L-M|/3$, a contradiction. Keep the punctured-domain quantifier from the derivative definition explicit.

items.title: The Wirtinger derivatives $\partial_z f$ and $\partial_{\bar z}f$, and antiholomorphic functions
Complex differentiability is equivalent to a complex-linear real total derivative, to $\partial_{\bar z}f=0$, and to real differentiability plus the Cauchy–Riemann equations
items.strategy: For $f=u+iv$ on an open set and $a$ in its domain, prove one four-way equivalence in a single item: (i) the complex difference quotient exists; (ii) $f$ is real totally differentiable and $Df(a)$ is multiplication by a complex number; (iii) $f$ is real totally differentiable and $\partial_{\bar z}f(a)=0$; (iv) $f$ is real totally differentiable and $u_x=v_y$, $u_y=-v_x$ at $a$. From (i), subtract $f'(a)h$ to obtain the real total-derivative remainder. Translate a real derivative matrix through the published coordinate model to show that complex-linearity is exactly the CR matrix form, and expand the Wirtinger formula to identify the same two real equations. Record $f'(a)=u_x+iv_x=v_y-iu_y=\partial_z f(a)$.

items.title: Complex differentiability at a point implies continuity there
items.strategy: Use the four-way theorem to obtain real total differentiability under the Euclidean identification, then apply the published local linear bound and continuity theorem. Translate the conclusion back through the metric dictionary.

items.title: Continuous first partial derivatives and the Cauchy–Riemann equations imply complex differentiability pointwise, and holomorphy when they hold throughout an open set
items.strategy: Let $f=u+iv$ on an open set and fix $a$. Assume all four first partials exist on a neighbourhood of $a$, are continuous at $a$, and satisfy CR at $a$. Apply the published continuous-partials theorem componentwise to get real total differentiability at $a$, then use the CR direction of the four-way theorem. Deduce the open-set corollary when the hypotheses hold at every point. State these exact hypotheses; do not replace them by the false assertion that bare existence of partials plus CR is sufficient.

items.title: Cartesian and polar forms of the Cauchy–Riemann equations agree away from the origin
items.strategy: On an open parameter set with $r>0$ and $re^{i\theta}$ in the domain, set $U(r,\theta)=u(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)$ and $V$ similarly. Use the real total-derivative chain rule and the real sine/cosine derivatives to transform the Cartesian equations into $U_r=r^{-1}V_\theta$ and $V_r=-r^{-1}U_\theta$, and reverse the invertible coordinate calculation. Also derive $f'(re^{i\theta})=e^{-i\theta}(U_r+iV_r)$. The statement must exclude $r=0$ and must not presume a global argument branch.

items.title: Linearity, product, reciprocal, and quotient rules for complex derivatives
items.strategy: At a common point of complex differentiability, prove the sum and scalar rules by linearity of limits. For the product insert and subtract $f(a)g(a+h)$ and use continuity of the differentiable factors. For $1/g$, factor the difference quotient and use $g(a)\ne0$ plus continuity to keep the denominator nonzero near $a$; combine with the product rule for the quotient. State the local nonvanishing set precisely and include the constant and identity derivatives as base cases.

items.title: The chain rule for complex derivatives
items.strategy: Regard both complex-differentiable maps as real totally differentiable with derivatives given by complex multiplication. Apply the published total-derivative chain rule; the composite of multiplication by $f'(a)$ and multiplication by $g'(f(a))$ is multiplication by their product. Invoke the four-way equivalence in reverse to recover complex differentiability and the formula $(g\circ f)'(a)=g'(f(a))f'(a)$.

items.title: The Wirtinger chain rule for compositions of real-differentiable complex-valued maps
items.strategy: For real-differentiable $f:U\to V$ and $g:V\to\mathbb C$, write the real differential of each map in the basis $(h,\bar h)$ supplied by its two Wirtinger derivatives. Apply the published real total-derivative chain rule and collect the coefficients of $h$ and $\bar h$. This gives $(g\circ f)_z=(g_w\circ f)f_z+(g_{\bar w}\circ f)\overline{f_{\bar z}}$ and $(g\circ f)_{\bar z}=(g_w\circ f)f_{\bar z}+(g_{\bar w}\circ f)\overline{f_z}$. Check the identity and conjugation maps as sign/conjugation tests, then recover the holomorphic chain rule when both barred derivatives vanish.

items.title: A conjugate difference quotient characterizes antiholomorphic maps
items.strategy: Assume for every $z$ in an open set that the limit $g(z)=\lim_{h\to0}(f(z+h)-f(z))/\bar h$ exists. Replace $h$ by $\bar k$ and conjugate the relevant linear model to prove real differentiability with differential $h\mapsto g(z)\bar h$; equivalently $f_z=0$ and $f_{\bar z}=g$. Conversely, if $f$ is real differentiable and antiholomorphic, its Wirtinger expansion has precisely this form, so division by $\bar h$ gives the limit. Keep the pointwise real-differentiability hypothesis explicit in the converse.

items.title: A holomorphic function with continuous complex derivative has $C^1$ real and imaginary components
items.strategy: For $f=u+iv$, the four-way theorem gives $u_x=\operatorname{Re}f'$, $v_x=\operatorname{Im}f'$, $u_y=-\operatorname{Im}f'$, and $v_y=\operatorname{Re}f'$. The published modulus formula gives $|\operatorname{Re}(w_1-w_2)|,|\operatorname{Im}(w_1-w_2)|\le|w_1-w_2|$, so both coordinate maps are continuous; continuity of $f'$ therefore makes all four first partials continuous. This is a conditional bridge only; do not use it to assume that every holomorphic derivative is continuous before the later regularity theory.

items.title: A continuous local inverse has derivative reciprocal to a nonzero complex derivative
items.strategy: Let $f:U\to V$ be a bijection between open neighbourhoods with inverse $g$ continuous at $b=f(a)$. If $f$ is complex differentiable at $a$ and $f'(a)\ne0$, rewrite the inverse difference quotient as $(z-a)/(f(z)-f(a))$ with $z=g(w)$. Continuity of $g$ sends $w\to b$ to $z\to a$, and the nonzero derivative makes the reciprocal limit legitimate. Conclude $g'(b)=1/f'(a)$. Keep continuity of the inverse as a hypothesis; no inverse-function theorem is available in this page's closure.

items.title: Complex polynomials are entire with the power-rule derivative, and rational functions are holomorphic wherever their denominator is nonzero
items.strategy: Prove the nonnegative integer power rule by induction from the identity and product rules, checking the constant power separately. Finite linear combinations give the displayed formal derivative of a polynomial. Apply the quotient rule to $P/Q$ on the open set where $Q\ne0$, with derivative $(P'Q-PQ')/Q^2$. State the zero polynomial and constant-denominator cases explicitly.

items.title: The complex exponential is entire and its complex derivative is itself
items.strategy: Use the published Cartesian formula $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$. The real exponential, sine, and cosine derivative theorems give continuous first partials, and direct calculation gives CR everywhere. Apply the exact $C^1$ converse and compute $\exp'(z)=u_x+iv_x=\exp(z)$. This proof bridges the already-published definition and Euler formula to complex differentiability without re-proving the power-series construction.

items.title: A holomorphic function with zero derivative on a domain is constant
items.strategy: For arbitrary points of a nonempty domain, use the published equivalence of connectedness and polygonal connectedness for open subsets of $\mathbb R^2$ to choose a finite polygonal path. On each line segment, apply the real total-derivative chain rule to the restriction of $f$; the four-way theorem makes the derivative zero. Apply the one-variable zero-derivative theorem to the real and imaginary components on the closed parameter interval, and concatenate the finitely many constant restrictions. The connectedness hypothesis is essential and is not replaced by mere openness.

items.title: A real-valued holomorphic function on a domain is constant
items.strategy: Write $f=u+iv$ with $v=0$. The CR equations force both first partials of $u$ to vanish and hence $f'=0$ pointwise. Apply the zero-derivative theorem on the domain.

items.title: A holomorphic function of constant modulus on a domain is constant
items.strategy: If the constant modulus is zero, modulus definiteness gives $f=0$. Otherwise differentiate $u^2+v^2=c^2$ in both real coordinates and use CR. The resulting two-by-two homogeneous system for $u_x,u_y$ has determinant $u^2+v^2=c^2>0$, so all four first partials vanish and $f'=0$. Finish with the zero-derivative theorem. This proof deliberately avoids the later maximum-modulus principle.

items.title: If both $f$ and $\bar f$ are holomorphic on a domain, then $f$ is constant
items.strategy: Write $f=u+iv$. CR for $f$ gives $u_x=v_y$ and $u_y=-v_x$, while CR for $\bar f=u-iv$ gives $u_x=-v_y$ and $u_y=v_x$. Combine the pairs to make every first partial zero, hence $f'=0$, and apply the domain theorem.

items.title: Orientation-preserving conformality for a real-differentiable complex map at a point
Plane similarities are complex or conjugate-complex multiplications; the orientation-preserving ones are exactly the nonzero complex multiplications
items.strategy: For a real-linear map with columns $p$ and $q$, the inner-product similarity condition makes the columns orthogonal with the same positive length. A positive signed area factor selects $q=(-p_2,p_1)$ and gives the matrix $[[a,-b],[b,a]]$, multiplication by $a+ib\ne0$; a negative factor selects the conjugate-complex form $h\mapsto\xi\bar h$. Conversely calculate inner products and the signed area factors $|\xi|^2$ and $-|\xi|^2$ directly. This separates angle preservation from orientation instead of silently building orientation into the word similarity.

items.title: A real-differentiable complex map is orientation-preserving conformal at a point exactly when it is complex differentiable there with nonzero derivative
items.strategy: If $f$ is complex differentiable, the four-way theorem identifies $Df(a)$ with multiplication by $f'(a)$; when this number is nonzero the similarity lemma gives oriented conformality. Conversely, the conformal derivative is a nonzero complex multiplication by the lemma, so the real-derivative condition in the four-way equivalence gives complex differentiability and identifies its nonzero derivative. State the pointwise convention, without assuming local or global injectivity.

items.title: The Jacobian determinant of a holomorphic map is $|f'|^2$ and is positive exactly where $f'\ne0$
items.strategy: Use the CR matrix $[[u_x,u_y],[v_x,v_y]]=[[a,-b],[b,a]]$ with $a+ib=f'$. Its two-by-two determinant is $a^2+b^2=|f'|^2$. Modulus definiteness makes this positive exactly for a nonzero derivative and zero exactly when the derivative vanishes; it can never be negative.

items.title: The $C^2$ real and imaginary parts of a holomorphic function satisfy Laplace's equation and form a harmonic-conjugate pair
items.strategy: Let $f=u+iv$ be holomorphic and assume explicitly that $u$ and $v$ are $C^2$. Differentiate $u_x=v_y$ in $x$ and $u_y=-v_x$ in $y$, then use Clairaut–Schwarz to obtain $u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0$. Differentiate the other way for $v_{xx}+v_{yy}=0$. At first use, say that a $C^2$ real function satisfying Laplace's equation is harmonic and that $v$ is a harmonic conjugate of $u$ when $u+iv$ is holomorphic. Do not claim here that every holomorphic function is automatically $C^2$ or that every harmonic function globally has a conjugate; those require later complex-analysis machinery.

items.title: If a holomorphic function has $C^2$ components, then its derivative is holomorphic
items.strategy: Write $f'=u_x+iv_x$. The $C^2$ hypothesis makes these two components $C^1$. Differentiate the CR equations and use equality of mixed partials to verify CR for $f'$. Apply the continuous-partials converse. Emphasize that this is a conditional first step, not the later theorem that arbitrary holomorphic functions possess derivatives of all orders.

items.title: The Hessian determinant of each $C^2$ holomorphic component is nonpositive; a nondegenerate critical point is a saddle
items.strategy: For either component $w$, harmonicity gives $w_{yy}=-w_{xx}$, so $\det H_w=-w_{xx}^2-w_{xy}^2\le0$. If a critical point has nonzero Hessian determinant, it is negative, hence the symmetric Hessian is indefinite and the published multivariable second-derivative test gives neither a local maximum nor a local minimum (a saddle). When the determinant is zero, state that the Hessian test is inconclusive.

pages.title: Complex Differentiability and the Cauchy–Riemann Equations: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: $z\mapsto z^2$ is entire with derivative $2z$, directly from the complex difference quotient
items.strategy: Factor $((z+h)^2-z^2)/h=2z+h$ for $h\ne0$ and take the complex limit. Also display $u=x^2-y^2$, $v=2xy$, verify CR as a consistency check, and verify directly that both satisfy Laplace's equation, so $v$ is a harmonic conjugate of $u$ under the page's $C^2$ convention.

items.title: The complex exponential satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations in Cartesian and polar form
items.strategy: First differentiate from the definition: the addition law gives $(e^{z+h}-e^z)/h=e^z(e^h-1)/h$, and the published power series gives $(e^h-1)/h=1+\sum_{n\ge2}h^{n-1}/n!\to1$ by a uniform bound for $|h|\le1$. Then compute the four Cartesian partials from $e^{x+iy}=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and recover $f'=f$. For $z=re^{i\theta}$, write $e^z=e^{r\cos\theta}(\cos(r\sin\theta)+i\sin(r\sin\theta))$, compute $U_r,U_\theta,V_r,V_\theta$, and verify both polar CR identities for $r>0$. At the origin use the Cartesian calculation, since polar coordinates are singular there.

items.title: $z\mapsto1/z$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ with derivative $-1/z^2$, directly from the difference quotient
items.strategy: For $z\ne0$ and sufficiently small $h$ with $z+h\ne0$, simplify $((z+h)^{-1}-z^{-1})/h=-1/(z(z+h))$ and use continuity of multiplication and reciprocal at the nonzero point. State that zero is excluded from the domain, not merely a point where the derivative formula fails.

items.title: A Möbius map $(az+b)/(cz+d)$ with $ad-bc\ne0$ is conformal wherever $cz+d\ne0$
items.strategy: Use the quotient rule to compute $f'(z)=(ad-bc)/(cz+d)^2$. The determinant hypothesis and domain condition make the derivative nonzero, so the pointwise conformality theorem applies. Treat $c=0$ and the unique pole when $c\ne0$ explicitly; make no global injectivity claim beyond the usual extended-plane setting, which is not yet defined.

items.title: The square map sends a Cartesian grid to two orthogonal families of parabolas away from its critical point
items.strategy: Under $w=z^2$, a vertical line $x=c$ has image $(u,v)=(c^2-y^2,2cy)$ and a horizontal line $y=c$ has image $(u,v)=(x^2-c^2,2cx)$. Eliminate the parameters to identify the parabolic arcs, and use the nonzero derivative $2z$ to prove their tangent directions remain orthogonal at every image of a grid crossing with $z\ne0$. At $z=0$ the derivative vanishes and the conformality conclusion is unavailable.

items.title: FALSE: real differentiability as a map $\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ implies complex differentiability; conjugation is the counterexample
items.strategy: For $f(z)=\bar z$, the real coordinate map $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$ is linear and hence totally differentiable everywhere. Its matrix $\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ is not a complex-multiplication matrix, equivalently $u_x=1\ne-1=v_y$, so the four-way theorem makes $f$ nowhere complex differentiable. Optionally confirm directly that real and imaginary increments give quotient limits $1$ and $-1$.

items.title: $z\mapsto|z|^2$ is complex differentiable exactly at $0$, with derivative $0$, but is holomorphic on no neighbourhood of $0$
items.strategy: At the origin the quotient $|h|^2/h=\bar h$ tends to zero. At $z=x+iy\ne0$, the real function has $u=x^2+y^2$ and $v=0$; CR would force $x=y=0$, so differentiability fails. Conclude that differentiability at one point need not extend to any neighbourhood.

items.title: $z\mapsto\operatorname{Re}z$ is real differentiable but nowhere complex differentiable
items.strategy: The real coordinate map is $(x,y)\mapsto(x,0)$, so its total derivative is constant. CR for a real-valued function would require both partials of its real component to vanish, but $u_x=1$. Equivalently, horizontal and vertical difference quotients are $1$ and $0$.

items.title: $z\mapsto|z|$ is nowhere complex differentiable
items.strategy: At zero compare $|t|/t$ along positive and negative real increments. At a nonzero point the modulus is real differentiable with nonzero gradient $(x/|z|,y/|z|)$; CR for a real-valued complex-differentiable function would force that gradient to vanish. Cover the origin and all nonzero points separately.

items.title: $x^3+3xy^2+i(y^3+3x^2y)$ is complex differentiable exactly on the coordinate axes but holomorphic nowhere
items.strategy: The polynomial components have continuous partials. Compute $u_x=v_y=3x^2+3y^2$ and $u_y=v_x=6xy$; CR holds exactly when $xy=0$, so the $C^1$ converse gives complex differentiability exactly on the two axes. Every neighbourhood of every axis point contains a point with $xy\ne0$, so no point has a neighbourhood on which the function is holomorphic.

items.title: FALSE: the Cauchy–Riemann equations at one point imply complex differentiability there
items.strategy: Define $f(0)=0$ and $f(z)=\bar z^2/z$ for $z\ne0$. Since $|f(z)|=|z|$, the function is continuous at zero. Compute the four coordinate partials at zero directly to get $u_x=v_y=1$ and $u_y=-v_x=0$, so CR holds. But $f(z)/z=\bar z^2/z^2$ equals $1$ on the real axis and $-1$ on the line $y=x$, so the complex derivative at zero does not exist.

items.title: FALSE: existence of partial derivatives satisfying Cauchy–Riemann everywhere on an open set implies holomorphy
items.strategy: Set $f(0)=0$ and $f(z)=\exp(-z^{-4})$ for $z\ne0$. Off zero it is holomorphic by the power, reciprocal, exponential, and chain rules, hence satisfies CR. Along both coordinate axes, $e^{-1/t^4}$ decays faster than $|t|$, so all four partials at zero exist and vanish; cite exponential domination for the estimate. Along $z=re^{i\pi/4}$ the value is $e^{1/r^4}$, so $f$ is unbounded in every neighbourhood of zero and therefore discontinuous and not complex differentiable there. Thus CR holds everywhere but holomorphy fails. As a sharper Wirtinger warning, note that $\bar f$ has $(\bar f)_z\equiv0$ continuously although its coordinate partials are discontinuous at zero.

items.title: FALSE: a holomorphic function with zero derivative on an arbitrary open set is constant
items.strategy: Take $U=\{\operatorname{Re}z<0\}\cup\{\operatorname{Re}z>0\}$ and set $f=0$ on the left half-plane and $f=1$ on the right. Each point has a neighbourhood on which $f$ is constant, so $f$ is holomorphic with derivative zero throughout $U$. Values on the two components differ, so $f$ is not constant. Explicitly identify the missing hypothesis as connectedness, hence the use of a domain in the theorem.

pages.title: Complex Power Series and Analytic Functions

items.title: Complex analytic functions as locally representable by convergent power series
Uniform convergence and the uniformly Cauchy condition for complex-valued functions, with the componentwise dictionary
A sequence of complex-valued functions converges uniformly if and only if it is uniformly Cauchy
items.strategy: Uniform convergence implies the uniformly Cauchy condition by the complex triangle inequality. Conversely, pointwise Cauchy sequences converge by completeness of the complex plane; hold one index fixed beyond the uniform Cauchy threshold and pass the other index to its pointwise limit to obtain one uniform error bound. Treat an empty domain vacuously.

items.title: A uniform limit of continuous complex-valued functions is continuous
items.strategy: Use the componentwise dictionary: uniform convergence in complex modulus implies uniform convergence of real and imaginary parts, and complex continuity is componentwise. Apply the published real uniform-limit theorem to both coordinates and recombine. Include an empty domain and arbitrary codomain-open-set points.

items.title: Weierstrass M-test for complex-valued function series
items.strategy: For each tail use the complex triangle inequality and the same convergent real majorant tail. This makes the partial sums uniformly Cauchy; pointwise completeness of the complex plane supplies the sum, and the componentwise dictionary makes the convergence uniform. Check an empty domain and zero majorants explicitly.

items.title: A complex power series converges absolutely and uniformly on every closed subdisc strictly inside its disc of convergence
items.strategy: Fix a closed subdisc of radius r<R. Cauchy–Hadamard gives convergence of the real majorant sum |c_n|r^n. Apply the complex M-test to c_n(z-a)^n, retaining the centre, R=0, and R=+infinity conventions and making no boundary-circle assertion.

items.title: A complex power series, its formal derivative, and its zero-constant-term formal antiderivative have the same radius
items.strategy: The complex radius is the radius of the real modulus-coefficient series. Apply the published real radius lemma to |c_n|; the modulus of the derived coefficient is n|c_n| and the modulus of the integrated coefficient is |c_n|/(n+1). Translate back without writing an applied canonical embedding.

items.title: Inside its disc of convergence a complex power series is holomorphic and may be differentiated term by term
items.strategy: Fix z in the disc and a slightly larger closed subdisc. Prove the finite complex power-difference identity inline by telescoping, then factor each monomial difference quotient. Uniformly dominate the resulting tails on the larger subdisc, pass the finite derivative formula to the limit, and identify the derivative series whose radius is unchanged. Treat the constant term and radius-zero case explicitly.

items.title: A complex power-series sum has complex derivatives of every order, obtained by repeated termwise differentiation
items.strategy: Iterate the termwise theorem because every derived series has the same radius. State the falling-factorial coefficient at order k and check k=0, k>n, and the zero series.

items.title: The coefficients of a complex power series are its derivatives at the centre divided by the corresponding factorials
items.strategy: Evaluate the nth termwise derivative at the centre. Every positive power vanishes, the nth term contributes n!c_n, and terms of lower degree have already disappeared. Include n=0 and use ordinary embedded-number notation only.

items.title: A complex power-series representation about a fixed centre has unique coefficients
items.strategy: If two series agree on a neighbourhood of their common centre, their derivatives of every order agree there. Apply the coefficient formula at the centre to each order, including the constant coefficient.

items.title: Every complex analytic function is holomorphic
items.strategy: At an arbitrary point use the local convergent power-series representation from the analytic definition. The termwise-differentiation theorem gives complex differentiability throughout that representation disc, hence at the chosen point. The empty-open-set case is vacuous.

items.title: The binomial double series for re-expanding a complex power series is absolutely convergent and may be regrouped
items.strategy: For |b-a|+|h|<R, apply the real re-expansion majorant lemma to the nonnegative coefficients |c_n|. The complex binomial theorem expands each term, and absolute convergence licenses regrouping by powers of h. Check h=0 and b=a.

items.title: A complex power-series sum re-expands about every interior point, at least to the distance from that point to the original boundary
items.strategy: Put z=b+h in the absolutely convergent binomial double series and regroup by h. Identify the new kth coefficient with f^(k)(b)/k! using termwise differentiation, and obtain convergence for |h|<R-|b-a|. Do not claim this lower bound is the exact new radius.

items.title: The sum of a complex power series is analytic throughout its open disc of convergence
items.strategy: At each interior point the re-expansion theorem supplies a positive-radius local series representing the same function. This is exactly the analytic definition, including the entire-radius case.

items.title: Sums and scalar multiples of convergent complex power series are represented coefficientwise on the common disc
items.strategy: On any point inside both radii, take finite partial sums and pass their exact linearity identity to the limit. The result converges locally uniformly on every smaller closed subdisc; include zero scalars and unequal radii.

items.title: Products of convergent complex power series are represented by their Cauchy-product coefficients on the common disc
items.strategy: At a point inside both radii, both numerical series converge absolutely. Apply the published complex Cauchy-product theorem and identify the finite convolution coefficient. Local uniform convergence on smaller closed subdiscs follows from the absolute coefficient majorant.

items.title: A composition of convergent complex power series has a convergent local power-series expansion when the inner sum maps the centre to the outer centre
items.strategy: Write the inner displacement as a zero-constant-term series H. Choose a small disc on which the absolute coefficient sum of H is below the outer radius. Expand each outer power by repeated Cauchy products; the scalar majorant is an absolutely convergent composition, so double-series regrouping gives a locally convergent series. Include a constant inner function.

items.title: A convergent complex power series with nonzero constant term has a convergent reciprocal power series locally
items.strategy: For f(a) nonzero write 1/f(z)=f(a)^(-1)/(1-H(z)), where H(a)=0. Continuity of the power-series sum makes |H|<1 on a smaller disc. Prove the finite complex geometric identity inline, compose H with the geometric series, and record the recursive reciprocal coefficients. The nonzero constant term is essential.

items.title: Complex analytic functions are closed under finite linear combinations, products, quotients with nonzero denominator, and composition
items.strategy: Choose compatible local expansions at an arbitrary point. Apply the coefficientwise sum/product results, the local reciprocal lemma when the denominator value is nonzero, and the local composition lemma after recentering the outer expansion at the inner value. State each natural domain exactly.

items.title: Every complex analytic function has a primitive on a neighbourhood of each point
items.strategy: Integrate a local representing power series coefficientwise, using the unchanged radius of the antiderivative series. Termwise differentiation recovers the original function. This is local only and makes no global simply-connectedness claim.

items.title: The exponential definitions of complex sine, cosine, hyperbolic sine, and hyperbolic cosine equal their entire power series
items.strategy: Substitute the entire exponential series at z, -z, iz, and -iz into the published definitions. Separate even and odd indices using absolute convergence and simplify the powers of i. Record all four series and their infinite radii without re-defining the functions.

items.title: Complex sine, cosine, hyperbolic sine, and hyperbolic cosine are entire with their standard derivatives
items.strategy: Differentiate the four entire series term by term and shift indices. Obtain sin'=cos, cos'=-sin, sinh'=cosh, and cosh'=sinh, including the constant terms.

items.title: The addition formulas for complex trigonometric and hyperbolic functions
items.strategy: Insert z+w into the published exponential definitions and use exp(z+w)=exp(z)exp(w). Collect the symmetric and antisymmetric combinations to obtain the sine, cosine, sinh, and cosh formulas for all complex z,w.

items.title: Complex sine and cosine are unbounded on the complex plane
items.strategy: For real y, the published trigonometric-hyperbolic dictionary gives sin(iy)=i sinh(y) and cos(iy)=cosh(y). Expand sinh and cosh by their exponential definitions. Since exp(y) tends to positive infinity while exp(-y) tends to zero, both moduli are unbounded along the imaginary axis. Keep y real and positive and make no boundedness claim on the real axis.

items.title: The zeros of complex sine are the integer multiples of pi, and the zeros of complex cosine are the odd half-integer multiples of pi
items.strategy: Rewrite sin z=0 as exp(2iz)=1 and apply the exact kernel formula. Rewrite cos z=0 as exp(2iz)=exp(i pi), then apply the fibre formula. Prove both converses by substitution and retain the integer quantifier.

items.title: Stolz approach regions at the boundary point 1 of the unit disc
Abel summation by parts for complex coefficients and their partial sums
items.strategy: For s_n=sum_{k=0}^n a_k, substitute a_n=s_n-s_{n-1} into a finite weighted sum and telescope. State both the finite identity and its tail form, checking the initial index and an empty finite range.

items.title: Abel's limit theorem: a convergent complex series is recovered by its power series along every Stolz approach to 1
items.strategy: Subtract the boundary sum so the partial sums tend to zero. Apply complex Abel summation to express the power series through those partial sums. Split at a fixed index; the finite head vanishes as z approaches 1, while the tail is bounded by the small partial-sum supremum times |1-z|/(1-|z|), which is bounded in a Stolz region. Handle the exact boundary point only as a limit and include radial approach as a corollary.

pages.title: Complex Power Series and Analytic Functions — Examples

items.title: The geometric series re-expanded about an arbitrary point of the unit disc
items.strategy: For |b|<1 rewrite 1/(1-z) as (1-b)^(-1) times the geometric series in (z-b)/(1-b). Verify the finite geometric identity directly, obtain coefficients (1-b)^(-k-1), and show the new radius is |1-b|.

items.title: The alternating harmonic power series tends to log 2 at the boundary point 1
items.strategy: Use the published real evaluation of the alternating harmonic series, regard its coefficients as complex, and apply the angular Abel theorem. State the series from its positive first index and make no logarithm-branch claim inside the disc.

items.title: The harmonic complex power series diverges at 1 and converges conditionally at every other point of the unit circle
items.strategy: For |z|=1 with z not equal to 1, the finite geometric identity bounds the partial sums of sum z^n by 2/|1-z|. Apply the complex Abel-summation tail identity with the positive decreasing weights 1/n, using the Archimedean reciprocal estimate to make the boundary term small. At z=1 the series is the divergent p-series with p=1, while at every boundary point the modulus series is the same divergent harmonic series, so all other convergence is conditional. Start at n=1 and never form 1/0.

items.title: A power series with reciprocal-square coefficients converges uniformly on the closed unit disc
items.strategy: For n starting at one, bound |z^n/n^2| by 1/n^2 on |z|<=1 and apply the complex M-test with the convergent real p-series. Contrast the boundary conclusion with what radius alone says, without evaluating the boundary sum.

items.title: The complex geometric series is not uniformly convergent on its open unit disc
items.strategy: Its nth term fails to tend uniformly to zero because the supremum of |z|^n over |z|<1 is one for every n. Nevertheless it converges pointwise by the finite geometric identity. Use no maximum-attainment claim on the open disc.

items.title: Equal radii do not determine convergence on the boundary circle
items.strategy: Compare the geometric series and the reciprocal-square coefficient series. Cauchy–Hadamard gives radius one to both; at z=1 the first has terms that do not tend to zero, whereas the second converges absolutely by the real p-series.

items.title: The lacunary power series with factorial exponents has radius one and diverges at 1
items.strategy: Set the coefficient of z^m to one when m=n! for some positive n and zero otherwise. Its coefficient-root limsup is one because ones occur arbitrarily far out, while all roots are at most one. At z=1 the nonzero terms do not tend to zero. Resolve the repeated exponent 1 by starting the factorial index at two or combining that finite duplication.

items.title: The real function 1/(1+x^2) is smooth on the real line but its Maclaurin series has radius one
items.strategy: Apply the finite geometric identity to 1/(1+x^2) to obtain sum (-1)^n x^(2n) for |x|<1. Cauchy–Hadamard gives radius one, while the quotient rule shows the real rational function is smooth for every real x. This illustrates complex singularities without invoking analytic continuation or the identity theorem.

items.title: Abel convergence of the alternating harmonic power series along a nonradial Stolz approach
items.strategy: Take z_k=1-1/k+i/(2k) for sufficiently large k. Check |z_k|<1 and a uniform bound on |1-z_k|/(1-|z_k|), then apply the angular Abel theorem to the alternating harmonic coefficients and their published sum log 2.

items.title: FALSE: convergence of a complex power series at one point other than its centre forces convergence everywhere
items.strategy: The geometric power series centered at zero converges at z=1/2 but diverges at z=2. Verify both claims from the finite geometric identity and the nth-term test, then state the correct radius dichotomy.

items.title: FALSE: complex sine and cosine are bounded on the complex plane
items.strategy: The unboundedness theorem gives explicit imaginary-axis witnesses: sin(iy)=i sinh(y) and cos(iy)=cosh(y), whose moduli grow without bound as y tends to positive infinity. Thus neither function admits a global complex-plane bound; distinguish this from their bounded real-axis restrictions.

pages.title: Contour Integration

items.title: Complex contours as planar rectifiable paths: the Euclidean, coordinate-BV, and piecewise-C1 dictionaries
Rectifiable complex contours, reversal, concatenation, closedness, and orientation
The complex line integral over a rectifiable path as a componentwise Riemann–Stieltjes integral
The absolute line integral over a rectifiable path using its arc-length function
Continuous integrands have complex and absolute line integrals along every rectifiable path
items.strategy: Write f=u+iv and gamma=x+iy. Rectifiability makes x and y continuous BV functions, and continuity of f along the compact parameter interval makes u and v continuous. Apply the real continuous-integrand/BV-integrator theorem to all four component integrals. For the absolute integral use the continuous nondecreasing arc-length function. Include singleton and constant paths.

items.title: For piecewise-C1 contours the Riemann–Stieltjes integral agrees with the parametric complex integral and the published real line integrals
items.strategy: On each smooth piece apply the real Stieltjes C1-integrator reduction to the four component integrals. Recombine them into integral f(gamma(t))gamma'(t) dt. Identify its real and imaginary parts with the published vector line integrals of (u,-v) and (v,u), and identify the absolute integral with the published scalar line integral. Sum over pieces and allow corners and zero-speed pieces.

items.title: Complex line integrals are linear in the integrand
items.strategy: Expand the real and imaginary parts of alpha f+beta g and apply real Stieltjes linearity in each component. Recombine the four identities into complex scalar linearity, including zero scalars and singleton paths.

items.title: Complex line integrals change sign under reversal and add under concatenation
items.strategy: For reversal apply the oriented Stieltjes convention after the decreasing affine parameter change, obtaining a minus sign for d gamma while the absolute integral is unchanged. For concatenation split each component Stieltjes integral at the join and use additivity. Check constant pieces and matching endpoints.

items.title: Complex and absolute line integrals are invariant under increasing continuous reparametrization
items.strategy: Let phi be a strictly increasing continuous bijection between nondegenerate compact intervals. Apply the exact real Riemann–Stieltjes change-of-variable theorem to each component and to the arc-length integrator, then recombine. Treat singleton intervals separately and state that decreasing reparametrization changes the complex integral's sign.

items.title: The fundamental inequality |integral f dz| <= integral |f| |dz| for rectifiable contours
items.strategy: Use tagged complex Stieltjes sums for the four component integrals. The complex triangle inequality bounds each sum by the corresponding tagged arc-length sum plus a uniform-continuity error controlled by polygonal length. Pass both limits and then remove the error. This preserves the sharp constant one, unlike separately bounding four real components.

items.title: ML estimate: a contour integral is bounded by a supremum bound times path length
items.strategy: If |f|<=M on the trace, monotonicity of the real Stieltjes integral against the nondecreasing arc-length function bounds the absolute line integral by M times s_gamma(b)-s_gamma(a)=M L(gamma). Combine with the fundamental inequality and include M=0 and L=0.

items.title: The absolute line integral of the constant function 1 is the length of the path
items.strategy: By definition the integral is the Stieltjes integral of one against s_gamma, which is the endpoint increment s_gamma(b)-s_gamma(a). Apply the defining endpoint values, including singleton and constant paths.

items.title: A primitive of a complex function on an open set
The line integral of a function with a continuous primitive is the primitive's endpoint increment along every rectifiable path
items.strategy: For a primitive F with continuous derivative f, uniform differentiability on the compact trace gives F(w)-F(z)=f(z)(w-z)+r with |r|<=epsilon|w-z| for sufficiently close trace points. Sum this identity over a fine partition of the rectifiable path. The main sums converge to the line integral, the endpoint increments telescope, and the total remainder is at most epsilon L(gamma). Let epsilon tend to zero. Include constant paths and avoid assuming the path is differentiable.

items.title: The integral of a continuous complex derivative over every closed rectifiable contour is zero
items.strategy: Apply the contour fundamental theorem to f=F'. Closedness identifies the two endpoint values, so their difference is zero. State continuity of F' explicitly and include constant loops.

items.title: The contour integral of a constant c is c times the endpoint displacement
items.strategy: The entire affine function F(z)=cz is a primitive of the constant c by the published complex derivative algebra. Apply the contour fundamental theorem and simplify. Include c=0 and a constant path.

items.title: For a continuous function on a complex domain, endpoint independence, zero closed-contour integrals, and existence of a primitive are equivalent
items.strategy: A primitive gives endpoint independence by the fundamental theorem, and endpoint independence gives zero on closed contours. Conversely fix a basepoint and define F(z) by integrating along a polygonal path, available because open connected plane sets are polygonally connected. Zero closed integrals makes F well-defined. For a small h use the final straight segment from z to z+h; its difference quotient is an average of f(z+th), which tends to f(z) by continuity. This proves F'=f. Check basepoint choice and both directions separately.

items.title: A uniformly convergent sequence of continuous integrands on a fixed contour permits passage of the limit through the complex line integral
items.strategy: Assume the limit integrand is continuous and state uniform convergence on the trace by its epsilon quantifiers. Apply the ML estimate to f_n-f. Its uniform error times L(gamma) tends to zero, so the integrals converge. Treat zero-length paths without dividing by length and do not cite the separate power-series page's uniform-convergence dictionary.

items.title: On a positively oriented circle about a, the integral of (z-a)^m is zero for every integer m except -1, and is 2 pi i for m=-1
items.strategy: Parametrize the circle by gamma(t)=a+r exp(it), 0<=t<=2 pi, with r>0. The piecewise-C1 agreement formula turns the integrand into i r^(m+1) exp(i(m+1)t). If m=-1 it is the constant i; otherwise integrate its explicit exponential primitive and use exp(2 pi i(m+1))=1. Check negative powers are defined because r>0.

items.title: The normalized integral (2 pi i)^(-1) integral dz/(z-a) around a positively oriented circle centred at a is 1
items.strategy: Specialize the circle monomial theorem to m=-1 and divide the nonzero complex number 2 pi i. The value is independent of the positive radius; no global winding-number theory or Cauchy theorem is invoked.

items.title: FALSE: every continuous complex-valued function on a domain has a primitive
items.strategy: On the punctured plane take f(z)=1/z, which is continuous. The punctured plane is a domain. If f had a primitive, its integral around every circle centred at zero would vanish, but the directly computed circle integral is 2 pi i. State the corrected zero-closed-contour criterion.

pages.title: Contour Integration — Examples

items.title: An exponential contour integral approximated by Riemann sums and evaluated by parametrization and a primitive
items.strategy: On the segment from 0 to 2+i pi/4, display a finite midpoint Riemann sum, then pass to the affine-parametric complex integral. Evaluate it both componentwise and from the primitive exp(z), obtaining exp(2+i pi/4)-1. This compares the Riemann-sum, parametric, and primitive methods without using the power-series page.

items.title: Integrating a complex polynomial along a segment and a parabola by a primitive and by parametrization
items.strategy: Begin with Howell–Mathews's componentwise warm-up integral of (t-i)^3 on a real interval. Then integrate f(z)=z from the same initial to terminal point along both their straight segment and their parabolic path. Compute parametrically and from the primitive z^2/2, verify that the endpoint values agree, and keep both orientations visible.

items.title: The integral of complex conjugation from -1 to 1 differs along a semicircle and a polygonal path
items.strategy: Parametrize Howell–Mathews's upper semicircle and their polygonal path from -1 to 1, compute the integral of conjugate(z) dz on each, and obtain the unequal values -pi i and -4i. This exhibits a continuous integrand without a primitive and checks concatenation signs directly.

items.title: ML bounds for rational integrands on a semicircular arc and a line segment
items.strategy: First choose a semicircle staying a positive distance from a pole, bound the denominator by the reverse triangle inequality, use length pi r, and apply ML. Then reproduce Howell–Mathews's segment from 2 to 2+i for 1/(z^2+1): the distances to i and -i give the stated product bound and the segment has length one.

items.title: Direct computation of the integral of 1/(z-a) around a semicircle and a full circle centred at a
items.strategy: Use gamma(t)=a+r exp(it) and cancel gamma'(t) against gamma(t)-a to obtain the constant i. First integrate from zero to pi to recover the upper-semicircle value i pi, then from zero to 2 pi for the full-circle value 2 pi i, and reverse the orientation to check the sign.

items.title: The unit-circle integral of exp(z)/z is 2 pi i by uniform termwise integration
items.strategy: On |z|=1 the exponential partial sums converge uniformly because the tail is bounded by the convergent numerical series sum 1/n!. Divide the finite sums by z, use finite linearity, and apply the integer-monomial circle formula: the n=0 term contributes 2 pi i and every n>=1 term contributes zero. The uniform-limit interchange theorem passes to exp(z)/z. The unit circle excludes z=0, so division is defined.

items.title: Assembling a keyhole contour from two radial segments and two circular arcs
items.strategy: Specify the four oriented pieces with matching endpoints, compute their lengths, and write the total integral as the signed sum supplied by concatenation. Do not evaluate it by Cauchy's theorem or introduce a logarithm branch; the point is rigorous contour bookkeeping.

items.title: The rectifiable Riemann–Stieltjes definition on an explicit polygonal contour with corners
items.strategy: Use Howell–Mathews's three-segment polygonal path, with its corner parametrization, and an affine integrand. Evaluate the four real Stieltjes components edge by edge, then verify agreement with the piecewise-C1 parametric formula. The corner derivatives need not agree.

items.title: Reversing orientation does not preserve a complex contour integral
items.strategy: Integrate the constant 1 along the segment from 0 to 1 and along its reversal. The values are 1 and -1 by the endpoint formula, while the absolute integrals agree. This separates oriented and unoriented integrals.

items.title: FALSE: the modulus of a contour integral always equals the absolute line integral
items.strategy: For f=1 on a positively oriented circle, the complex integral is zero by the endpoint formula, whereas the absolute line integral is the positive circumference. State the correct fundamental inequality and its equality need not hold.

items.title: FALSE: contour length depends only on the trace and ignores multiplicity
items.strategy: Compare one traversal of a circle with two traversals. They have the same trace but the second path has twice the speed integral and twice the length. Use an explicit parametrization and retain the positive radius hypothesis.

items.title: FALSE: parametrization independence makes orientation reversal leave every contour integral unchanged
items.strategy: Use the segment integral of the constant 1. The orientation-preserving theorem applies only to increasing reparametrizations; reversal is decreasing and changes the sign from 1 to -1. Quote the hypotheses without widening them.
