items.title: The covariant and contravariant hom-assignments and the hom-bifunctor of a locally small category
The assignments $\mathcal C(a,-)$ and $\mathcal C(-,a)$ are functors to $\mathbf{Set}$
items.strategy: For a morphism $u:b\to c$, define the covariant action by postcomposition $f\mapsto u\circ f$ and the contravariant action by precomposition $g\mapsto g\circ u$. Associativity gives preservation of composition, and the identity laws give preservation of identities.

items.title: The hom-assignment $\mathcal C(-,-):\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\times\mathcal C\to\mathbf{Set}$ is a bifunctor
items.strategy: Send $(h:a'\to a,u:b\to b')$ to $f\mapsto u\circ f\circ h$. Check identity and composition componentwise; associativity also shows that precomposition and postcomposition commute, so the two one-variable hom-functors assemble into one bifunctor.

items.title: Generalized elements and their shapes
Presheaves, covariantly and contravariantly representable functors, and representations
Initial and terminal objects are exactly the representations of the constant singleton functor
items.strategy: For the covariant case, a representation $\mathcal C(I,-)\cong 1$ says that every hom-set out of $I$ is a singleton, exactly the initial-object condition. Apply the same argument to $\mathcal C(-,T)\cong1$ for terminal objects, including the empty-category obstruction.

items.title: Initial and terminal objects are unique up to a unique isomorphism
items.strategy: Between two initial objects there is one morphism in each direction. Each composite is an endomorphism of an initial object and hence must be its unique endomorphism, the identity; uniqueness of the isomorphism follows from uniqueness of the forward morphism. Dualize for terminal objects.

items.title: Evaluation at the identity gives $\operatorname{Nat}(\mathcal C(a,-),F)\cong F(a)$ and proves that the natural-transformation collection is a set
items.strategy: Define evaluation by $\alpha\mapsto\alpha_a(1_a)$. For $x\in F(a)$ construct $\alpha^x_c(f)=F(f)(x)$, check naturality, and prove the two constructions inverse using the naturality square for $f:a\to c$. Only after this explicit bijection is constructed identify the natural-transformation collection with a set; no choice is used.

items.title: The Yoneda bijection $\operatorname{Nat}(\mathcal C(a,-),F)\cong F(a)$ is natural in both $a$ and $F$
items.strategy: Use the explicit evaluation bijection. For $h:a\to a'$, verify that precomposition with $\mathcal C(h,-):\mathcal C(a',-)\Rightarrow\mathcal C(a,-)$ corresponds to $F(h)$; for $\eta:F\Rightarrow G$, verify that postcomposition by $\eta$ corresponds to $\eta_a$. These two equations establish the two naturality squares without assuming a functor category for a large source.

items.title: For a presheaf $P$, $\operatorname{Nat}(\mathcal C(-,a),P)\cong P(a)$ naturally in $a$ and $P$
items.strategy: Apply the covariant Yoneda lemma to $\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}$. Translate its covariant hom-functor, object morphisms, and naturality equations back to the stated presheaf variance.

items.title: Local smallness does not make every natural-transformation collection a set, but the Yoneda construction proves sethood in the representable-source case
The Yoneda assignment and the small-source Yoneda functor, traditionally called the Yoneda embedding
The Yoneda functor is fully faithful, and it is a full embedding when its object map is injective
items.strategy: Specialize contravariant Yoneda to $P=\mathcal C(-,b)$ to obtain $\operatorname{Nat}(\mathcal C(-,a),\mathcal C(-,b))\cong\mathcal C(a,b)$. Check that the inverse sends $f:a\to b$ to postcomposition by $f$, exactly the morphism action of $y$; the bijection gives fullness and faithfulness with no global smallness needed for the hom-set claim. Under the library's stronger terminology, add the conditional object-injectivity clause before calling this a full embedding.

items.title: Objects $a$ and $b$ are isomorphic exactly when $\mathcal C(-,a)$ and $\mathcal C(-,b)$ are naturally isomorphic
items.strategy: An isomorphism $a\to b$ is sent by Yoneda to a natural isomorphism. Conversely, full faithfulness lifts a natural isomorphism and its inverse to morphisms $a\to b$ and $b\to a$; faithfulness turns the two inverse equations into the corresponding equations in $\mathcal C$.

items.title: Universal elements of covariant functors and presheaves
A representation is equivalently a universal element with a unique factorisation property
items.strategy: For covariant $F$, send a representation $\theta:\mathcal C(R,-)\cong F$ to $u=\theta_R(1_R)$ and use Yoneda's inverse formula to show $\theta_c(f)=F(f)(u)$. Conversely the stipulated unique factorization makes each such map bijective, and functoriality makes the family natural. Apply the dual argument to presheaves.

items.title: Representing objects are unique up to a unique isomorphism compatible with their universal elements
items.strategy: Given universal elements $(R,u)$ and $(R',u')$ for the same covariant functor, use universality to obtain the unique maps $i:R\to R'$ and $j:R'\to R$ carrying one universal element to the other. Functoriality and uniqueness force $ji=1_R$ and $ij=1_{R'}$, and also force uniqueness of the compatible isomorphism; dualize for presheaves.

items.title: The category of elements of a covariant functor or a presheaf
Universal elements are initial in a covariant category of elements and terminal in a presheaf category of elements
items.strategy: Unpack a morphism $(R,u)\to(c,x)$ in the covariant category of elements: it is exactly a morphism $f:R\to c$ satisfying $F(f)(u)=x$, so initiality is precisely the universal-factorization condition. The presheaf equation reverses the arrow and yields terminality.

items.title: Universal arrows from an object to a functor and from a functor to an object
Universal arrows to a functor are initial in comma categories, and universal arrows from a functor are terminal
items.strategy: An arrow in $(X\downarrow U)$ from $(R,\eta)$ to $(C,f)$ is a morphism $h:R\to C$ with $U(h)\eta=f$, exactly the unique factorization in a universal arrow from $X$ to $U$. Unpack $(U\downarrow X)$ dually for universal arrows from $U$ to $X$.

pages.title: Universal Properties, Representables and the Yoneda Lemma — Examples

items.title: A Cartesian product represents $X\mapsto\mathbf{Set}(X,A)\times\mathbf{Set}(X,B)$
items.strategy: Use $A\times B$ with its projections. Send $f:X\to A\times B$ to its two coordinate maps, send a pair $(g,h)$ to $x\mapsto(g(x),h(x))$, and check that these operations are inverse and natural in $X$.

items.title: A tagged disjoint union represents $X\mapsto\mathbf{Set}(A,X)\times\mathbf{Set}(B,X)$
items.strategy: Construct $A\sqcup B=(A\times\{0\})\cup(B\times\{1\})$. Restriction along the two injections sends a map out of the union to a pair of maps; define the inverse piecewise on the two tags and verify uniqueness and naturality.

items.title: The function set $B^A$ represents $X\mapsto\mathbf{Set}(X\times A,B)$
items.strategy: Curry a map $f:X\times A\to B$ to $x\mapsto(a\mapsto f(x,a))$ and uncurry a map $X\to B^A$ by evaluation. The two formulas are inverse and commute with precomposition in $X$.

items.title: The free word monoid on $X$ represents $M\mapsto\mathbf{Set}(X,U(M))$
items.strategy: Form the monoid $X^*$ of finite words under concatenation and the one-letter map $j:X\to X^*$. Extend $f:X\to U(M)$ to the product of the letters in a word, prove this is the unique unital monoid homomorphism extending $f$, and check naturality in $M$. Also verify that monoids and unital homomorphisms form a locally small category and that $U$ is a functor.

items.title: The free group on $X$ represents $G\mapsto\mathbf{Set}(X,U(G))$
items.strategy: Apply the published free-group universal property to obtain a bijection $\mathbf{Grp}(F(X),G)\cong\mathbf{Set}(X,U(G))$. Show that postcomposition by a group homomorphism agrees with postcomposition of the underlying set map, proving naturality; for a singleton $X$, identify $F(X)$ with the infinite cyclic group.

items.title: $\mathbb Z[x]$ represents the underlying-set functor on unital rings
items.strategy: For an arbitrary unital ring $R$ and $r\in R$, define evaluation by $\sum_i a_i x^i\mapsto\sum_i(a_i1_R)r^i$. Integer scalars are central, so the convolution calculation proves multiplicativity without assuming $R$ commutative. Show that every unital homomorphism $\mathbb Z[x]\to R$ is forced by the image of $x$, and verify naturality under postcomposition.

items.title: The one-point space represents the underlying-set functor on $\mathbf{Top}$
items.strategy: A map from the one-point space $1$ to $X$ is determined by its unique image point, and every such map is continuous because each preimage is either empty or all of $1$. This gives $\mathbf{Top}(1,X)\cong U(X)$, naturally under continuous maps.

items.title: A representable presheaf on a poset is the indicator of a principal down-set
items.strategy: View a poset $P$ as a category and fix $p\in P$. Compute $P(-,p)$ at $q$: it is a singleton when $q\le p$ and empty otherwise. The unique possible restriction maps display the presheaf completely and identify its nonempty support with the principal down-set of $p$.

items.title: The functor $D(X)=X\sqcup X$ on $\mathbf{Set}$ is not covariantly representable
items.strategy: Define $D$ on a function by applying it separately to the two tags. If $D\cong\mathbf{Set}(R,-)$, evaluation at a singleton would give a bijection from the two-element set $D(1)$ to the singleton $\mathbf{Set}(R,1)$, an immediate contradiction for every set $R$.

items.title: Two singleton sets give canonically isomorphic representations of the identity functor on $\mathbf{Set}$
items.strategy: Represent the identity functor by $\{0\}$ and by $\{1\}$ through evaluation at the unique point. The unique bijection $\{0\}\to\{1\}$ is the unique isomorphism carrying one universal point to the other, illustrating compatibility rather than merely an arbitrary isomorphism.

items.title: The Yoneda embedding of the walking-arrow category computed objectwise
items.strategy: For the category $0\xrightarrow{u}1$, tabulate $y(0)$ and $y(1)$ on both objects and on $u^{\mathrm{op}}$, then compute $y(u):y(0)\Rightarrow y(1)$. The resulting natural-transformation sets reproduce the three hom-sets and their composition.

items.title: For a monoid action, Yoneda says that an equivariant map from the regular action is determined by the identity element
items.strategy: View a monoid $M$ as its one-object category and a functor $BM\to\mathbf{Set}$ as a left $M$-set $X$. Identify $BM(*,-)$ with the left regular action on $M$; evaluation at the identity sends an equivariant map $M\to X$ to a point of $X$, with inverse $x\mapsto(m\mapsto m\cdot x)$.

items.title: The Yoneda lemma requires its category to be small
items.strategy: Refute the claim by the proved theorem: its construction uses only that each $\mathcal C(a,c)$ is a set. The large locally small category $\mathbf{Set}$ supplies a concrete category outside the small case, while the same evaluation-and-inverse formulas still apply.

items.title: Non-isomorphic objects can have naturally isomorphic representable presheaves
items.strategy: A natural isomorphism $\mathcal C(-,a)\cong\mathcal C(-,b)$ lifts by full faithfulness to mutually inverse morphisms $a\to b$ and $b\to a$. This contradicts non-isomorphism and directly refutes the claim.

pages.title: Limits and Colimits

items.title: Constant diagrams, cones, cocones, and their morphisms
Limits and colimits as terminal cones and initial cocones, with existence and uniqueness in their universal properties
Any two limits, or any two colimits, of one diagram are uniquely isomorphic compatibly with their structure maps
items.strategy: Regard limits as terminal objects of the cone category. The two terminal universal properties give comparison arrows in opposite directions; uniqueness forces both composites to be identities and also forces the comparison to commute with every leg. Repeat in the cocone category for colimits, including both the existence and uniqueness clauses rather than asserting uniqueness up to isomorphism abstractly.

items.title: A limiting cone for a diagram is exactly a colimiting cocone for the formally dual diagram in the opposite category
items.strategy: Write the dual diagram and reverse every arrow in the cone equations. Verify that cones and their morphisms become cocones and their morphisms with composition reversed, so terminality becomes initiality. State the licensing rule explicitly: a proof by duality is available only after the hypotheses and conclusion have been translated into this exact formal dual.

items.title: Limits of empty diagrams are terminal objects, and colimits of empty diagrams are initial objects
items.strategy: For the unique diagram from the empty category, show that a cone with apex X contains no legs and that a cone morphism is just a morphism between apices because all compatibility equations are vacuous. Terminality of the cone is therefore precisely terminality of X; apply the exact formal dual for the colimit assertion.

items.title: Products and coproducts as limits and colimits of discrete diagrams, including their existence-and-uniqueness equations
Equalizers and coequalizers as limits and colimits of a parallel pair
Pullbacks and pushouts as limits and colimits of cospans and spans
Kernels and cokernels in a category with zero morphisms as equalizers and coequalizers
The legs of a limiting cone are jointly monic, and the legs of a colimiting cocone are jointly epic
items.strategy: If two arrows into the limit have equal composites with every leg, each is a cone morphism from the same cone to the limiting cone. Uniqueness in the limit universal property makes the arrows equal. Obtain the colimit clause by translating the proof through the established formal duality proposition.

items.title: Every equalizer is a monomorphism, and every coequalizer is an epimorphism
items.strategy: An equalizer cone has one structure arrow, so joint monicity of its legs is ordinary monicity of that arrow. Apply the dual clause to the one-legged coequalizer cocone.

items.title: A pullback of a monomorphism is a monomorphism, and a pushout of an epimorphism is an epimorphism
items.strategy: In a named pullback square, suppose two arrows become equal after the projection opposite the given monomorphism. Compose the pullback equation with both arrows and cancel through the given monomorphism to obtain equality after the other projection; joint monicity of the pullback legs then gives equality. Reverse the named square and all arrows for the pushout clause.

items.title: Pullback and pushout pasting: two adjacent squares give the outer universal square exactly when the remaining square is universal
items.strategy: Name a composable rectangle with left and right squares. First assume both small squares are pullbacks: factor a test cone through the right square and then through the left, and run uniqueness in the reverse order. Next assume the left square and the outer rectangle are pullbacks: for a test cone over the right cospan, use the outer property to obtain an arrow and use the left property plus its uniqueness to prove that its composite has the required right component; outer uniqueness then proves uniqueness. State the symmetric version with right square fixed, and obtain the pushout assertions only by exact formal duality.

items.title: Assuming Choice, cardinality of a small category and κ-small diagrams
Finite, small, and large limits and colimits; complete and cocomplete categories
A cone over an identity diagram is weakly initial, and the identity diagram has a limit exactly when the category has an initial object
items.strategy: A cone λ:ΔL⇒id_C supplies a leg L→C for every object, so L is weakly initial. If λ is limiting, its component λ_L factors the cone through itself; uniqueness forces λ_L=1_L, and then the cone equations show that every f:L→C equals λ_C, making L initial. Conversely, the unique arrows from an initial object I form a cone over id_C; for any other cone, its component at I gives the unique factorization, with all triangles forced by the cone equations. This is a genuinely large-diagram statement and is not a consequence of ordinary completeness.

items.title: Set has all small limits, realized as compatible tuples in a set-indexed product
items.strategy: For a small diagram D:J→Set, form the product over the set of objects of J and cut it down to tuples satisfying D(u)(x_j)=x_k for every arrow u:j→k. Coordinate projections form a cone. Given any cone, its legs assemble its unique tuple-valued map, and the cone equations put every value in the compatible subset; equality of maps follows coordinatewise. Treat the empty object set explicitly, where the product is a singleton and compatibility is vacuous.

items.title: Set has all small colimits, realized as a quotient of a set-indexed disjoint union
items.strategy: For a small diagram D:J→Set, take tagged pairs (j,x) and the equivalence relation generated by (j,x)∼(k,D(u)(x)) for every arrow u:j→k. The quotient maps form a cocone. A cocone defines a function on tagged pairs constant on the generating relation, hence on its equivalence closure, so the quotient universal property gives the unique induced function. Check the empty diagram separately: the tagged union and its quotient are empty, the initial set.

items.title: Every small limit can be constructed as an equalizer between products over the objects and arrows of the index category
items.strategy: For D:J→C with J small, form P=∏_j D(j) and Q=∏_{u:j→k}D(k). Define s,t:P→Q by the u-coordinate s_u=D(u)p_j and t_u=p_k. An equalizer e:L→P supplies legs p_j e satisfying every cone equation. Conversely a cone gives a map to P whose two composites to Q agree coordinatewise, so it factors uniquely through e; equalizer uniqueness plus product uniqueness proves the limit uniqueness clause. Include the empty J case, where P is terminal and Q is terminal.

items.title: Every small colimit can be constructed as a coequalizer between coproducts over the arrows and objects of the index category
items.strategy: Apply the exact formal dual of the product–equalizer construction: use the coproduct over arrows as the source, the coproduct over objects as the target, and on the summand for u:j→k use respectively the j-injection and the composite through D(u) into the k-injection. Verify that the coequalizer cocone equations and both clauses of its universal property are precisely the dualized equations.

items.title: A category is complete exactly when it has all small products and equalizers, and cocomplete exactly when it has all small coproducts and coequalizers
items.strategy: The forward directions specialize completeness or cocompleteness to the relevant small discrete and parallel-pair shapes. The reverse directions invoke the product–equalizer and coproduct–coequalizer constructions for an arbitrary small index category. Keep both directions and the empty product or coproduct cases explicit.

items.title: Finite, nonempty finite, and connected finite (co)limit criteria in terms of products, equalizers, pullbacks, terminal objects, and their duals
items.strategy: Restrict the object-and-arrow product construction to finite index categories to prove finite limits from finite products and equalizers. Replace a finite product by terminal objects and iterated binary products, and prove the pullback formulations using equalizers as pullbacks along a diagonal and binary products as pullbacks over a terminal object. For nonempty and connected finite shapes, identify exactly which empty or disconnected product data disappear. Prove the reverse implications by specializing to the named shapes, then formally dualize every clause for finite colimits.

items.title: Preservation, reflection, and creation of limits and colimits; continuous and cocontinuous functors
A functor preserves a chosen limit exactly when its canonical comparison to the chosen target limit is an isomorphism, and dually for colimits
items.strategy: Given a limiting cone λ for D and a chosen limiting cone μ for FD, use μ's universal property to obtain the unique comparison c with μ_j c=Fλ_j. If Fλ is limiting, its universal property constructs an inverse to c and uniqueness proves both composite identities. Conversely an isomorphism c transports the existence and uniqueness clauses from μ to Fλ. Reverse the arrows for the colimit comparison.

items.title: Fully faithful functors reflect limits and colimits
items.strategy: Suppose F sends a cone λ to a limiting cone. For any cone in the source, fullness lifts the unique mediating arrow supplied in the target; faithfulness turns the target leg equations into the required source equations and also turns equality of their images into uniqueness. Apply the same argument in opposite categories for colimits.

items.title: Equivalences preserve, reflect, and create limits and colimits in the isomorphism-invariant sense
items.strategy: Choose a quasi-inverse and the unit and counit natural isomorphisms. Transport cones and their mediating arrows through the two functors, using full faithfulness for reflection and essential surjectivity plus the counit to lift a limiting apex and its legs. Verify the lifted universal property and uniqueness, and explain why this proves ordinary isomorphism-invariant creation but not strict on-the-nose creation. Dualize for colimits.

items.title: A functor that creates limits of a given shape lifts their existence and preserves the created limits, and dually for colimits
items.strategy: Start with a diagram whose image has a limit. Apply the existence clause in the definition of creation to lift an isomorphic limiting cone; the defining uniqueness of the lift makes it a source cone, and reflection built into creation proves it is limiting. Its image is the chosen target limit up to the specified isomorphism, so the comparison criterion proves preservation. Repeat with all arrows reversed.

items.title: Chosen limits and colimits of a fixed small shape assemble into limit and colimit functors
items.strategy: Let J be small and choose a limiting cone for every J-diagram in C. For a natural transformation α:D⇒E, compose the chosen legs of D with the components of α; naturality makes a cone over E, whose chosen limit supplies a unique induced arrow. Use equality after every chosen leg to prove preservation of identities and composition. This defines lim_J:[J,C]→C; apply the exact formal dual for colim_J.

items.title: A limit for each diagram need not provide a chosen limit functor without a simultaneous choice of representatives
Every covariantly representable functor to Set preserves all existing small limits
items.strategy: First take Hom_C(X,−). For a limiting cone L→D, send f:X→L to the compatible tuple of composites with the limit legs. The limit universal property supplies an inverse from every compatible tuple, and both inverse equations follow from existence and uniqueness. A natural isomorphism from a representable functor transports this preservation result to every covariantly representable functor. State the required smallness of the index so the Set-valued limit is a set.

items.title: Hom(X,−) is continuous, while Hom(−,X) sends every existing small colimit to a limit of sets
items.strategy: Apply representable preservation directly to Hom(X,−). For Hom(−,X), view a colimit in C as a limit in C^op and apply the same theorem there; unpacking the opposite diagram gives the natural bijection between maps out of the colimit and compatible families of maps from its objects. Record both existence and uniqueness in this bijection.

items.title: For small source and index categories, chosen target limits and colimits compute the corresponding functor-category limits and colimits pointwise
items.strategy: Let A and J be small and D:J→[A,C], with a chosen J-shaped limit of D(−)(a) for each a. For each arrow h:a→b, the natural-transformation components form a cone at b after postcomposition; the limit at b supplies a unique map between the pointwise apices. Prove functoriality by equality after all limit legs, then prove the legs are natural and verify the functor-category universal property componentwise, including uniqueness of the mediating natural transformation. Dualize the full construction for colimits.

items.title: If A is small, then [A,C] is complete or cocomplete whenever C is respectively complete or cocomplete
items.strategy: For an arbitrary small index J, completeness or cocompleteness of C supplies every required pointwise J-shaped limit or colimit. Choice selects one for every object of the small source A; invoke the pointwise theorem and retain its small-source hypotheses, so no functor category with a large source is formed.

items.title: For a small category, the Yoneda functor preserves and reflects all existing small limits
items.strategy: Each evaluation component of the Yoneda image is Hom(c,−), so representable preservation and pointwise computation prove preservation. The published full faithfulness of Yoneda and the reflection proposition prove reflection. Keep the source category small so the presheaf category and Yoneda functor exist under the library's set-based convention.

items.title: Iterated small limits commute: either order is canonically isomorphic to the limit over the product category
items.strategy: For small J,K and D:J×K→C, identify a cone over D with a J-indexed cone of K-indexed cones. Applying the two universal properties successively gives the same bijection from an arbitrary apex to compatible families indexed by pairs (j,k), hence both iterated limits and the product-indexed limit represent the same cone functor. Use unique compatible isomorphisms to obtain the canonical comparison and its inverse, including the cases where either index category is empty.

items.title: Filtered categories and filtered colimits, including nonemptiness and eventual equality
Two representatives in a filtered colimit of sets are equal exactly when they become equal at one common later stage
items.strategy: For a small filtered diagram D, define a relation on tagged elements by (j,x)≈(k,y) when some object l receives arrows j→l and k→l whose images of x and y agree. Reflexivity is immediate, symmetry reverses the witnesses, and transitivity uses filteredness to compare the two intermediate stages and then to coequalize the resulting parallel arrows. This equivalence relation contains exactly the generating identifications in the Set-colimit quotient, proving both directions of the criterion.

items.title: Filtered colimits commute with finite limits in Set
items.strategy: Use the explicit quotient construction of a filtered colimit. Surjectivity of the comparison map is proved by choosing representatives for finitely many coordinates and using filteredness repeatedly to move them to one common stage; the finite cone equations then become true at one later stage by eventual equality. For injectivity, representatives that agree coordinatewise become equal after finitely many further stages, again combined into one stage by filteredness. Include the empty finite limit: both sides are singleton because filtered categories are nonempty.

items.title: Final and initial functors via nonempty connected comma categories
Assuming Choice, precomposition with a final functor does not change colimits, and precomposition with an initial functor does not change limits
items.strategy: For a final u:A→B between small categories and F:B→C, restriction sends every cocone over F to one over Fu. Given a cocone over Fu, choose an object (a,b→u(a)) of each nonempty comma category, use its arrow to define the b-component, and use connectedness to prove independence of the choice; comma morphisms and cocone equations prove natural compatibility. These constructions are inverse, so the two cocone functors are naturally isomorphic and representability gives existence in either case and the canonical colimit isomorphism. Apply the exact formal dual to initial functors and limits.

items.title: Grp is complete and cocomplete
items.strategy: Products are Cartesian products with componentwise multiplication, and equalizers are the subgroups on which a parallel pair agrees, so the completeness criterion applies. For coproducts, construct the free group on the tagged disjoint union of underlying sets and quotient by the normal closure of the relations imposing each factor's multiplication and identity; verify the resulting injections have the coproduct universal property. Coequalize f,g by quotienting the codomain by the normal closure of all f(x)g(x)^{-1}. The cocompleteness criterion then gives every small colimit.

items.title: Top is complete and cocomplete, and its underlying-set functor preserves all small limits and colimits
items.strategy: For a small diagram, take its Set-limit and give it the initial topology induced by all limit projections; the characteristic property of initial topologies proves that the set-theoretic mediating map is continuous exactly when its composites are, establishing the limit universal property. Dually, give the Set-colimit the final topology induced by all cocone maps and verify the colimit property. The underlying sets and functions are unchanged by these topology constructions, so the comparison maps for the underlying-set functor are identities and it preserves both.

items.title: For every ring R, the category R-Mod is complete and cocomplete
items.strategy: Products use componentwise addition and scalar multiplication, while equalizers are submodules, so the completeness criterion applies. Construct a coproduct as the module of finitely supported functions on the tagged disjoint union of the underlying modules, quotiented by the submodule generated by the relations enforcing addition and scalar multiplication in each summand; its coordinate inclusions satisfy the coproduct universal property. Coequalize f,g:M→N by N modulo the submodule generated by f(m)−g(m). Verify both existence and uniqueness of induced homomorphisms, then apply the cocompleteness criterion.

items.title: A poset category is complete exactly when every small family has an infimum, and cocomplete exactly when every small family has a supremum
items.strategy: Translate cones and cocones in a poset category into lower and upper bounds. Because parallel arrows are unique, the equalizer and coequalizer conditions are automatic, while products and coproducts are precisely infima and suprema, including the empty family as the top and bottom elements. Apply the completeness and cocompleteness criteria in both directions; when both conditions hold this is exactly a complete lattice.

items.title: Assuming Choice, a small category with products or coproducts indexed by the cardinality of its morphism set is a preorder
items.strategy: Assume Choice, let κ be the cardinality of the morphism set, and suppose distinct parallel arrows f,g:A→B exist. Form the κ-indexed product of B. Every subset S of κ determines a morphism A→B^κ whose coordinate is f on S and g off S; distinct subsets give distinct morphisms by projection, yielding an injection P(κ)→Mor(C). Cantor gives |P(κ)|>κ, contradicting the definition of κ. Apply formal duality for κ-indexed coproducts.

items.title: Assuming Choice, every small complete category and every small cocomplete category is a preorder
items.strategy: For a small category C, its morphism collection has a cardinal κ. Completeness supplies the κ-indexed product of every constant κ-family, and cocompleteness supplies the corresponding coproduct. Apply the cardinality-sized product or coproduct theorem in the respective case.

pages.title: Limits and Colimits: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: Products in Set are Cartesian products and coproducts are tagged disjoint unions
items.strategy: For products, map a function into the Cartesian product to its coordinate functions and recover it uniquely from those coordinates, including the empty family. For coproducts, use tagged pairs, define a map by cases on the tag, and prove uniqueness on every summand.

items.title: Equalizers in Set are agreement subsets and coequalizers are quotients by the generated equivalence relation
items.strategy: For f,g:X→Y, verify that the inclusion of {x:f(x)=g(x)} has the equalizer existence and uniqueness property. For the coequalizer, quotient Y by the least equivalence relation containing every pair (f(x),g(x)); prove a map descends exactly when it equalizes f and g, then invoke quotient uniqueness.

items.title: Pullbacks in Set are fibre products and pushouts are quotients of tagged disjoint unions
items.strategy: For X→Z←Y, use the subset of X×Y on which the two structure maps agree and prove the unique pairing map. For X←Z→Y, quotient the tagged union X⊔Y by the equivalence relation generated by identifying the two images of every z; the quotient universal property proves both clauses of the pushout universal property.

items.title: A pullback in Top is the fibre product with the subspace topology inherited from the product
items.strategy: Take the Set-theoretic fibre product inside X×Y with the product topology and then its subspace topology. The projections are continuous. A pair of continuous maps with equal composites has the unique set-theoretic pairing, whose map to the product is continuous and whose range lies in the fibre product; the subspace characteristic property proves continuity of the factor.

items.title: The equalizer of two group homomorphisms is their agreement subgroup
items.strategy: For f,g:G→H, show E={x∈G:f(x)=g(x)} contains the identity and is closed under products and inverses. The inclusion equalizes f and g. Any homomorphism whose composites agree has image in E and therefore factors uniquely through the inclusion as a homomorphism.

items.title: The colimit of an increasing chain of sets is its union
items.strategy: For inclusions X_0⊆X_1⊆⋯, use the ordinary union with the inclusion maps. Compatible maps out of the chain agree whenever an element appears at two stages, so define the induced map on the union by any containing stage and prove this is well-defined and unique. Relate it to the tagged-union quotient without assuming the stages are disjoint.

items.title: In a poset regarded as a category, products are infima, coproducts are suprema, and equalizers are automatic
items.strategy: Translate a cone over a discrete family into a lower bound and its unique factorization into the greatest-lower-bound inequalities; uniqueness is automatic because a poset category has at most one arrow. Reverse the order for coproducts. Parallel arrows are equal whenever they exist, so their identity arrow is an equalizer and coequalizer.

items.title: The singleton set and trivial group are terminal, while the empty set and trivial group are initial
items.strategy: List the unique functions X→{∗} and ∅→X, then the unique homomorphisms G→1 and 1→G, and check the group homomorphism laws. Invoke the empty-diagram proposition to identify the corresponding limits and colimits, noting that the trivial group is both initial and terminal whereas Set's two objects differ.

items.title: Assuming Choice, nonempty sets have all small products but a parallel pair with no equalizer and hence a diagram with no limit
items.strategy: Under AC, a product of nonempty sets is nonempty, so the full subcategory Set_nonempty has every small product, including the empty product. Take the two constant maps from a singleton to a two-element set with different values: their agreement subset is empty, and no nonempty set can carry an equalizing map, so the pair has no cone and no equalizer. This isolates why products alone do not construct arbitrary limits.

items.title: A monotone functor between poset categories preserves every monomorphism but need not preserve pullbacks
items.strategy: Let P have 0<a<1 and 0<b<1 with a,b incomparable, and let Q be the two-element chain. Send 0 to 0 and a,b,1 to 1. Every arrow in a poset category is monic, so monomorphisms are preserved. The pullback of a→1←b is 0 in P, but the pullback of 1→1←1 is 1 in Q, so the canonical comparison 0→1 is not an isomorphism.

items.title: A limit in a full subcategory need not be the ambient limit
items.strategy: Use the poset P with 0<q<m<a and 0<q<m<b, where a and b are incomparable, and its full subposet Q={0,q,a,b}. The product of a and b is m in P but q in Q. Fullness preserves all hom-sets between retained objects yet does not supply the omitted ambient limiting object, so the inclusion does not preserve this product.

items.title: Filtered colimits in Set need not commute with countably infinite products
items.strategy: For i≥1 let M_{i,j}={1,…,i} for every positive integer j, with inclusions as i grows. The product at stage i consists of sequences uniformly bounded by i, so its filtered colimit contains exactly bounded positive-integer sequences. Taking filtered colimits first gives the positive integers in every coordinate, whose countable product also contains unbounded sequences. The canonical comparison is therefore not surjective.

items.title: FALSE: every category has all small limits
items.strategy: The category of nonempty sets and all functions has no equalizer for two distinct constant maps from a singleton to a two-element set, because no nonempty set supports even an equalizing cone. Since the parallel-pair index is finite and therefore small, this is a small diagram without a limit.

items.title: FALSE: a functor preserving binary products and equalizers must preserve all finite limits
items.strategy: Take the constant functor from the terminal category to Set at the empty set. It preserves every binary product and every equalizer because the relevant source and target cones are all carried to identities on the empty set. It does not preserve the terminal object: the unique source object is terminal, while the empty set is not terminal in Set. This isolates the missing nullary-product hypothesis in the finite-limit criterion.

items.title: FALSE: the underlying-set functor Top→Set fails to preserve some small limit
items.strategy: Use the explicit construction of Top-limits: the underlying set is exactly the Set-limit and only the initial topology is added. Thus every canonical comparison is the identity bijection, so the claimed counterexample cannot exist. Contrast this with reflection: a set-theoretic limiting cone need not carry the topology required to be limiting in Top.

items.title: FALSE: colimits in Grp are computed by taking the Set-colimit of the underlying diagram
items.strategy: Use the empty diagram. Its colimit in Grp is the initial trivial group, whose underlying set is a singleton, whereas its colimit in Set is the empty set. Therefore the underlying-set functor Grp→Set does not preserve even this small colimit, so underlying Set-colimits cannot compute all group colimits.

items.title: Under the definable-class diagram convention, the empty set is the product of the large family of all sets
items.strategy: Any cone over the discrete class diagram of all sets includes a function from its apex to the empty-set factor, so its apex must be empty. There is exactly one cone with empty apex, consisting of the empty functions to every set, and every cone therefore factors through it uniquely. This shows that some large diagrams have limits even though completeness asserts only small limits.

items.title: Adjunction by unit, counit, and the triangle identities
The unit-counit definition imposes no local-smallness hypothesis
An adjoint equivalence is an adjunction whose unit and counit are natural isomorphisms
items.strategy: Compare the two definitions component by component. An adjoint equivalence already supplies functors, an invertible unit, an invertible counit, and the same two triangle identities, so forgetting invertibility gives an adjunction. Conversely, an adjunction with invertible unit and counit satisfies the published definition of adjoint equivalence. Relate this characterization to the theorem equipping every equivalence as an adjoint equivalence.

items.title: Adjuncts and transposition under an adjunction
The unit and counit transpose formulas are mutually inverse
items.strategy: For a morphism $u:Fc\to d$, expand $(u^\flat)^\sharp$ as $\varepsilon_d\circ FG(u)\circ F\eta_c$, use naturality of $\varepsilon$, and finish with the triangle identity at $c$. Dually expand $(v^\sharp)^\flat$ for $v:c\to Gd$, use naturality of $\eta$, and finish with the other triangle identity. Keep the types of every whiskered component visible.

items.title: Under local smallness, transposition gives the natural hom-set bijection, and conversely
items.strategy: Use the preceding inverse-formula lemma to obtain a bijection $\mathcal D(Fc,d)\cong\mathcal C(c,Gd)$. Verify naturality separately in $c$ and $d$ by functoriality and naturality of the unit and counit. Conversely, transpose the identity morphisms under a given natural family to define $\eta_c$ and $\varepsilon_d$; derive their naturality from the two-variable naturality squares and derive both triangle identities from the two inverse laws. Finally prove uniqueness because any unit and counit inducing the family must be those transposes of identities.

items.title: A square commutes if and only if its transposed square commutes
items.strategy: Write the naturality equation for the hom-set bijection in both variables. Applying transposition to one route around a square produces the corresponding route around the transposed square; injectivity of the bijection gives the forward implication. Apply inverse transposition for the reverse implication. State both orientations so later mate calculations can cite the typed form directly.

items.title: Unit components are initial in comma categories, and counit components are terminal
items.strategy: Regard $\eta_c:c\to GFc$ as a universal arrow from $c$ to $G$: a morphism $c\to Gd$ has the unique transpose $Fc\to d$. Invoke the published equivalence between universal arrows and initial comma objects. Apply the dual argument to the counit $FGd\to d$.

items.title: The unit-counit, hom-set, unit-universal, and counit-universal encodings of an adjunction are equivalent
items.strategy: Organize the implications without conflating their size assumptions. Unit-counit data give the hom-set correspondence when the hom-classes are sets; the correspondence recovers the unit and counit by transposing identities. The unit components are universal by transposition, and a natural family of universal unit components reconstructs the counit and triangle identities; prove the counit version dually. State the local-smallness qualification only on the hom-set encoding.

items.title: A left adjoint exists exactly when chosen initial objects are supplied in every comma category
items.strategy: If $F\dashv G$, use each unit component as the initial object of $c\downarrow G$. Conversely, take as data one initial object $(Fc,\eta_c)$ in each comma category; the explicit choice is part of the hypothesis. Use its unique arrows to define $F$ on morphisms, then verify identities, composition, and naturality by uniqueness and obtain the adjunction from the universal-unit encoding. State the dual criterion for a right adjoint using terminal objects in $G\downarrow d$, obtained by passing to opposite categories.

items.title: Chosen objectwise universal arrows assemble uniquely into a left adjoint
items.strategy: For a supplied family $(Fc,\eta_c)$ universal from $c$ to $G$, define $Ff$ as the unique morphism satisfying $G(Ff)\eta_c=\eta_{c'}f$. The uniqueness clause proves $F(1)=1$ and $F(gf)=F(g)F(f)$ and also proves naturality of $\eta$. Transposition along the universal arrows gives a natural hom-class correspondence and hence the unit-counit adjunction. Prove uniqueness of the functor structure from the same defining square.

items.title: A supplied pointwise right adjoint extends uniquely to a functor
items.strategy: Assume an object assignment $d\mapsto Gd$ and representations $\mathcal D(F-,d)\cong\mathcal C(-,Gd)$ natural in the source variable. For $h:d\to d'$, use Yoneda uniqueness to define the unique $Gh:Gd\to Gd'$ representing postcomposition by $h$. Identity and composition follow because their induced natural transformations agree, and the construction makes the representing isomorphisms natural in $d$. The object assignment is data, so the proof performs no proper-class selection.

items.title: Objectwise existence does not itself supply a class-sized choice of adjoint values
Adjoints are unique up to a unique natural isomorphism compatible with the adjunction data
items.strategy: Given $F\dashv G$ and $F'\dashv G$, transpose each unit component for one adjunction through the other to obtain comparison maps $F\to F'$ and $F'\to F$. Naturality follows from transposition of squares. Their composites commute with the relevant units, so universal uniqueness makes them identities. The same argument proves that the comparison is the unique natural isomorphism compatible with the units, and the counit compatibility follows by taking mates.

items.title: Adjunctions compose with the composite unit and counit formulas
items.strategy: For $F\dashv G$ and $F'\dashv G'$, define $\bar\eta=G\eta'F\circ\eta$ and $\bar\varepsilon=\varepsilon'\circ F'\varepsilon G'$. Verify that these are natural with the indicated types. Expand each composite triangle, use naturality to interchange the middle pieces, and apply the two original triangle identities in sequence. This direct recheck avoids treating composition as a slogan.

items.title: An adjunction induces postcomposition and precomposition adjunctions on legitimate functor categories
items.strategy: Whisker the unit and counit pointwise to define the postcomposition adjunction $F_*\dashv G_*$ on $[\mathcal J,\mathcal C]$ and $[\mathcal J,\mathcal D]$, and verify the triangle identities componentwise. For precomposition, use the contravariant arrangement of the same hom-set transposition on natural transformations. State the smallness conditions that ensure the displayed functor categories are locally small, while noting that the unit-counit construction itself is formal whenever those categories are legitimate.

items.title: Natural transformations have mates under a pair of adjunctions
items.strategy: For two adjunctions and functors across their source and target categories, define the right mate of a natural transformation by inserting the first unit, whiskering the transformation, and applying the second counit. Define the inverse construction symmetrically. Expand both composites and use naturality plus the triangle identities to prove the constructions inverse. Then calculate that identities and compatible horizontal and vertical pastings correspond, with order dictated by the typed pasting diagrams.

items.title: Conjugation preserves invertibility but the general mates correspondence need not
An adjunction restricts to an equivalence on the subcategories fixed by its unit and counit
items.strategy: Take the full subcategory of objects $c$ for which $\eta_c$ is invertible and the full subcategory of objects $d$ for which $\varepsilon_d$ is invertible. The triangle identities show that $F$ and $G$ carry these objects into the opposite fixed subcategory. Restrict the functors and the unit and counit; their components are natural isomorphisms, so the restrictions form an equivalence.

items.title: Fullness and faithfulness of a right adjoint are detected by its counit
items.strategy: Under the adjunction bijection, the map on hom-classes induced by $G$ corresponds by Yoneda to precomposition with the counit. Use cancellation to show injectivity of every hom map exactly when each counit component is epic, and use a preimage of the identity to show surjectivity exactly when each counit component has a left inverse. Combine the clauses for full faithfulness, and prove the unit statement by duality.

items.title: Adjoint triple $L\dashv M\dashv R$
An adjoint triple induces adjunctions between its associated endofunctors
items.strategy: Let $L\dashv U\dashv R$ with $L,R:\mathcal D\to\mathcal C$ and $U:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D$. Apply composition first to $U\dashv R$ and then $L\dashv U$ to obtain $LU\dashv RU$ on $\mathcal C$. Apply it in the other order to obtain $UL\dashv UR$ on $\mathcal D$. Write the two composite units and counits from the formulas in the composition theorem and check their types; this unit-counit proof carries no local-smallness hypothesis.

items.title: Mutually left and mutually right adjoint contravariant functors
Galois connection between preorders
A Galois connection between posets satisfies $FGF=F$ and $GFG=G$
items.strategy: Let $A$ and $B$ be posets and let $F:A\to B$ and $G:B\to A$ form a Galois connection. From $F\dashv G$ obtain $a\le GFa$ and $FGb\le b$. Apply monotonicity to derive $FGFa\le Fa\le FGFa$ and $GFGb\le Gb\le GFGb$; antisymmetry gives $FGF=F$ and $GFG=G$. For preorders the same inequalities instead give the natural isomorphisms $FGF\cong F$ and $GFG\cong G$.

items.title: In a poset adjunction the triangle identities are automatic
items.strategy: A natural transformation between monotone maps of posets is a pointwise inequality, and between any fixed source and target there is at most one morphism. Once the unit inequalities $c\le GFc$ and counit inequalities $FGd\le d$ exist, both sides of either triangle identity are parallel morphisms and therefore equal. Relate the inequalities back to the defining Galois equivalence.

items.title: Right adjoints preserve every limit that exists
items.strategy: Let $F\dashv G$ and let $(L,\lambda)$ limit a diagram $D$ in the domain of $G$. Given a cone $\mu:c\Rightarrow GD$, transpose each leg by the explicit counit formula $\varepsilon_{D_j}\circ F(\mu_j)$; naturality of the counit verifies the cone equations. Factor this cone uniquely through $L$, transpose the mediating morphism back using the unit, and use both triangle identities to prove existence and uniqueness. The proof uses no smallness or local-smallness hypothesis and applies to an arbitrary diagram for which the displayed limit exists.

items.title: Left adjoints preserve every colimit that exists
items.strategy: Pass to opposite categories, where $F\dashv G$ becomes $G^{op}\dashv F^{op}$ and a colimit becomes a limit. Apply preservation of limits by the right adjoint $F^{op}$ and translate the result back by the category-theoretic duality principle.

items.title: The direct preservation theorem carries no size hypothesis
Under local smallness, representable functors give a second proof that right adjoints preserve small limits
items.strategy: For a small diagram $D$ and object $c$, use the adjunction isomorphism to identify $\mathcal C(c,G\lim D)$ with $\mathcal D(Fc,\lim D)$. Representability carries the latter to the limit of $\mathcal D(Fc,D-)$, and adjunction identifies this with the limit of $\mathcal C(c,GD-)$. Naturality and Yoneda identify the canonical comparison $G\lim D\to\lim GD$ as an isomorphism. Keep local smallness and smallness explicit because this route is set-valued.

items.title: Left exact and right exact functors
A right adjoint is left exact and a left adjoint is right exact
items.strategy: Specialize preservation of all existing limits and colimits to finite indexing categories, then unfold the definitions of left exactness and right exactness. No existence claim is added: the conclusion concerns finite limits or colimits that exist in the relevant source category.

items.title: Right adjoints preserve monomorphisms and left adjoints preserve epimorphisms
items.strategy: Characterize a monomorphism $f:x\to y$ by the square with both top and left arrows $1_x$ and both bottom and right arrows $f$: it is a pullback exactly when $f$ is monic. Apply a right adjoint and its preservation of this existing pullback to conclude that the image of $f$ is monic. Pass to opposite categories for the dual assertion that every left adjoint preserves epimorphisms.

items.title: Chosen limits and colimits are adjoint to the diagonal functor
items.strategy: Fix a small shape $\mathcal J$. For supplied choices of all $\mathcal J$-limits, use the published assembly theorem to obtain $\lim_{\mathcal J}$. Identify morphisms $c\to\lim D$ with cones $\Delta c\Rightarrow D$, hence with morphisms $\Delta c\to D$ in the functor category, naturally in both variables; this gives $\Delta\dashv\lim_{\mathcal J}$. Apply the dual construction to supplied colimits. Do not infer the required choices from objectwise existence.

items.title: Direct image, preimage, and universal image form an adjoint triple on power sets
items.strategy: For $f:A\to B$, define $f_!(S)=f[S]$, retain $f^{-1}(T)$ for preimage, and define $f_*(S)=\{b\in B:f^{-1}[\{b\}]\subseteq S\}$. Prove $f[S]\subseteq T$ iff $S\subseteq f^{-1}[T]$, and $f^{-1}[T]\subseteq S$ iff $T\subseteq f_*(S)$, including empty fibres. Thus $f_!\dashv f^{-1}\dashv f_*$. State explicitly that this page reserves $f_!$ for direct image and $f_*$ for universal image, opposite to Riehl's star/subscript convention.

items.title: The image-preimage adjunctions explain the set-operation preservation laws
The free-group functor is left adjoint to the underlying-set functor
items.strategy: Use the published free-group universal property to assign to every function $X\to U(G)$ its unique extending homomorphism $F(X)\to G$. Define $F$ on functions by extending the composite of the generator map with the function; uniqueness proves functoriality and naturality of the unit. The universal-arrow assembly theorem then gives $F\dashv U$, and uniqueness of free groups shows independence from the chosen reduced-word model.

items.title: The free-module functor is left adjoint to the underlying-set functor
items.strategy: For a fixed unital ring $R$, use the universal property of $R^{(X)}$ to identify $R$-linear maps $R^{(X)}\to M$ with functions $X\to U(M)$. Define the action on set maps by extending the induced map on standard basis elements; uniqueness proves functoriality and naturality. Apply objectwise universal-arrow assembly and check the empty basis case is the zero module with its unique map.

items.title: Finite words satisfy the free-monoid universal property
items.strategy: Construct the word set as the indexed union $X^*=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}X^n$, with the unique function on $0$ as the empty word, and define concatenation by the two finite function pieces. Verify sethood, associativity, and the empty-word identity. Given $u:X\to M$ into a monoid, define $\widehat u$ by multiplying the images of the letters in order; induction on word length proves preservation of concatenation. Any homomorphism extending $u$ has this value on every word, proving uniqueness, including the empty word.

items.title: The free-monoid functor is left adjoint to the underlying-set functor
items.strategy: Use the finite-word universal property to define $X\mapsto X^*$ and define the image of a function letterwise. Universal uniqueness proves identity and composition laws and gives the natural hom-set bijection between monoid homomorphisms $X^*\to M$ and functions $X\to U(M)$. Conclude the adjunction by universal-arrow assembly without citing the published B-leaf representation example.

items.title: Abelianisation is left adjoint to the inclusion of abelian groups
items.strategy: For a homomorphism $f:G\to A$ with $A$ abelian, calculate that every commutator maps to the identity, so $[G,G]\subseteq\ker f$. Apply the quotient-group universal property to factor $f$ uniquely through $q_G:G\to G^{ab}$. Use the same uniqueness to define abelianisation on morphisms and prove functoriality and naturality. This local proof avoids citing the published universality theorem, whose home is outside the declared page closure.

items.title: Discrete topology, underlying set, and indiscrete topology form an adjoint triple
items.strategy: Define $D$ and $I$ on maps by the underlying functions. Every function from a discrete space is continuous, giving $D\dashv U$, and every function into an indiscrete space is continuous, giving $U\dashv I$. Verify naturality of both identity-on-functions bijections and identify the units and counits. The empty set and singleton require no exception.

items.title: Under the ultrafilter lemma and dependent choice, Stone-Cech compactification is left adjoint to the compact-Hausdorff inclusion
items.strategy: Use the published Stone-Cech universal property: every map from a Tychonoff space $X$ to a compact Hausdorff space extends uniquely across $\eta_X:X\to\beta X$. The extension uniqueness defines $\beta$ on morphisms and proves functoriality and naturality of the unit. Apply universal-arrow assembly to obtain the adjunction. Preserve exactly the ultrafilter-lemma and dependent-choice assumptions inherited by the published construction and target-embedding lemma.

items.title: The underlying-set functor on fields has no left adjoint
items.strategy: If $F\dashv U:\mathbf{Field}\to\mathbf{Set}$, then the adjunction sends the unique map from the empty set into every underlying field to a unique field homomorphism from $F(\varnothing)$ into every field, making $F(\varnothing)$ initial. But a unital field homomorphism preserves characteristic, while $\mathbb F_2$ and $\mathbb F_3$ are fields of different characteristics; no field can map to both. Therefore no such initial field, and hence no left adjoint, exists.

items.title: Coextension of scalars $\operatorname{Hom}_R(S,M)$ carries its canonical left $S$-module structure
items.strategy: For a unital homomorphism $\varphi:R\to S$ and a left $R$-module $M$, view $S$ as a left $R$-module and set $(s\cdot f)(t)=f(ts)$. Verify that $s\cdot f$ is $R$-linear and check associativity, the unit law, and distributivity pointwise. For an $R$-linear map $M\to M'$, postcomposition is $S$-linear, so the construction is functorial.

items.title: Coextension of scalars is right adjoint to restriction of scalars
items.strategy: For $\varphi:R\to S$, an $S$-linear map $\alpha:N\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(S,M)$ is sent to the $R$-linear map $n\mapsto\alpha(n)(1)$. Conversely, from $u:\operatorname{Res}N\to M$ define $\widehat u(n)(s)=u(sn)$. Check $R$-linearity in $s$, $S$-linearity in $n$, and that evaluation and currying are inverse and natural in $N$ and $M$. Thus $\operatorname{Res}\dashv\operatorname{Hom}_R(S,-)$; no tensor-product or extension-of-scalars claim is made.

items.title: Currying gives the adjunction $-\times A\dashv(-)^A$ in $\mathbf{Set}$
items.strategy: For sets $A,X,Y$, send $h:X\times A\to Y$ to $\widehat h:X\to Y^A$ with $\widehat h(x)(a)=h(x,a)$, and send $k:X\to Y^A$ to $(x,a)\mapsto k(x)(a)$. Extensionality proves the constructions inverse, and substitution proves naturality in $X$ and $Y$. The published A-page function-set construction ensures $Y^A$ is an ordinary set; no B-leaf exponential example is cited.

items.title: A unit and counit determine an adjunction without the triangle identities
items.strategy: Refute the claim in the one-object category whose endomorphism monoid is the two-element group. Take both functors to be the identity, the unit to be the identity transformation, and the counit to be the nonidentity central element. Both families are natural, but each triangle composite is the nonidentity element rather than the identity, so the data are not an adjunction.

items.title: Left adjoints preserve limits
items.strategy: Use the free-group left adjoint. The terminal set is a singleton, but in the reduced-word model its empty word and its one-letter generator are distinct, so its free group is not the terminal group. Hence this left adjoint fails to preserve even the terminal-object limit, while the valid theorem says left adjoints preserve colimits.

items.title: Every functor with a left adjoint also has a right adjoint
items.strategy: The underlying-set functor $U:\mathbf{Grp}\to\mathbf{Set}$ has the free-group functor as a left adjoint. If $U$ also had a right adjoint, then $U$ would be a left adjoint and would preserve initial objects. The initial group is trivial and its underlying set is a singleton, which is not the initial empty set, so no right adjoint to $U$ exists.

items.title: The hom-set form of an adjunction needs no size hypothesis
items.strategy: The expression $\mathcal D(Fc,d)\cong\mathcal C(c,Gd)$ as an isomorphism of sets presupposes that both hom-classes are sets. Exhibit a one-object large category whose endomorphism class is the proper class of all ordinals, with composition given by ordinal addition and identity $0$; associativity and the identity clauses make it a category, while Burali-Forti makes its single hom-class non-set-sized. Thus the hom-set expression is not Set-valued there, whereas the unit-counit definition still makes sense for legitimate functors and natural transformations between such categories.

pages.title: Adjunctions Units and Counits — Examples

items.title: The unit inserts generators as one-letter words and the counit evaluates words in the free-group adjunction
items.strategy: For a set $X$, identify the unit $X\to U F(X)$ with the one-letter-word inclusion. For a group $G$, identify the counit $F U(G)\to G$ with evaluation of a reduced word in elements of $G$. Check both triangle identities on generators, after which equality of homomorphisms follows from the free universal property; include $X=\varnothing$ and the trivial group.

items.title: The unit inserts basis vectors and the counit evaluates formal linear combinations in the free-vector-space adjunction
items.strategy: Specialize the free-module adjunction to a field $k$. The unit sends $x$ to the standard basis vector $e_x$; the counit sends a formal finite sum of vectors to its actual linear combination. Check the triangle identities first on basis vectors and then by linearity, including the empty basis and the zero vector space.

items.title: Vanishing sets and vanishing ideals form a contravariant Galois connection
items.strategy: For a field $k$, subsets $S\subseteq k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, and subsets $X\subseteq k^n$, define $V(S)$ as their common zero set and $I(X)$ as the polynomials vanishing on $X$. Prove $X\subseteq V(S)$ iff $S\subseteq I(X)$ directly from evaluation. Verify that $I(X)$ is an ideal and that both assignments reverse inclusion. Deduce the closure identities $VIV=V$ and $IVI=I$ without invoking the Nullstellensatz.

items.title: Finite directed paths form the free category on a quiver
items.strategy: For a small quiver, take vertices as objects and finite composable edge paths as morphisms, with empty paths as identities and concatenation as composition. Verify the category laws. Any quiver morphism into the underlying quiver of a category extends by composing edge images along paths; induction on path length proves uniqueness and naturality, yielding the free-category adjunction. Define the quiver interface within the example so no published examples-page item is cited.

items.title: The inclusion of groupoids into categories is left adjoint to the maximal-subgroupoid functor
items.strategy: For a small groupoid $G$ and a small category $C$, every functor $G\to C$ sends each morphism of $G$ to an isomorphism, so it factors uniquely through the maximal subgroupoid $\operatorname{Core}(C)$. Show that a functor $C\to D$ restricts to $\operatorname{Core}(C)\to\operatorname{Core}(D)$ and that the factorisation bijection $\operatorname{Cat}(G,C)\cong\operatorname{Gpd}(G,\operatorname{Core}(C))$ is natural. Hence the inclusion $\mathbf{Gpd}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{Cat}$ is left adjoint to $\operatorname{Core}$.

items.title: Frobenius reciprocity for group representations without tensor products
items.strategy: For a subgroup $H\le G$ and a field $k$, define a representation directly as a vector space with a linear group action. Model $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G(V)$ as the vector space of functions $f:G\to V$ satisfying $f(gh)=h^{-1}f(g)$ whose support meets only finitely many right cosets, with $(a\cdot f)(g)=f(a^{-1}g)$. Define $j_V(v)$ to be supported on $H$ with $j_V(v)(h)=h^{-1}v$. For an $H$-equivariant linear map $u:V\to\operatorname{Res}_H^G W$, set $\widehat u(f)=\sum_{gH\in G/H}g\cdot u(f(g))$ over the finitely many support cosets; prove independence of representatives and $G$-equivariance. The inverse sends a $G$-map $T$ to $T\circ j_V$. Decompose $f$ as $\sum_{gH}g\cdot j_V(f(g))$ to prove the inverse laws and then verify naturality. This constructs $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G\dashv\operatorname{Res}_H^G$ directly, using neither group algebras nor tensor products.

items.title: A componentwise family of morphisms need not be a natural transformation and hence need not be a unit
items.strategy: On $\mathbf{Set}$ take $F=G=1$. Let the component at the specific two-element set be its transposition and let every other component be the identity. For the inclusion of a singleton into that two-element set, the naturality square fails. Thus even correctly typed components $X\to GFX$ do not constitute a unit without naturality.

items.title: A wrong counit can be natural while both triangle identities fail
items.strategy: Use the one-object category of the two-element group and take $F=G=1$. Choose the identity unit and the nonidentity central element as counit. Naturality holds because the group is abelian, but both triangle composites equal the nonidentity element. Replacing the counit by the identity recovers the identity adjunction, isolating the triangle failure.

items.title: A floor-division and multiplication adjunction between natural-number preorders
items.strategy: Fix a positive natural number $m$. On the natural numbers with their usual order, define $F(n)=mn$ and $G(r)=\lfloor r/m\rfloor$ using Euclidean division. Prove $mn\le r$ iff $n\le\lfloor r/m\rfloor$, then read off the unit and counit inequalities and verify $FGF=F$ and $GFG=G$. The case $m=1$ is the identity adjunction; positivity excludes division by zero.

pages.title: The Erdős–Hajnal Property and Homogeneous Sets

items.title: Homogeneous vertex sets and the homogeneous number $\operatorname{hom}(G)=\max{\omega(G),\alpha(G)}$
The Erdős–Hajnal property and an Erdős–Hajnal constant for a hereditary graph class
Every smaller positive exponent is again an Erdős–Hajnal constant
items.strategy: Let $0<\delta\le\epsilon$ and let $G$ be a nonempty graph in the class, with $n=|V(G)|\ge1$. From $\log n\ge0$ and monotonicity of the exponential, deduce $n^\delta\le n^\epsilon$, then apply the defining bound. Treat $n=1$ explicitly so no zero-base real power is invoked.

items.title: Every nonempty $n$-vertex graph satisfies $\operatorname{hom}(G)\ge \tfrac12\log_2 n$
items.strategy: Put $k=\lfloor\tfrac12\log_2 n\rfloor+1$. The published Ramsey bound gives a clique or stable set of size $k$ once $n\ge\binom{2k-2}{k-1}$. Bound the middle binomial coefficient by the total number $2^{2k-2}$ of subsets of a $(2k-2)$-set, and use $2k-2\le\log_2 n$. Conclude $\operatorname{hom}(G)\ge k>\tfrac12\log_2 n$, including $n=1$.

items.title: For every $t\ge1$, the class of $K_t$-free graphs has the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: For $t=1$ the class has no nonempty member, and for $t=2$ every member is empty. Let $t\ge3$. For all sufficiently large $n$, choose $s=\lfloor\tfrac12 n^{1/(t-1)}\rfloor$ with $s\ge t-2$. Apply the published Ramsey theorem with parameters $t,s$: since $\binom{t+s-2}{t-1}\le(t+s-2)^{t-1}\le(2s)^{t-1}\le n$, every $K_t$-free $n$-vertex graph has a stable set of size at least $s$. For large $n$, $s\ge n^{1/t}$. Reduce the positive exponent if necessary so that the finite initial range is covered by the elementary bound $\operatorname{hom}(G)\ge2$ for $n\ge2$, and treat $n=1$ separately.

items.title: Every $P_3$-free graph $G$ satisfies $\operatorname{hom}(G)\ge\sqrt{|V(G)|}$
items.strategy: If two nonadjacent vertices lie in one connected component, take a shortest path between them. Its first three vertices induce $P_3$: consecutive vertices are adjacent, while an edge joining the first and third would shorten the path. Hence every component is a clique. If the component orders are $c_1,\ldots,c_r$, then $\omega(G)\ge\max_i c_i$, while one vertex from each component is a stable set and gives $\alpha(G)\ge r$. Therefore $|V(G)|=\sum_i c_i\le r\max_i c_i\le\alpha(G)\omega(G)\le\operatorname{hom}(G)^2$. Take nonnegative square roots and identify $\sqrt n=n^{1/2}$; thus the $P_3$-free class has Erdős–Hajnal constant $1/2$.

items.title: For every $n\ge16$ there is an $n$-vertex graph with $\operatorname{hom}(G)<3\log_2 n$
items.strategy: Take $G\sim G(n,1/2)$ and $k=\lceil3\log_2 n\rceil$. Let $X$ count $k$-subsets inducing either a clique or a stable set. For each subset the probability is $2\cdot2^{-\binom{k}{2}}$, so linearity gives $\mathbb E X=2\binom nk2^{-\binom{k}{2}}\le2n^k2^{-k(k-1)/2}<1$; verify the last exponent inequality from $\log_2 n\ge4$. The first-moment method gives $X=0$, and every larger homogeneous set would contain a homogeneous $k$-subset, so $\operatorname{hom}(G)\le k-1<3\log_2n$.

items.title: The hereditary class of all finite graphs does not have the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Assume an exponent $\epsilon>0$ works for every graph. The logarithm-versus-power limit makes $3\log_2n<n^\epsilon$ for all sufficiently large $n$; choose such an $n\ge16$ and contradict the random-graph upper-bound theorem. Spell out the harmless change from natural to base-two logarithm.

items.title: A hereditary class has the Erdős–Hajnal property exactly when its complementary class does, with the same constants
items.strategy: Complementation bijects the two classes and swaps cliques with stable sets, hence preserves $\operatorname{hom}$. Apply the defining inequality in each direction, using that complementation is an involution. Record the fixed-pattern consequence: $H$ and $\overline H$ have the same Erdős–Hajnal constants.

items.title: Every graph on at most three vertices has the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Up to isomorphism and complementation, a graph on at most three vertices is one of $K_1,K_2,K_3$, or $P_3$. The complete cases have the property by the $K_t$-free theorem, the path case has exponent $1/2$, and complement invariance supplies their complements. Check the null pattern separately if graphs of order zero are admitted by the final Statement.

items.title: The Erdős–Hajnal property and each of its constants pass to hereditary subclasses
items.strategy: If $\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal C$, every nonempty graph tested for $\mathcal D$ is already tested for $\mathcal C$. Restrict the same inequality and keep the exponent unchanged.

items.title: If $H$ is an induced subgraph of $H'$ and $H'$ has the Erdős–Hajnal property, then $H$ has it with every constant of $H'$
items.strategy: Composition of induced embeddings shows that every $H$-free graph is $H'$-free when $H$ embeds inducedly in $H'$. Thus the $H$-free class is a hereditary subclass of the $H'$-free class; apply subclass monotonicity. State the direction carefully, since reversing this inclusion is a common error.

items.title: The single-forbidden-graph and finite-nonempty-family formulations of the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture are equivalent
items.strategy: For the forward direction, given a finite nonempty family $\mathcal F$, choose $H\in\mathcal F$; every $\mathcal F$-free graph is $H$-free, so the single-pattern assertion and subclass monotonicity supply an exponent. For the reverse direction apply the family assertion to the singleton family ${H}$. Make clear that this is an equivalence between two universally quantified conjectures, not an equivalence for one fixed family and each of its members.

items.title: The Erdős–Hajnal conjecture: every fixed forbidden induced graph admits a positive exponent

pages.title: The Erdős–Hajnal Property and Homogeneous Sets — Examples

items.title: $K_n$ and $\overline K_n$ both have homogeneous number $n$
items.strategy: Compute $\omega$ and $\alpha$ directly in the two graphs, including $n=0$, and take their maximum.

items.title: For positive $a,b$, $\operatorname{hom}(K_{a,b})=\max{2,a,b}$
items.strategy: A clique contains at most one vertex from each side and an edge supplies a 2-clique, while a stable set lies in one side and either whole side works. Take the larger of the clique and stability numbers; keep both sides nonempty as stated.

items.title: The self-complementary five-cycle satisfies $\operatorname{hom}(C_5)=2$
items.strategy: Exhibit an edge and a nonedge, then show every three vertices in a five-cycle contain both an edge and a nonedge. Give an explicit isomorphism from $C_5$ to its complement to illustrate complement invariance.

items.title: The classes of complete graphs and of empty graphs have Erdős–Hajnal constant $1$
items.strategy: Each nonempty graph in either class has homogeneous number equal to its order, so the defining inequality holds with exponent $1$. Check heredity under induced subgraphs and use complementation to relate the two examples.

items.title: Every hereditary graph class of bounded order has the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Let $\mathcal C$ be hereditary, and suppose every graph in $\mathcal C$ has at most $N$ vertices. Choose a positive exponent $\epsilon$ with $N^\epsilon\le2$ when $N\ge2$. Every nonempty graph has a homogeneous set of size at least one, and every graph with at least two vertices has one of size at least two. Handle $N\le1$ separately.

items.title: Forbidding $P_3$ and forbidding $\overline{P_3}$ have the same Erdős–Hajnal constants
items.strategy: Identify $\overline{P_3}$ as an edge plus an isolated vertex, apply the forbidden-pattern complement dictionary, and then apply complement invariance of homogeneous number and EH constants.

items.title: The universal logarithmic Ramsey guarantee cannot be replaced by any universal positive power
items.strategy: Fix $\epsilon>0$, choose $n$ large enough that $3\log_2n<n^\epsilon$, and invoke the constructed $n$-vertex graph with homogeneous number below $3\log_2n$. This supplies a counterexample for every proposed universal exponent.

items.title: Every hereditary graph class has the Erdős–Hajnal property
items.strategy: Refute the statement with the hereditary class of all finite graphs and the published corollary showing that this class has no positive EH exponent.
